Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 1:

(p-433) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Isra' (the Night Journey)

This surah is Meccan, except for three verses: the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We revealed to you⦆ [al-Isra': 73], and His words: ﴿And indeed, they were about to drive you out of the land⦆ [al-Isra': 76]. They were revealed when the delegation of Thaqif came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and when the Jews said: "This is not the land of the prophets." And the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance⦆ [al-Isra': 80], and His words: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it⦆ [al-Isra': 107], to the end of the verse. Ibn Mas'ud said, concerning Bani Isra'il, al-Kahf and Maryam: "They are among the earliest (al-'ataq al-ula) and they are of my old (talad) possessions," meaning that they are from his earlier acquisition.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing.⦆

The wording of the verse requires that Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, took His servant by night, who is Muhammad ﷺ. The exegetes said: (p-434) its meaning is: "He traveled with His servant." It appears that "asra" is transitive by means of the hamza to an omitted object, its estimated meaning being: "The angels took His servant by night." This is because it would be objectionable to attribute "asra" (which, in the sense of "sara," gives the meaning of movement, like "mashā," "jarā," "ahdara" and "intaqala") to Allah, the Exalted and Majestic. It is not fitting to attribute any of these to Him when we find an alternative. Yet when the Law has expressed something of this kind, such as the words of the Exalted in the hadith: "I come to him walking, and I come to him running," that is understood by way of interpretation in the manner that frees it from attributing temporal events (to Him). And "asra" in this verse comes out eloquent, as we have mentioned, and does not need a strained figurative usage in such a wording, for it is more binding on the notion of movement than "ataytuhu" and "fa-ata Allahu bunyanahum" [al-Nahl: 26]. It is also possible that "asra" means "sara" by omission of a modifier, like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah took away their light⦆ [al-Baqarah: 17]. The Night Journey is reported in all the collections of hadith and was related from the Companions in every region of Islam, so it is mass-transmitted (mutawatir) in this respect. Al-Naqqash mentioned twenty Companions among those who related it. The majority of the Companions related it, and most of the scholars received from them that the Night Journey was with his person ﷺ, and that he rode al-Buraq from Mecca and reached Bayt al-Maqdis and prayed in it. Hudhayfa and others related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not dismount from al-Buraq at Bayt al-Maqdis nor enter it. Hudhayfa said: "Had he prayed in it, prayer in it would have been prescribed for you." And that he rode al-Buraq in Mecca and did not dismount from it (p-435) until he returned to his house, except in his ascent to the heaven. 'A'isha and Mu'awiya said: "The Night Journey was only of the soul of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; his person did not leave his bed, and it was only a vision in which he saw the realities from his Lord, the Exalted and Majestic." al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq permitted it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The hadith is lengthy in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, so we have abridged its text in this book. And riding al-Buraq, according to these people, would be among what was seen in sleep. Ibn al-Musayyab and Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said, in the book of al-Tabari: "al-Buraq is the mount of Ibrahim with which he used to visit the Sacred House."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They mean: he came and returned the same day, and that from his dwelling in al-Sham. The correct view is that held by the majority. Had it been a dream, Quraysh would not have been able to vilify (him), nor would Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, have been distinguished by his affirmation, nor would Umm Hani have said to him: "Do not tell the people of this, for they will call you a liar," among other proofs.

He argued for the view of 'A'isha by the words of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people⦆ [al-Isra': 60].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This admits of the other view, because the sight of the eye is also called "ru'ya" (vision). He also argued that some hadiths say: "I awoke while I was in al-Masjid al-Haram," and this admits that he was returned from the Night Journey to sleep. The view of 'A'isha was objected to on the grounds that she was a child, did not witness it, and did not narrate from the Prophet ﷺ. As for Mu'awiya, he was a disbeliever at that time, not a witness to the event, a child, and did not narrate from the Prophet ﷺ.

His words, the Exalted: "Subhana" is an indeclinable verbal noun (masdar ghayr mutamakkin), for it does not take the varieties of i'rab (grammatical case inflection), nor does the article "al-" enter upon it, and no form "fa'ala" comes from it; "sabbaha" means "qala subhana Allah," so "sabbaha" is only used as a reference to "subhana." It is not declinable because it has two added letters at its end, and it is definite by being a proper noun (ma'rifa bi-l-'alamiyya), and its being put in an annexed construction does not increase its definiteness. All of this is the view of Sibawayh regarding it. A group said: its accusative is by way of address (nida'), as if he said: "O Glory of Him who took (His servant) by night."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, and its meaning is: "as a declaration of Allah's transcendence (tanzih)." Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Fayyad, one of the Ten, related that he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "What is the meaning of 'Subhan Allah'?" He said: "It is the declaration of Allah's transcendence above every evil." According to the view of Sibawayh, the governing element (al-'amil) in it is a verb that is of its meaning, not of its wording, since it does not govern from its own wording "fa'ala"; this is like "qa'ada al-qurfusa'" and "ishtamala al-samma'," so the estimate for him is: "I declare the transcendence of Allah, a declaration (tanzihan)," and "subhana" took the place of your saying "tanzihan."

A group of the exegetes said: "asra" is an intransitive verb, which is made transitive here by the preposition, and you say: "asra al-rajul" and "sara" with the same meaning, when he traveled by night. I have mentioned what appears in the wording from the standpoint of doctrine. Hudhayfa and Ibn Mas'ud recited: "asra bi-'abdihi min al-layli min al-masjid al-haram."

His words, the Exalted: ﴿from al-Masjid al-Haram⦆. Anas ibn Malik said: he meant the mosque surrounding the Ka'ba itself, and al-Tabari preferred this, saying: it is what is known when this name is mentioned. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "While I was near the House, between sleeping and waking." 'Abd ibn Humayd al-Kashshi mentioned in his tafsir, from Sufyan al-Thawri, that he said: (p-437) the Prophet ﷺ was taken by night from the shi'b of Abu Talib. Another group said: "al-Masjid al-Haram" is all of Mecca, and they relied on the words of the Exalted: ﴿You will surely enter al-Masjid al-Haram⦆ [al-Fath: 27], and the great destination here is Mecca. Some of this group related from Umm Hani that she said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in my house on the night of the Night Journey," and some of it was related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The roof of my house opened," and this accords with the words of Umm Hani, may Allah be pleased with her.

It was, according to Muqatil, a year before the Hijra, and Qatada said the same; it was also said: a year and a half, which 'Urwa related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. It was in Rajab. It was also said: on the night of the seventeenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, when the Prophet ﷺ was fifty-one years, nine months and twenty days old. What is established is that it was after the splitting of the chest (shaqq al-sahifa). It was also said: after the Pledge of al-'Aqaba. A delusion (wahm) occurs in the two Sahihs in the case of Sharik ibn Abi Namir in this matter, for he related the hadith of the Night Journey and said in it: "And that was before revelation came to him." There is no disagreement among the scholars of hadith that this is a delusion on the part of Sharik.

"al-Masjid al-Aqsa" is the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, and it was called "al-Aqsa" in the sense that at that time it was the furthest of the excellent houses of Allah from the Ka'ba. It is possible that by "al-Aqsa" he means "the distant," without comparison between it and others, and the purpose would be to show the wonder of the Night Journey to such a distance in a single night.

(p-438) The blessing around it is from two aspects: the first is prophethood, the laws and the messengers who were in that region and its surroundings and its gatherings; the second is the bounties of trees, waters and the fertile land which Allah singled out for al-Sham. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Allah blessed what lies between al-'Arish and the Euphrates, and singled out Filastin for sanctification."

His words, the Exalted: ﴿that We might show him of Our signs⦆ mean: that We might show Muhammad, with his own eye, Our signs in the heavens, the angels, the Garden, the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and other wonders that he saw that night. It is also possible that it means: that We might show Muhammad ﷺ to the people as a sign, that is, the Prophet ﷺ would be a sign in that Allah performs this act for a human being, and in this case the seeing would be seeing of the heart.

There is no disagreement that in this Night Journey the five daily prayers were prescribed upon this Community. His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing⦆ are a warning from Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, to the disbelievers for their denial of Muhammad ﷺ regarding the matter of the Night Journey. It is thus a subtle and eloquent allusion to that, meaning: He is the Hearer of what you say, the Seer of your deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 2–4:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying]: "Do not take other than Me as a trustee."﴾ ﴿[You are] the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book: "You will surely cause corruption on earth twice, and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance."﴾

He joined His saying, "And We gave," to what is implied in His saying, ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1], by way of an implied predicate, as if He had said: "We took Our servant by night and showed him Our signs." "Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah. The pronoun in "jaalnahu" (We made it) may refer back to "al-Kitab," and it may refer back to Moses, peace be upon him.

His saying, "Alla tattakhidhu" (that you not take), may be in a place of accusative [i.e., nasb] with the implied sense of "karahiyah" (out of aversion), and it may be in a place of genitive [i.e., khafd] with the implied sense of "bi-allā tattakhidhū" (so that you do not take). It is also possible that "an" (that) is explanatory, meaning "ay" (namely), as in His saying, ﴿Go on and be steadfast﴾ [Sad: 6]. In that case it is with a command in that verse, and here, in our verse, it is with a prohibition. The meaning in these readings is: We made that so that you would not take, O offspring. It is possible that "dhurriyyata" (offspring) is an object, and it is possible that "an" is superfluous. A verb of saying is implied in the speech, its implied form being: "We said to them: Do not take." As for implying the verb of saying without making "an" superfluous, it is not sound, because what follows a verb of saying is either a sentence that is reported, or a paraphrase of speech that is not the same speech. So the verb of saying works on the paraphrase, as when you say, to someone who said "There is no god but Allah": "You have spoken the truth." His saying, "Allā tattakhidhū," is in the second-person address; this was stated by Abu 'Ali.

The majority of readers recited "Allā tattakhidhū" in the second-person address. Abu 'Amr alone recited "Allā yattakhidhū" with a "ya" (third-person masculine) in the form of the absent party. This is the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Isa, and Abu Raja'.

"Al-Wakil" (the trustee) is on the pattern "fa'il" from "tawakkul" (reliance), meaning one relied upon in affairs. Thus, by this sense, one would be taking him as a deity. Mujahid said: "wakilan" means "a partner."

The majority of readers recited "dhurriyyata" with a dammah on the dhal. 'Amir recited it with a fathah. Zayd ibn Thabit, Aban ibn 'Uthman, and also Mujahid recited it with a kasrah. All of these are with a shaddah on the ra' and the ya'. It is narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit with a fathah on the dhal, with the ra' eased and the ya' doubled, on the pattern "fa'iliyah." The word "dhurriyyah" is on the pattern "fa'ulah"; its root is "dhururah," in which the second ra' was changed to ya' and assimilated, and then the ra' was given a kasrah to harmonize with the ya'. All of these readers recited "dhurriyyata" in the accusative. That is sound, either as an object of "yattakhidhu," in which case the meaning is: that no human being should be taken as a deity besides Allah; or as a vocative, meaning "O offspring," in which case it addresses the whole world. Some people said: This is not sound except on the reading of whoever recited "Allā tattakhidhū" with a "ta" from above. It is not permissible on the reading of whoever recited with a "ya" from below, because the verb is for an absent party while the vocative is for an addressed party. Moving from the absent to the address is only made easy when the speech indicates the intended meaning, and in the vocative there is no indication except with extreme forced interpretation. It may also be in the accusative with an implied "a'nī" (I mean). It may also be in apposition to "wakilan," and this too involves forced interpretation.

A group recited "dhurriyyatu" with a damma (nominative), as an apposition to the pronoun that is the subject of "yattakhidhū." This also is valid on the reading with "ya," but it is not permissible on the reading with "ta," because an addressed pronoun is not replaced by apposition. If you say, "I struck you, Zayd," as an apposition, it is not permissible.

His saying: ﴿[You are] the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ — He expressed it with this phrase about the people intended in the verse, according to the difference mentioned, and because in this phrase there is an enumeration of the blessing upon people in the salvation that led to their existence. Disbelief and disobedience are ugly along with this blessing. Those who were carried with Noah and then propagated were his sons from his loins, since he is "Adam the Lesser," and everyone on earth today is of his lineage. This is the view of the majority, and al-Tabari narrated it from Qatada and Mujahid. Even if others were with him, they did not propagate. Al-Naqqash said: Noah's name was 'Abd al-Jabbar. Ibn al-Kalbi said: his name was Faraj. He was described as grateful because he used to praise Allah in every state and for every blessing, for food, drink, clothing, the call of nature, and other things. (ﷺ). This was said by Salman al-Farisi, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Abi Maryam, and Qatada.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel﴾, [to the end of the verse]. Al-Tabari said: the meaning of "qadayna" (We decreed) is "faraghna" (We finished/determined). It was reported from another that he said: "qadayna" here means "akhbarna" (We informed). It was reported from others that they said: "qadayna" means: "in the Mother of the Book" (Umm al-Kitab, the source-book with God).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What causes confusion in this place is the construction of "qadayna" with "ila" (to). My summary of the speech is that this matter is among what Allah, the Exalted, decreed in the Mother of the Book upon the Children of Israel and obligated them with it. Then He informed them of it in the Torah through the tongue of Moses. When here He intended to inform them of both matters together in brevity, He made "qadayna" indicate the enforcement in the Mother of the Book, and joined to it "ila," indicating the delivery of that to the Children of Israel. The intended meaning is understood through these words. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained once by saying: "And We decreed to the Children of Israel" means "We informed them," and said another time: it means "We decreed upon them." "Al-Kitab" here is the Torah, because the oath in His saying, blessed and exalted, "You will surely cause corruption," is not consistent with "al-Kitab" being the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi recited "fi al-kutub" (in the books) in the plural. Abu Hatim said: the reading of the people is in the singular. The majority recited "latufsidunna" with a damma on the ta' and a kasrah on the sin. 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited "latafsudunna" with a fathah on the ta' and a damma on the sin and the dal. Ibn 'Abbas, Nasr ibn 'Asim, and Jabir ibn Zayd recited "latufsadunna" with a damma on the ta', a fathah on the sin, and a damma on the dal. His saying, the Exalted: "wa-latu'lunna" means: you will surely behave arrogantly against obedience to those who command obedience to Allah, and you will seek loftiness and corruption on earth, and you will oppress those over whom you have power to oppress, and the like of this.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The implication of these verses is that Allah, the Exalted, informed the Children of Israel in the Torah that disobedience, transgression, and disbelief in the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, that they had among them, in the messengers, the books, and other things, would occur from them. He would send upon them a nation that would overcome them, kill them, and humiliate them. Then He would have mercy on them after that, give them the upper hand again, and return them to their former state of ascendancy. Then sins and ingratitude for blessings, oppression and killing, and disbelief in Allah from some of them would occur, so Allah would send upon them another nation that would destroy their homes, kill them, and expel them with a severe expulsion. It is said that the time between the two occurrences, from the end of the first to the beginning of the second, was two hundred and ten years of eternal rule with prophets; and it is said it was seventy years.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 2–4:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying]: "Do not take other than Me as a trustee."﴾ ﴿[You are] the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant.﴾ ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book: "You will surely cause corruption on earth twice, and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance."﴾

He joined His saying, "And We gave," to what is implied in His saying, ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1], by way of an implied predicate, as if He had said: "We took Our servant by night and showed him Our signs." "Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah. The pronoun in "jaalnahu" (We made it) may refer back to "al-Kitab," and it may refer back to Moses, peace be upon him.

His saying, "Alla tattakhidhu" (that you not take), may be in a place of accusative [i.e., nasb] with the implied sense of "karahiyah" (out of aversion), and it may be in a place of genitive [i.e., khafd] with the implied sense of "bi-allā tattakhidhū" (so that you do not take). It is also possible that "an" (that) is explanatory, meaning "ay" (namely), as in His saying, ﴿Go on and be steadfast﴾ [Sad: 6]. In that case it is with a command in that verse, and here, in our verse, it is with a prohibition. The meaning in these readings is: We made that so that you would not take, O offspring. It is possible that "dhurriyyata" (offspring) is an object, and it is possible that "an" is superfluous. A verb of saying is implied in the speech, its implied form being: "We said to them: Do not take." As for implying the verb of saying without making "an" superfluous, it is not sound, because what follows a verb of saying is either a sentence that is reported, or a paraphrase of speech that is not the same speech. So the verb of saying works on the paraphrase, as when you say, to someone who said "There is no god but Allah": "You have spoken the truth." His saying, "Allā tattakhidhū," is in the second-person address; this was stated by Abu 'Ali.

The majority of readers recited "Allā tattakhidhū" in the second-person address. Abu 'Amr alone recited "Allā yattakhidhū" with a "ya" (third-person masculine) in the form of the absent party. This is the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Isa, and Abu Raja'.

"Al-Wakil" (the trustee) is on the pattern "fa'il" from "tawakkul" (reliance), meaning one relied upon in affairs. Thus, by this sense, one would be taking him as a deity. Mujahid said: "wakilan" means "a partner."

The majority of readers recited "dhurriyyata" with a dammah on the dhal. 'Amir recited it with a fathah. Zayd ibn Thabit, Aban ibn 'Uthman, and also Mujahid recited it with a kasrah. All of these are with a shaddah on the ra' and the ya'. It is narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit with a fathah on the dhal, with the ra' eased and the ya' doubled, on the pattern "fa'iliyah." The word "dhurriyyah" is on the pattern "fa'ulah"; its root is "dhururah," in which the second ra' was changed to ya' and assimilated, and then the ra' was given a kasrah to harmonize with the ya'. All of these readers recited "dhurriyyata" in the accusative. That is sound, either as an object of "yattakhidhu," in which case the meaning is: that no human being should be taken as a deity besides Allah; or as a vocative, meaning "O offspring," in which case it addresses the whole world. Some people said: This is not sound except on the reading of whoever recited "Allā tattakhidhū" with a "ta" from above. It is not permissible on the reading of whoever recited with a "ya" from below, because the verb is for an absent party while the vocative is for an addressed party. Moving from the absent to the address is only made easy when the speech indicates the intended meaning, and in the vocative there is no indication except with extreme forced interpretation. It may also be in the accusative with an implied "a'nī" (I mean). It may also be in apposition to "wakilan," and this too involves forced interpretation.

A group recited "dhurriyyatu" with a damma (nominative), as an apposition to the pronoun that is the subject of "yattakhidhū." This also is valid on the reading with "ya," but it is not permissible on the reading with "ta," because an addressed pronoun is not replaced by apposition. If you say, "I struck you, Zayd," as an apposition, it is not permissible.

His saying: ﴿[You are] the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ — He expressed it with this phrase about the people intended in the verse, according to the difference mentioned, and because in this phrase there is an enumeration of the blessing upon people in the salvation that led to their existence. Disbelief and disobedience are ugly along with this blessing. Those who were carried with Noah and then propagated were his sons from his loins, since he is "Adam the Lesser," and everyone on earth today is of his lineage. This is the view of the majority, and al-Tabari narrated it from Qatada and Mujahid. Even if others were with him, they did not propagate. Al-Naqqash said: Noah's name was 'Abd al-Jabbar. Ibn al-Kalbi said: his name was Faraj. He was described as grateful because he used to praise Allah in every state and for every blessing, for food, drink, clothing, the call of nature, and other things. (ﷺ). This was said by Salman al-Farisi, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Abi Maryam, and Qatada.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel﴾, [to the end of the verse]. Al-Tabari said: the meaning of "qadayna" (We decreed) is "faraghna" (We finished/determined). It was reported from another that he said: "qadayna" here means "akhbarna" (We informed). It was reported from others that they said: "qadayna" means: "in the Mother of the Book" (Umm al-Kitab, the source-book with God).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What causes confusion in this place is the construction of "qadayna" with "ila" (to). My summary of the speech is that this matter is among what Allah, the Exalted, decreed in the Mother of the Book upon the Children of Israel and obligated them with it. Then He informed them of it in the Torah through the tongue of Moses. When here He intended to inform them of both matters together in brevity, He made "qadayna" indicate the enforcement in the Mother of the Book, and joined to it "ila," indicating the delivery of that to the Children of Israel. The intended meaning is understood through these words. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained once by saying: "And We decreed to the Children of Israel" means "We informed them," and said another time: it means "We decreed upon them." "Al-Kitab" here is the Torah, because the oath in His saying, blessed and exalted, "You will surely cause corruption," is not consistent with "al-Kitab" being the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi recited "fi al-kutub" (in the books) in the plural. Abu Hatim said: the reading of the people is in the singular. The majority recited "latufsidunna" with a damma on the ta' and a kasrah on the sin. 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited "latafsudunna" with a fathah on the ta' and a damma on the sin and the dal. Ibn 'Abbas, Nasr ibn 'Asim, and Jabir ibn Zayd recited "latufsadunna" with a damma on the ta', a fathah on the sin, and a damma on the dal. His saying, the Exalted: "wa-latu'lunna" means: you will surely behave arrogantly against obedience to those who command obedience to Allah, and you will seek loftiness and corruption on earth, and you will oppress those over whom you have power to oppress, and the like of this.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The implication of these verses is that Allah, the Exalted, informed the Children of Israel in the Torah that disobedience, transgression, and disbelief in the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, that they had among them, in the messengers, the books, and other things, would occur from them. He would send upon them a nation that would overcome them, kill them, and humiliate them. Then He would have mercy on them after that, give them the upper hand again, and return them to their former state of ascendancy. Then sins and ingratitude for blessings, oppression and killing, and disbelief in Allah from some of them would occur, so Allah would send upon them another nation that would destroy their homes, kill them, and expel them with a severe expulsion. It is said that the time between the two occurrences, from the end of the first to the beginning of the second, was two hundred and ten years of eternal rule with prophets; and it is said it was seventy years.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 5–7:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿So when the promise of the first of the two came, We sent against you servants of Ours, of great might, and they ranged through the houses; and it was a promise fulfilled.﴾ ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them, and We aided you with wealth and sons, and We made you more numerous in manpower.﴾ ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls; and if you do evil, it is for them. So when the promise of the Hereafter came, [We sent them] to disgrace your faces, and to enter the Masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy completely whatever they had conquered.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "ūlāhumā" (the first of them) refers back to "marratayn" (two times). He expressed evil by the word "promise" (al-wa'd) because the punishment has been explicitly mentioned; and when "promise" is not used absolutely, it is permissible for it to be applied to evil.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "ʿabīdan" (slaves), and people differed greatly, and in widely divergent ways, about the servants who were sent and about the form of the event. It is narrated that the Children of Israel disobeyed and killed Zakariyyā (peace be upon him), so Sanḥārīb, king of Babylon, invaded them; so said Ibn Isḥāq and Ibn Jubayr. Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Jālūt from the people of al-Jazīra invaded them. It is related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr that he said in a lengthy hadith: the last to invade them was a king named Khurdūsh, and his commander, named Hūrzādhān, took charge of killing them in retaliation for the blood of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā; he then withheld from the Children of Israel and settled, out of respect for the blood of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (peace be upon them both). It was also said: the first to invade them was Ṣakhhābīn, king of Rome. It was also said: it was Bukhtanṣar. It is related that he had earlier entered, in an army of Persians, while being obscure and working in the king's kitchen; he observed, through the injustice of the Children of Israel, what the Persians did not know, because he used to mingle with them. When the army returned, this was mentioned to the greatest king; after a period, the king made him commander of an army and sent him, and he ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, killed them, and expelled them. Then he returned and found the king had died, so he ruled in his place, and his condition continued until he ruled the earth after that.

A group said: Bukhtanṣar only invaded them in the final instance when they disobeyed and killed Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (peace be upon them both). The manner of his killing was that the king wanted to marry his wife's daughter, and Yaḥyā (peace be upon him) forbade him from this; this was grievous to his wife, so she adorned her daughter and made her pour wine for the king, and said to her: "When the king seeks you for yourself, refuse him until the king gives you whatever you wish; and when he says to you, 'Wish from me whatever you want,' then say to him: 'The head of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā.'" The girl did this; the king refused her twice, and granted her in the third instance. The head was brought on a basin, and its tongue was speaking, saying: "It is not lawful for you." The blood of Yaḥyā (peace be upon him) flowed and did not stop; the king placed dust upon it until it equalled the city wall, and the blood still gushed forth. When the king whom Allah sent against them invaded them—according to the difference concerning him—he killed of them for the blood until it subsided after killing seventy thousand. This is the implication of this report, and in some of its narrations there is addition and omission. A group related that Ashiʿyā (Isaiah) admonished them and reminded them of Allah and His blessings in a lengthy discourse, whose text al-Ṭabarī quoted; and Ashiʿyā mentioned at its end Muhammad (ﷺ) and gave glad tidings of him. The Children of Israel rushed at him, and he fled from them, and came upon a tree which split open for him until he entered it, and it closed over him. Then Satan presented to them a fringe of his garment, so they took a saw, sawed the tree, and cut it in its middle, and they killed him. At that point Allah sent against them, in the final instance, [the king].

Al-Zahrāwī related from Qatāda stories that Zakariyyā was the companion of the tree, and that when Maryam became pregnant they said: "You neglected our master's daughter until she committed fornication." So they sought him, and he fled from them until he entered the tree, and they sawed him. A group related that Bukhtanṣar was the grandson of Sanḥārīb the first king. A group related that the one who invaded them last was Sābūr Dhū al-Aktāf. Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) also said: when they returned, Allah empowered over them three kings from Persia: Sandābādān, Shahrayāzān, and another. Mujāhid said: in the first instance there came to them a force from Persia which ranged through the houses and roamed about, but there was no fighting and no killing among the Children of Israel; then the armies withdrew from them, and they prevailed and were aided with wealth and sons, until they disobeyed and transgressed. Then in the second instance there came to them one who killed them, overcame them in their stronghold, and destroyed them until the end of time.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-jāsū khilāl al-diyār﴾ (they ranged through the houses), and "diyār" means dwellings and homes. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-liyadkhulū al-masjid kamā dakhalūhu awwala marra﴾ (and to enter the mosque as they entered it the first time) refutes the saying of Mujāhid that in the first instance there was no domination and no fighting; for does one enter the mosque except after domination and fighting? And a historian has said: "They ranged through the alleys." Al-Ṭabarī mentioned in this verse lengthy stories, some of which pertain to the verses and most of which do not; and these meanings are not established, so I have abridged them.

His saying, exalted is He: "baʿathnā" (We sent) may mean that Allah sent a messenger to the king of that nation commanding him to raid the Children of Israel, so the sending was by command; and it may mean that He expressed "sending" by what was cast into the heart of the king who invaded them. People read "fa-jāsū" with a jīm, and Abū al-Samāl read "fa-ḥāsū" with a ḥāʾ; both have the meaning of overpowering and entering by force, and from it comes "al-ḥawāss" (the senses). It was said to Abū al-Samāl: "The reading is only 'jāsū' with a jīm," and he said: "jāsū and ḥāsū are one."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This indicates a choice of reading, not a transmitted narration; for this reason prayer is not valid with it or with its like. Al-Jumhūr read "khilāl," and al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "khalal," and in both cases it is put in the accusative as an adverb of place.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them﴾: the verse is an expression of what Allah said to the Children of Israel in the Torah; and "radadnā" is put in place of "narudd," since at the time of their being informed the matter had not yet occurred; but because Allah's promise is in the utmost certainty that it will occur, He expressed its future by the past tense. This return is after the first deportation, as we have described; the Children of Israel then prevailed over Bayt al-Maqdis and ruled in it, and their condition was good for a while of time, and Allah gave them wealth and children, and made them, when they went forth, more numerous than most people. Al-Ṭabarī said: "We made you the most numerous group that goes forth from among them." Qatāda said: "They were most numerous in manpower in the time of Dawūd (peace be upon him)." And "nafīran" may be the plural of "nafar," like "kalb" and "kalīb," and "ʿabd" and "ʿabīd"; or it may be a form *fa'īl* in the sense of *fā'il*, i.e., "We made you more numerous in one who goes forth."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, "nafīr" is a name for the group that goes forth, named by the verbal noun; and Tubba' al-Ḥimyarī has said:

*Then honour, by Qaḥṭān, a father, and by the Ḥimyarites, honour a nafīr.*

And they say: "neither in the caravan nor in the nafīr," meaning the gathering of Quraysh that went out from Makkah to Badr.

When Allah, exalted is He, said to them, "Thus I shall do to you," He followed this with their admonition in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls﴾. The meaning is: you are taken to account by your own deeds; that is not injustice nor a imposition upon you. ﴿The promise of the Hereafter﴾ means: of the two times mentioned. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to disgrace your faces﴾: the *lām* is the *lām* of command; it was said: the meaning is "We sent them in order that they might disgrace," so the *lām* is entirely the *lām* of "in order that," and the pronoun refers to the servants of great might. Al-Jumhūr read "li-yasūʾū" with a *yāʾ*, a plural with a hamza between two wāws; ʿĀṣim, in the narration of Abū Bakr, and Ibn ʿĀmir read "li-yasūʾa" with a *yāʾ* and an open hamza in the singular; al-Kisāʾī—and it is narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him)—read "li-nasūʾa" with the *nūn* of majesty; Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read "li-nasūʾanna" with a light *nūn*, being the *lām* of command; ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) read "la-yasūʾanna" with an open *lām*, being the *lām* of oath—and the agent is Allah, mighty and majestic. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "li-yusīʾa" with a *yāʾ* dammed and without a wāw; in the codex of Anas: "li-yasūʾa wajhakum" in the singular. He singled out the faces for mention because they are the places that indicate what is in a person of good or evil. "al-Masjid" means the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis. "Tabbara" means: to corrupt and destroy with violence; and His saying: ﴿mā ʿalaw﴾ means: what they overcame of the regions and ruled of the lands; it was said: "mā" is temporal, and the meaning is: the period of their elevation and domination over the lands. "Tabbara" in its precise sense: to return a thing to fragments, like the gold or silk dust and the like, which is its crushing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 5–7:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿So when the promise of the first of the two came, We sent against you servants of Ours, of great might, and they ranged through the houses; and it was a promise fulfilled.﴾ ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them, and We aided you with wealth and sons, and We made you more numerous in manpower.﴾ ﴿If you do good, you do good for your own souls; and if you do evil, it is for them. So when the promise of the Hereafter came, [We sent them] to disgrace your faces, and to enter the Masjid as they entered it the first time, and to destroy completely whatever they had conquered.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "ūlāhumā" (the first of them) refers back to "marratayn" (two times). He expressed evil by the word "promise" (al-wa'd) because the punishment has been explicitly mentioned; and when "promise" is not used absolutely, it is permissible for it to be applied to evil.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "ʿabīdan" (slaves), and people differed greatly, and in widely divergent ways, about the servants who were sent and about the form of the event. It is narrated that the Children of Israel disobeyed and killed Zakariyyā (peace be upon him), so Sanḥārīb, king of Babylon, invaded them; so said Ibn Isḥāq and Ibn Jubayr. Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Jālūt from the people of al-Jazīra invaded them. It is related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr that he said in a lengthy hadith: the last to invade them was a king named Khurdūsh, and his commander, named Hūrzādhān, took charge of killing them in retaliation for the blood of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā; he then withheld from the Children of Israel and settled, out of respect for the blood of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (peace be upon them both). It was also said: the first to invade them was Ṣakhhābīn, king of Rome. It was also said: it was Bukhtanṣar. It is related that he had earlier entered, in an army of Persians, while being obscure and working in the king's kitchen; he observed, through the injustice of the Children of Israel, what the Persians did not know, because he used to mingle with them. When the army returned, this was mentioned to the greatest king; after a period, the king made him commander of an army and sent him, and he ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, killed them, and expelled them. Then he returned and found the king had died, so he ruled in his place, and his condition continued until he ruled the earth after that.

A group said: Bukhtanṣar only invaded them in the final instance when they disobeyed and killed Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā (peace be upon them both). The manner of his killing was that the king wanted to marry his wife's daughter, and Yaḥyā (peace be upon him) forbade him from this; this was grievous to his wife, so she adorned her daughter and made her pour wine for the king, and said to her: "When the king seeks you for yourself, refuse him until the king gives you whatever you wish; and when he says to you, 'Wish from me whatever you want,' then say to him: 'The head of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā.'" The girl did this; the king refused her twice, and granted her in the third instance. The head was brought on a basin, and its tongue was speaking, saying: "It is not lawful for you." The blood of Yaḥyā (peace be upon him) flowed and did not stop; the king placed dust upon it until it equalled the city wall, and the blood still gushed forth. When the king whom Allah sent against them invaded them—according to the difference concerning him—he killed of them for the blood until it subsided after killing seventy thousand. This is the implication of this report, and in some of its narrations there is addition and omission. A group related that Ashiʿyā (Isaiah) admonished them and reminded them of Allah and His blessings in a lengthy discourse, whose text al-Ṭabarī quoted; and Ashiʿyā mentioned at its end Muhammad (ﷺ) and gave glad tidings of him. The Children of Israel rushed at him, and he fled from them, and came upon a tree which split open for him until he entered it, and it closed over him. Then Satan presented to them a fringe of his garment, so they took a saw, sawed the tree, and cut it in its middle, and they killed him. At that point Allah sent against them, in the final instance, [the king].

Al-Zahrāwī related from Qatāda stories that Zakariyyā was the companion of the tree, and that when Maryam became pregnant they said: "You neglected our master's daughter until she committed fornication." So they sought him, and he fled from them until he entered the tree, and they sawed him. A group related that Bukhtanṣar was the grandson of Sanḥārīb the first king. A group related that the one who invaded them last was Sābūr Dhū al-Aktāf. Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) also said: when they returned, Allah empowered over them three kings from Persia: Sandābādān, Shahrayāzān, and another. Mujāhid said: in the first instance there came to them a force from Persia which ranged through the houses and roamed about, but there was no fighting and no killing among the Children of Israel; then the armies withdrew from them, and they prevailed and were aided with wealth and sons, until they disobeyed and transgressed. Then in the second instance there came to them one who killed them, overcame them in their stronghold, and destroyed them until the end of time.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fa-jāsū khilāl al-diyār﴾ (they ranged through the houses), and "diyār" means dwellings and homes. Al-Ṭabarī mentioned in this verse lengthy stories, some of which pertain to the verses and most of which do not; and these meanings are not established, so I have abridged them.

His saying, exalted is He: "baʿathnā" (We sent) may mean that Allah sent a messenger to the king of that nation commanding him to raid the Children of Israel, so the sending was by command; and it may mean that He expressed "sending" by what was cast into the heart of the king who invaded them. People read "fa-jāsū" with a jīm, and Abū al-Samāl read "fa-ḥāsū" with a ḥāʾ; both have the meaning of overpowering and entering by force, and from it comes "al-ḥawāss" (the senses). It was said to Abū al-Samāl: "The reading is only 'jāsū' with a jīm," and he said: "jāsū and ḥāsū are one."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This indicates a choice of reading, not a transmitted narration; for this reason prayer is not valid with it or with its like. Al-Jumhūr read "khilāl," and al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "khalal," and in both cases it is put in the accusative as an adverb of place.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them﴾: the verse is an expression of what Allah said to the Children of Israel in the Torah; and "radadnā" is put in place of "narudd," since at the time of their being informed the matter had not yet occurred; but because Allah's promise is in the utmost certainty that it will occur, He expressed its future by the past tense. This return is after the first deportation, as we have described; the Children of Israel then prevailed over Bayt al-Maqdis and ruled in it, and their condition was good for a while of time, and Allah gave them wealth and children, and made them, when they went forth, more numerous than most people. Al-Ṭabarī said: "We made you the most numerous group that goes forth from among them." Qatāda said: "They were most numerous in manpower in the time of Dawūd (peace be upon him)." And "nafīran" may be the plural of "nafar," like "kalb" and "kalīb," and "ʿabd" and "ʿabīd"; or it may be a form *fa'īl* in the sense of *fā'il*, i.e., "We made you more numerous in one who goes forth."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, "nafīr" is a name for the group that goes forth, named by the verbal noun; and Tubba' al-Ḥimyarī has said:

*Then honour, by Qaḥṭān, a father, and by the Ḥimyarites, honour a nafīr.*

And they say: "neither in the caravan nor in the nafīr," meaning the gathering of Quraysh that went out from Makkah to Badr.

Allah, exalted is He, says to the remnant of the Children of Israel: ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾ if you obey concerning yourselves and remain upright. "It may be" (ʿasā) expresses hope concerning them. This promise is not a promise of the return of their dominion. It is that He will show mercy to those among them who obey. Following ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, and Muḥammad ﷺ was among their obedience, but they did not do so. They returned to disbelief and disobedience, so the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, returned to them. He imposed humiliation upon them, killed them, and made them abased at the hand of every nation. Here Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He gave three kings power over them.

Al-Ḥaṣīr (the prison, or confining place) is a form (faʿīl) from al-ḥaṣr (confinement). It means a prison, that is, it confines them. Mujāhid, Qatādah, and others explained it in this sense. It is also said that al-Ḥaṣīr is from ḥaṣr for the king (meaning the royal court or assembly). From this is the verse of Labīd:

"And an assembly of stiff-necked men, as if they were jinn standing at the door of the Ḥaṣīr."

It is also said that the two sides of a person's body are called ḥaṣīrān, because they confine him. From this is the verse of al-Ṭirimmāḥ:

"A little while she lingers to attend to her need, then she was raised up upon every ... of the two ḥaṣīrs, stout-bodied."

Al-Ḥasan said: "al-Ḥaṣīr" in the verse means that which is spread out and laid down, like the well-known mat (ḥaṣīr) among people.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That ḥaṣīr is derived from ḥaṣr.

As for Allah's statement, ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides﴾ and the rest of the verse: "yahdī" in this verse means "yurshidu" (guides). It may also be taken to mean "yadʿū" (calls). By "allatī" (that which) He means the state and the way. A group said: ﴿to that which is most upright﴾ is the statement "There is no god but Allah."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first meaning is more general. The word of sincerity and other statements and actions are included in the state that is most upright, compared with every state set against it. The restriction to "most upright" without mentioning "than such-and-such" is a concise expression. The meaning is understood: that which is most upright than everything that differs from it, so it is the ultimate in uprightness. He restricted the believers to doing righteous deeds, since this is the perfection of faith, even if faith in itself does not require it. The believer who acts alone has a share in righteous deeds through his faith. "Al-ajr al-kabīr" (the great reward) is Paradise. Likewise, wherever it occurs in the Book of Allah, "a great bounty and a great reward" refers to Paradise.

[p. 447]

As for Allah's statement, the first "anna" is in the position of an accusative governed by "yubashshiru" (gives glad tidings). The second "inna" is conjoined to the first and is included in the sphere of the glad tidings given to the believers. The Qur'an gave them glad tidings of Paradise and that the disbelievers have a painful punishment. This is because the believers' knowledge of this is a joy to them. In this glad tidings there is also, by implication, a warning to the disbelievers. This is what the wording of the verse requires. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhūr, meaning the main body of recitation authorities) read "wa-yubashshiru" with a damma on the yāʾ, a fatḥa on the bāʾ, and a kasra on the shīn. Ibn Masʿūd, Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, and Ṭalḥah read "wa-yubashshiru" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, a sukūn on the bāʾ, and a damma on the shīn. "Aʿtadnā" means: we prepared and made ready. From it comes ʿattād (equipment). "Al-alīm" means the painful.

As for Allah's statement, ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾: the wāw was dropped from "yadʿu" in the written codex (al-muṣḥaf, the Uthmanic copy), because they wrote what was pronounced. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and Mujāhid said: this verse was revealed to censure what people do by invoking curses upon their wealth and children at times of anger and distress. Allah informs that they invoke evil at such a time just as they invoke good at a time of composure. If Allah were to answer their supplication, He would destroy them. But Allah, exalted is He, overlooks and does not answer the supplication of the distressed and hasty. Then He offered some partial excuse, that man has an innate haste. "Al-insān" here, it is said, refers to the species, according to what is in creation of this trait. Mujāhid and others said this. Salmān al-Fārisī and Ibn ʿAbbās said: it refers to Ādam, peace be upon him, in that when the spirit was breathed into his head he sneezed and saw, and when the spirit moved through his body, reaching his legs before the rest, he was impressed with himself and went walking hastily toward that, but he could not manage it. The wording of this verse alludes to that. The meaning is: you are people of an inherited haste from your father.

It is related that the Prophet ﷺ was made a captive and placed in fetters in the house of Sawdah bint Zamʿah. Sawdah heard his groaning and was concerned, and she said to him: "What is wrong with you?" He said: "The pain of the fetter." So she stood up and loosened it for him, and he became quiet. Then she slept, and he contrived to free himself and escaped. The Prophet ﷺ looked for him at dawn and was informed of what had happened. He said: "May Allah cut off her hands." Sawdah was alarmed, raised her hands toward the sky, and feared that her supplication would be answered. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah has made my supplication in such a situation a mercy upon the one for whom I supplicate, because I am a human being who becomes angry and hasty. So let Sawdah lower her hands."

[p. 448]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 17, verses 12–14:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day visible, that you might seek bounty from your Lord and that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. And everything We have explained in detail.﴾ ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (ṭā'ir) to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open.﴾ ﴿"Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner."﴾

"Āyah" (sign): the marker set up for reflection and lesson. As for His words, "fa-maḥawnā" (then We effaced): a group said that the reason for the fa' (then), indicating sequence, is that God created the sun and the moon both shining, then after that He effaced the moon. Gabriel effaced it with his wings three times, and from that point came its spots and its being only luminous. Another group, and this is the apparent meaning, said: His words "then We effaced" mean only in the original creation of it. This is like your saying, "I built my house, then it began with the foundation, then it continued," where you do not intend by the fa' a sense of sequence. The apparent wording of the verse requires four signs, especially for one who holds that the moon is the effaced one and the sun is the visible one. But if one estimates the effaced thing as the darkness of the night and the visibility as the light of the day, it is possible for the verse to include only two signs, on the basis that there is a part of attributing a thing to itself. As for His words "mubṣiratan" (visible), it is like your saying, "a night that sleeps and wakes": that is, one sleeps in it and one wakes in it. Likewise, "an ayah mubṣirah" means one sees in it and with it.

Al-Ṭabarī related from some of the Kufans that he said: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

[p. 449] "Ask me about whatever you wish." Ibn al-Kawwā' said: "What is the blackness that is in the moon?" 'Alī said to him: "May Allah fight you! Why did you not ask about the matter of your religion and your Hereafter? That is the effacing of the night."

Allah the Exalted made the day visible so that people might seek sustenance and the bounty of Allah. He made the moon differ from the state of the sun so that by it the number of years and the reckoning of months and days might be known. Knowledge of that in the Sharī'ah comes from the direction of the moon, not from the direction of the sun.

His words "kulla shay'" (everything) are in the accusative, governed by a verb understood which the apparent wording indicates; its estimate is: "And We have explained everything in detail." It was also said that "wa-kulla" is coordinated with "wal-ḥisāb" (and the reckoning), so it is an object of "li-ta'lamū" (that you might know). "Tafṣīl" (detailed explanation) is clarification by mentioning the distinctions between things and removing their causes, until the right is distinguished from the doubt that has occurred in it.

His words: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (the verse). His saying "kulla" is in the accusative, governed by a verb to be estimated. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajā', and Ibn Mujāhid read "ṭayrahu fī 'unuqih" (his omen on his neck). Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Ṭā'iruhu" is what has been decreed for him and upon him. Allah, blessed and exalted, addressed the Arabs in this verse in terms they knew. That was because it was their custom to take omens (tayammun and tashā'um) from birds, whether they came from the right (sāniḥah) or from the left (bāriḥah). This became so common that they did the same with gazelles and the animals of the wilderness, and they called all of that "taṭayyur" (taking omens; tiyarah). They believed that such an omen decreed what a person encounters of good and evil. So Allah the Exalted informed them, in this verse, in the most concise wording and most eloquent allusion, that everything a person meets of good or evil has already been preceded by decree, and that his share, his deed, and his earning are fastened to his neck. This is in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾. So He expressed the share and the deed by the bird, since the two are inseparable. This was said by Mujāhid and Qatādah, according to the belief of the Arabs about taking omens, and their saying about matters, "upon the auspicious bird," and "with the luckiest bird," and from it what "flew" in argument and in the arrow-lot. Like the saying of Umm al-'Alā' al-Anṣāriyyah: "There flew for us, among those who came with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Hijrah, 'Uthmān ibn Maẓ'ūn," meaning that was our share. [p. 450] The origin of all this is from the birds, which in their view decided the meeting of good and evil. This was nullified by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no contagion (ʿadwā) and no omen-taking (ṭiyarah)."

His words ﴿in his neck﴾ also follow the usage of the Arabs in attributing to the neck whatever is an obligation, a necklace, a trust, and the like. Like their saying, "My blood is on the neck of so-and-so," and like the saying of al-A'shā:

*"I have hung poetry about your neck, O Salāmah, possessor of bounty,
and a thing is wherever it is placed."*

This is common. Similar to it is their attributing what is earning, crime, and sin to the hand, since the hand is the origin of earning.

Abū Ja'far, Nāfi', and the people read "wa-nukhriju" (and We bring out) with the plural of majesty, "kitāban" (a record) in the accusative. Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Ibn Muḥayṣin read "yakhruju" with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the rā', as an imperfect verb, "kitāban," meaning: his bird, which is a metaphor for his deed, comes out for him as a record. Al-Ḥasan – among these – read "kitābun" with the nominative. Abū Ja'far also read "wa-yukhraju" with a ḍammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the rā', in the passive voice whose agent is not named, "kitāban," meaning: his bird. He also read "kitābun." A group read "wa-yukhriju" with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the rā', meaning: Allah brings out. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "fī 'unuqihi yaqra'uhu [p. 451] yawm al-qiyāmah kitāban yalqāhu manshūran." This record is the human's deed and his sins.

The majority read "yalqāhu" with a fatḥah on the yā', sukūn on the lām, and light pronunciation of the qāf. Ibn 'Āmir alone read "yulaqqāhu" with a ḍammah on the yā', fatḥah on the lām, and shaddah on the qāf. This is the reading of al-Ḥasan according to one report, and of Abū Ja'far al-Jaḥdarī.

His words: ﴿Read your record﴾ – "It will be said to him" has been omitted from the speech for brevity, since the apparent wording indicates it. "Al-ḥasīb" means the reckoner, and its accusative is as a specification (tamyīz). Al-Ṭabarī related from al-Ḥasan that he said: "O son of Adam, a scroll has been unfolded for you, and two noble angels have been appointed over you: one on your right writes your good deeds, and the other on your left guards your bad deeds. So possess what you wish, or diminish, or increase, until when you die your scroll is folded and placed on your neck with you in your grave, until you come out on the Day of Resurrection with a record you will find spread open. 'Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner.' By Allah, the one who made you the reckoner of your own soul has been just with you."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On the basis of these words which al-Ḥasan mentioned, the bird is what is gathered with Adam of his deed in his grave, so reflect on his wording. This is also the saying of Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Qatādah said regarding His words ﴿Read your record﴾: that on that day everyone who could not read will read.

His words: ﴿Read your record﴾ – "It will be said to him" has been omitted from the speech for brevity, since the apparent wording indicates it. "Al-ḥasīb" means the reckoner, and its accusative is as a specification (tamyīz). Al-Ṭabarī related from al-Ḥasan that he said: "O son of Adam, a scroll has been unfolded for you, and two noble angels have been appointed over you: one on your right writes your good deeds, and the other on your left guards your bad deeds. So possess what you wish, or diminish, or increase, until when you die your scroll is folded and placed on your neck with you in your grave, until you come out on the Day of Resurrection with a record you will find spread open. 'Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner.' By Allah, the one who made you the reckoner of your own soul has been just with you."

On the basis of these words which al-Ḥasan mentioned, the bird is what is gathered with Adam of his deed in his grave, so reflect on his wording. This is also the saying of Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Qatādah said regarding His words ﴿Read your record﴾: that on that day everyone who could not read will read.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 17, verses 12–14:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day visible, that you might seek bounty from your Lord and that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. And everything We have explained in detail.﴾ ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird (ṭā'ir) to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open.﴾ ﴿"Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner."﴾

"Āyah" (sign): the marker set up for reflection and lesson. As for His words, "fa-maḥawnā" (then We effaced): a group said that the reason for the fa' (then), indicating sequence, is that God created the sun and the moon both shining, then after that He effaced the moon. Gabriel effaced it with his wings three times, and from that point came its spots and its being only luminous. Another group, and this is the apparent meaning, said: His words "then We effaced" mean only in the original creation of it. This is like your saying, "I built my house, then it began with the foundation, then it continued," where you do not intend by the fa' a sense of sequence. The apparent wording of the verse requires four signs, especially for one who holds that the moon is the effaced one and the sun is the visible one. But if one estimates the effaced thing as the darkness of the night and the visibility as the light of the day, it is possible for the verse to include only two signs, on the basis that there is a part of attributing a thing to itself. As for His words "mubṣiratan" (visible), it is like your saying, "a night that sleeps and wakes": that is, one sleeps in it and one wakes in it. Likewise, "an ayah mubṣirah" means one sees in it and with it.

Al-Ṭabarī related from some of the Kufans that he said: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

[p. 449] "Ask me about whatever you wish." Ibn al-Kawwā' said: "What is the blackness that is in the moon?" 'Alī said to him: "May Allah fight you! Why did you not ask about the matter of your religion and your Hereafter? That is the effacing of the night."

Allah the Exalted made the day visible so that people might seek sustenance and the bounty of Allah. He made the moon differ from the state of the sun so that by it the number of years and the reckoning of months and days might be known. Knowledge of that in the Sharī'ah comes from the direction of the moon, not from the direction of the sun.

His words "kulla shay'" (everything) are in the accusative, governed by a verb understood which the apparent wording indicates; its estimate is: "And We have explained everything in detail." It was also said that "wa-kulla" is coordinated with "wal-ḥisāb" (and the reckoning), so it is an object of "li-ta'lamū" (that you might know). "Tafṣīl" (detailed explanation) is clarification by mentioning the distinctions between things and removing their causes, until the right is distinguished from the doubt that has occurred in it.

His words: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ (the verse). His saying "kulla" is in the accusative, governed by a verb to be estimated. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajā', and Ibn Mujāhid read "ṭayrahu fī 'unuqih" (his omen on his neck). Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Ṭā'iruhu" is what has been decreed for him and upon him. Allah, blessed and exalted, addressed the Arabs in this verse in terms they knew. That was because it was their custom to take omens (tayammun and tashā'um) from birds, whether they came from the right (sāniḥah) or from the left (bāriḥah). This became so common that they did the same with gazelles and the animals of the wilderness, and they called all of that "taṭayyur" (taking omens; tiyarah). They believed that such an omen decreed what a person encounters of good and evil. So Allah the Exalted informed them, in this verse, in the most concise wording and most eloquent allusion, that everything a person meets of good or evil has already been preceded by decree, and that his share, his deed, and his earning are fastened to his neck. This is in the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾. So He expressed the share and the deed by the bird, since the two are inseparable. This was said by Mujāhid and Qatādah, according to the belief of the Arabs about taking omens, and their saying about matters, "upon the auspicious bird," and "with the luckiest bird," and from it what "flew" in argument and in the arrow-lot. Like the saying of Umm al-'Alā' al-Anṣāriyyah: "There flew for us, among those who came with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Hijrah, 'Uthmān ibn Maẓ'ūn," meaning that was our share. [p. 450] The origin of all this is from the birds, which in their view decided the meeting of good and evil. This was nullified by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no contagion (ʿadwā) and no omen-taking (ṭiyarah)."

*"I have hung poetry about your neck, O Salāmah, possessor of bounty,
and a thing is wherever it is placed."*

This is common. Similar to it is their attributing what is earning, crime, and sin to the hand, since the hand is the origin of earning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 15–17:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment. No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. And We would never punish until We have sent a Messenger.﴾ ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they transgress therein, and the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah? And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾

The meaning of this verse is that each person is held to account for himself and not for another. It is narrated that its occasion of revelation was that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi said to the people of Mecca: "Disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ), and your sin will be on me." So this verse was revealed, meaning: al-Walid does not carry your sins, and the sin of each (p-452) individual is upon himself. A group said: the reference to guidance in the verse was revealed concerning Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad, and the reference to going astray concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

"Wazara" means "he carried," and "al-wizr" means "the burden." From this comes "wazir" of a ruler, that is, one who bears the weight of his rule. With this verse 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, argued in refuting the one who said that the dead person is punished by the weeping of the living over him. The essence of that meaning is that punishment only occurs when the weeping was part of the deceased's custom and he was its cause, as the Arabs used to do.

As for His saying, ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a Messenger﴾, a group, which is the majority, said: this applies to the ruling of this world, meaning that Allah does not destroy a nation with punishment except after sending a messenger to them and warning them. Another group said: this is general in this world and the Hereafter.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The summary of this meaning is that the purpose of the verse in this place is to inform about the worship of Allah the Exalted among the nations in this world, and by this the threat draws near to the disbelievers of Mecca. What confirms this is what follows of His description of what occurs when Allah intends to destroy a town, and of His informing about the multitude of generations He destroyed. Nevertheless, the apparent meaning from the Book of Allah the Exalted in other places, and from reflection, is that Allah the Exalted does not punish in the Hereafter except after the sending of the messengers, as in His saying: ﴿Every time a group is cast into it, its keepers ask them, "Did no warner come to you?"﴾ [al-Mulk: 8] ﴿They say, "Yes."﴾ [al-Mulk: 9]. The apparent sense of "kullama" (every time) is restriction. And as in His saying: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24]. As for reasoning, the sending of Adam, peace be upon him, with monotheism, and the establishment of beliefs among his descendants, and the setting up of proofs indicating the Creator, together with soundness of the intellect, obligates every person of sound mind to believe and follow the law of Allah. Then this was renewed in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, after the drowning of the disbelievers. This verse also, the possibilities of its wording allow something like this. It is also possible, as a hypothesis, that there are people to whom no message reached, among them the people of the intervals (ahl al-fatarat) between prophets, whose existence some scholars have estimated. As for what is reported, that Allah will send messengers to them on the Day of Resurrection, and to the insane and children, this is a hadith that is not authentic, and what the Sharia requires does not imply it, namely that the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾, the verse. In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "We sent the greatest of its criminals" (ba'athna akabira mujrimiha). "Qarya" (town) means a gathered city, derived from "qaraytu al-ma'a fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the basin), if I gathered it. It is not from "qara'a" (to recite), which is hamzated, although both share the meaning of gathering. The majority read "amarna" in the past tense, from "amara," the opposite of "nahá" (forbade). Nafi' and Ibn Kathir, in some of what is narrated from them, read "a'marna" with a lengthened hamza, meaning "we multiplied." This is also narrated from al-Hasan, and it is the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, with a variant from him; and from al-A'raj, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read with it. The Arabs say "amira al-qawm" when the people increased, and Allah the Exalted made them increase (amarahum), which takes a transitive form with the hamza. Abu 'Amr, with a variant, read "ammarna" with a doubled mim. This is the reading of Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu al-'Aliya, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

Al-Tabari said: the first reading means: "We commanded them to obey, but they disobeyed and transgressed therein," and this is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. The second means: "We multiplied them." The third is from imara (rule), meaning: "We made them rulers over the people."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "The best interpretation of 'amarna' is that it means 'we multiplied,' the verb being transitive by a form that is not transitive, as you say: raja'a and raja'tuhu (he returned and I returned it), and shataret 'aynuhu and shatartuha (his eye squinted and I made it squint). So you say: amara al-qawm (the people increased) and Allah ammarahum (made them increase), meaning kathharahum (multiplied them). 'A'marna' is an intensification of 'amarna' with the hamza, and 'ammarna' is an intensification of it by doubling. There is no basis for 'ammarna' being from imara (rule), because their leadership would only be one after another, while the destruction occurs during the period of one of them."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The response to what Abu 'Ali said is that the command, although it includes the affluent and others, singled out the affluent for mention, since their wickedness is the one that has an effect on the corruption of the town, and they are the bulk of misguidance, while others follow them. As for "ammarna" from imara (rule), it is correct in two ways. One is that it does not mean rule over a kingdom, but rather that they command and are obeyed. The Arabs say of one who commands a person, even if he is not a king, "he is an amir" (commander). From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

When the guide of a youth in the lands,
the chest of the spear, obeys the commander.

From this is the saying of Mu'awiya to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when 'Umar ordered him to take retaliation for the slap of 'Amr ibn al-'As: "Indeed, over me is a commander; I do not decide a matter without him," meaning by Mu'awiya his father. Al-A'sha meant that when a man grows old, becomes blind, and is guided by a staff, he obeys whoever commands him. From this is the saying of another:

The people blame the commander when
they err in what is right, and the guide is not blamed.

Moreover, if one intended rule over a kingdom in the verse, the meaning would be fine, because when Allah gives rule over a nation to an affluent man who transgresses, then after him another like him rules, and so on, the corruption grows, disbelief spreads, and they deserve punishment, and it descends upon them at the hands of the last of their kings. Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "amirna" with a kasra on the mim, and al-Nahhas related it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. I do not establish a basis for this reading, unless "amira al-qawm" is intransitive in its own form, for the Arabs say "amira banu fulan" when they increased. From this is the saying of Labid:

If they are envied, they will be brought low, and if they increase
one day they will become for scarcity and annihilation.

From this is: "Indeed the matter of Ibn Abi Kabsha has increased (laqad amira amru ibn abi kabsha)." Al-Farra' rejected this reading. It is related that "amira" is transitive from Abu Zayd al-Ansari. "Al-mutraf" is the wealthy one of the wealth, indulgent in luxury, and "al-turfa" is blessing. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "a town, We sent the greatest of its criminals, and they plotted therein." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then the word becomes due against it﴾ means Allah's threat against it which their messenger had spoken. "Al-tadmir" is destruction together with effacing the traces and demolishing the structures. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

They were for them like the camel of Thamud, when
it wailed for a time, so He destroyed them with destruction.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed﴾, the verse. "Kam" (how many) is in the accusative position governed by "ahlakna" (We destroyed). This mention of the multitude of those whom Allah destroyed from the generations is an example for Quraysh and a threat, meaning: you are not far from what those people incurred of punishment, if you deny your Prophet. People differed concerning the length of a generation (qarn). Ibn Sirin related from the Prophet (ﷺ): forty. It was said other than this, close to it. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa said: a generation is one hundred and twenty years. A group said: a generation is one hundred years, and this is the most sound view, which the hadith supports in his (ﷺ) saying: "The best of people is my generation (qarni)." Muhammad ibn al-Qasim related, from his in-law 'Abd Allah ibn Busr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand on my head and said: "This boy will live a qarn." I said: "How long is a qarn?" He said: "One hundred years." Muhammad ibn al-Qasim said: we kept counting for him until he completed one hundred years, and he died, may Allah have mercy on him. The ba' in His saying "bi-rabbika" (by your Lord) is superfluous (za'ida), and the sense is: "sufficient is your Lord." This ba' generally comes in praise or dispraise, and it seems to convey the meaning: "be content with your Lord," that is, how sufficient He is in this. "Kafa" may also come without a ba', as in the words of the poet:

Grey hair and Islam suffice a man as a deterrent.

And as in the saying of another:

The guidance of a man informs me about his absent companion;
guidance suffices, concerning what is hidden of a man, as an informer.

they err in what is right, and the guide is not blamed.

Moreover, if one intended rule over a kingdom in the verse, the meaning would be fine, because when Allah gives rule over a nation to an affluent man who transgresses, then after him another like him rules, and so on, the corruption grows, disbelief spreads, and they deserve punishment, and it descends upon them at the hands of the last of their kings. Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "amirna" with a kasra on the mim, and al-Nahhas related it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. I do not establish a basis for this reading, unless "amira al-qawm" is intransitive in its own form, for the Arabs say "amira banu fulan" when they increased. From this is the saying of Labid:

If they are envied, they will be brought low, and if they increase
one day they will become for scarcity and annihilation.

From this is: "Indeed the matter of Ibn Abi Kabsha has increased (laqad amira amru ibn abi kabsha)." Al-Farra' rejected this reading. It is related that "amira" is transitive from Abu Zayd al-Ansari. "Al-tadmir" is destruction together with effacing the traces and demolishing the structures. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

They were for them like the camel of Thamud, when
it wailed for a time, so He destroyed them with destruction.

This mention of the multitude of those whom Allah destroyed from the generations is an example for Quraysh and a threat, meaning: you are not far from what those people incurred of punishment, if you deny your Prophet. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa said: a generation is one hundred and twenty years. A group said: a generation is one hundred years, and this is the most sound view, which the hadith supports in his (ﷺ) saying: "The best of people is my generation (qarni)."
