The ba' in His saying "bi-rabbika" (by your Lord) is superfluous (za'ida), and the sense is: "sufficient is your Lord." This ba' generally comes in praise or dispraise, and it seems to convey the meaning: "be content with your Lord," that is, how sufficient He is in this. "Kafa" may also come without a ba', as in the words of the poet:

Grey hair and Islam suffice a man as a deterrent.

And as in the saying of another:

The guidance of a man informs me about his absent companion;
guidance suffices, concerning what is hidden of a man, as an informer.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 15–17:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self, and whoever goes astray only goes astray to its detriment. No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾

The meaning of this verse is that each person is held to account for himself and not for another. It is narrated that its occasion of revelation was that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi said to the people of Mecca: "Disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ), and your sin will be on me." So this verse was revealed, meaning: al-Walid does not carry your sins, and the sin of each (p-452) individual is upon himself. A group said: the reference to guidance in the verse was revealed concerning Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad, and the reference to going astray concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

"Wazara" means "he carried," and "al-wizr" means "the burden." From this comes "wazir" of a ruler, that is, one who bears the weight of his rule. With this verse 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, argued in refuting the one who said that the dead person is punished by the weeping of the living over him. The essence of that meaning is that punishment only occurs when the weeping was part of the deceased's custom and he was its cause, as the Arabs used to do.

As for His saying, ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a Messenger﴾, a group, which is the majority, said: this applies to the ruling of this world, meaning that Allah does not destroy a nation with punishment except after sending a messenger to them and warning them. Another group said: this is general in this world and the Hereafter.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The summary of this meaning is that the purpose of the verse in this place is to inform about the worship of Allah the Exalted among the nations in this world, and by this the threat draws near to the disbelievers of Mecca. What confirms this is what follows of His description of what occurs when Allah intends to destroy a town, and of His informing about the multitude of generations He destroyed. Nevertheless, the apparent meaning from the Book of Allah the Exalted in other places, and from reflection, is that Allah the Exalted does not punish in the Hereafter except after the sending of the messengers, as in His saying: ﴿Every time a group is cast into it, its keepers ask them, "Did no warner come to you?"﴾ [al-Mulk: 8] ﴿They say, "Yes."﴾ [al-Mulk: 9]. The apparent sense of "kullama" (every time) is restriction. And as in His saying: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24]. As for reasoning, the sending of Adam, peace be upon him, with monotheism, and the establishment of beliefs among his descendants, and the setting up of proofs indicating the Creator, together with soundness of the intellect, obligates every person of sound mind to believe and follow the law of Allah. Then this was renewed in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, after the drowning of the disbelievers. This verse also, the possibilities of its wording allow something like this. It is also possible, as a hypothesis, that there are people to whom no message reached, among them the people of the intervals (ahl al-fatarat) between prophets, whose existence some scholars have estimated. As for what is reported, that Allah will send messengers to them on the Day of Resurrection, and to the insane and children, this is a hadith that is not authentic, and what the Sharia requires does not imply it, namely that the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾, the verse. In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "We sent the greatest of its criminals" (ba'athna akabira mujrimiha). "Qarya" (town) means a gathered city, derived from "qaraytu al-ma'a fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the basin), if I gathered it. It is not from "qara'a" (to recite), which is hamzated, although both share the meaning of gathering. The majority read "amarna" in the past tense, from "amara," the opposite of "nahá" (forbade). This is the reading of Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, Abu al-'Aliya, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and it is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "The best interpretation of 'amarna' is that it means 'we multiplied,' the verb being transitive by a form that is not transitive, as you say: raja'a and raja'tuhu (he returned and I returned it), and shataret 'aynuhu and shatartuha (his eye squinted and I made it squint). When the guide of a youth in the lands,

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 17, verses 18–22:**

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have appointed for him Hell, he will burn therein, reproached and banished.﴾ ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it while he is a believer, those – their striving will be appreciated.﴾ ﴿To each We extend, to these and to those, from the gift of your Lord. And the gift of your Lord has never been restricted.﴾ ﴿See how We have favored some of them over others, and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾ ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.﴾

The meaning: whoever desires the immediate worldly life, and believes in nothing else, and does not believe in the Hereafter, then he empties his hope and his belief for this world. Allah the Exalted hastens for whomever of these people He wills what this seeker wills, or what Allah wills, according to the reading of the one who recites "nashā'" with the letter nūn. His words, ﴿for whom We intend﴾, are a sufficient condition on both readings. Then Allah the Exalted appoints Hell for all who desire the immediate life, in the manner of disbelief, whether He gave them what they wished in it or deprived them of it. Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī said: "for whom We intend" means "his destruction." Most reciters read "nashā'" with nūn, while Nāfi' also read "yashā'" with yā'. "Al-madhūr" means humiliated, distanced, abased, and one who is subject to wrath.

His words, ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾ – the verse. The meaning: whoever desires the Hereafter with the desire of certainty in it, in Allah and in His Messenger.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

All of that is linked by mutual necessity.

Then He stipulated for the seeker of the Hereafter that he strive for it with its striving, which is persistence in good deeds and good words according to the ruling and methods of the Sharī'ah. Those – Allah appreciates their striving. Allah does not appreciate any deed or striving without rewarding for it and forgiving by means of it. Among this is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of the man who gave water to the thirsty dog: "So Allah appreciated it from him, and forgave him."

His words, ﴿To each We extend﴾ – the verse. "Kullan" is in the accusative governed by "numidd." "Amdadtu al-shay'" means when you add to a thing from other than its kind, and "madadtu" means when you add to it from its own kind. It is said that both have the same meaning; one says "madda" and "amadda." "Hā'ulā'" is a substitute for "kullan," so it is in the accusative position. His words, ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾, may mean: from the acts of obedience for those who desire the Hereafter, and the acts of disobedience for those who desire the immediate life. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with him). It may also mean by the gift the provision of this world. This is the interpretation of al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, meaning that Allah, blessed and exalted, provides in this world for the seekers of the Hereafter who are believers and the seekers of the immediate life who are disbelievers, and extends to them of His gift from it; differentiation and disparity occur only in the Hereafter. This meaning accords with His words, ﴿and the gift of your Lord has never been restricted﴾, meaning that His provision in this world does not narrow for believer or disbeliever. Yet this expression is hardly suited to one whom He extends with sins that destroy him.

"Al-maḥẓūr" means the prevented.

His words, ﴿See how We have favored some of them over others﴾ – a verse that clearly indicates that the gift in the preceding verse is provision. Accordingly, Muḥammad (ﷺ) is to look at Allah, blessed and exalted, favoring some over others in provision, the like, forms, nobility, status, and portions. Clearly, the favoring that the Prophet (ﷺ) looks at is that Allah gave some people obedience leading to Paradise, and gave others disbelief leading to the Fire. This is the view of al-Ṭabarī, and this concerns the consideration of the favoring of one group over another. According to the other interpretation, the consideration is of the favoring of one individual over another among believers and disbelievers, however you pair them. Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, informed that the greatest distinction occurs in the Hereafter. His words, ﴿greater in degrees﴾, are not in the wording "greater than what," but in meaning – necessarily – greater in degrees than everything that is attached to it, in existence or by supposition. Likewise His words, ﴿and greater in preference﴾.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Some scholars held that these degrees and this favoring are only among believers. Al-Ṭabarī related in this regard a hadith whose text is: "Indeed, between the highest level of Paradise and its lowest is a degree like the star seen in the eastern and western horizons."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is said: Allah has satisfied them all, so no one envies another, and no one wishes to exchange that for anything else.

His words, ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾ – the verse. The address is to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is all of creation, as al-Ṭabarī and others said. "Al-dhamm" here applies from Allah the Exalted and from those of sound intellect against a person who makes a stick or a stone superior to himself, singles it out with honor, attributes divinity to it, and associates it with Allah, who created him, provided for him, and bestowed His blessings upon him. "Al-khidhlān" in this context means Allah withdrawing His support and not guaranteeing victory for him. "Al-makhdhūl" is one whom those who ought to support him do not support. "Al-khādhil" is the gazelle that abandons its young. From this same root is the verse of al-Ra'ī:

*They killed Ibn 'Affān, the Caliph, in a state of ihrām,*
*and he strove, but I have not seen one like him forsaken.*

*and he strove, but I have not seen one like him forsaken.*

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 17, verses 18–22:**

And the gift of your Lord has never been restricted.﴾ ﴿See how We have favored some of them over others, and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾ ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken.﴾

(p-460) The words of the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "Uff," nor rebuke them, but speak to them a generous word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small." Your Lord knows best what is in your souls; if you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him).﴾

"Qaḍā" (decreed) in this verse means: commanded, obligated, and made incumbent upon you. This is also what people have said. I say: the meaning is, "Your Lord has decreed His command, ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾," and these words contain nothing but a command to restrict worship to God alone. That is the thing decreed, not the act of worship itself. In the speech of the Arabs, "qaḍā" means to complete something and make it firm, and what is decreed here is the command.

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the word is "wa-waṣṣā" (and enjoined), and this is the recitation of his companions, of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Maymun ibn Mihran, and likewise it is found with Ubayy ibn Ka'b. al-Ḍaḥḥak said: "Among some people, 'waṣṣā' was mistakenly written as 'qaḍā' when the waw and the ṣad were confused at the time the codex was written."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. The recitation is transmitted through a chain of narration. Abu Hatim has mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, a statement like that of al-Ḍaḥḥak, and he said concerning Maymun ibn Mihran that he said: "Indeed, according to the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, there is a light," and God the Exalted said: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah and that which We revealed to you﴾ [al-Shura: 13]. Then Ibn Hatim deemed it unlikely that Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said that, and he said: "If we said this, the heretics would attack our codex."

The pronoun in "ta'budu" (you worship) refers to all of creation, and on this interpretation the early generations and the majority proceeded. A man asked al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, saying: "He divorced his wife three times." Al-Hasan said to him: "You have disobeyed your Lord, and your wife has become irrevocably separated from you by three." The man said: "That was decreed upon me." Al-Hasan said to him, and he was eloquent: "What God decreed is not what God commanded," and he recited this verse. People said: "Al-Hasan has spoken about predestination (qadar)."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that "qaḍā" retains its well-known meaning in speech, and that the pronoun in "ta'budu" refers to the believers among mankind until the Day of Resurrection. But on the first interpretation, His saying ﴿and to parents, goodness﴾ is a conjunction with the first "an" (that), meaning: God commanded that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. On this possibility that we have mentioned, His saying ﴿and to parents, goodness﴾ is detached from the first, for He informed them of the decree of God, blessed and exalted, and then commanded them to be good to their parents.

"Immā" (whether) is conditional. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read "yablughanna" (reach). It is narrated from Ibn Dhakwan "yablughan" with the nun lightened. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yablughān" (reach), and this is the recitation of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Yahya, Talha, al-A'mash, and al-Jahdari; here the nun is the heavy nun (nun al-tawkid) introduced for emphasis, and it is not the dual nun. So, according to the first two recitations, His saying "aḥaduhumā" (one of them) is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "yablughanna," and it is a partitive substitute (badal muqassim), like the words of the poet:

"I was like one with two legs: one healthy, and a man whom time struck, so it became paralyzed."

(p-462) It is also possible that "aḥaduhumā" is the subject (fa'il), and His saying ﴿or both of them﴾ is a conjunction with it, and this would be according to the dialect of the one who says "akalūnī al-barāghīth" (the fleas ate me). Some grammarians have mentioned this for this verse, but Sibawayh did not consider this dialect to have any place in the Noble Qur'an.

Abu 'Amr read "uffin" with a kasra on the fa' and without tanwin. This is the recitation of Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr. Nafi', al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and 'Isa read "uffin" with a kasra and tanwin. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "uffa" with a fatha on the fa'. Abu al-Sammal read "uffu" with a damma on the fa'. Ibn 'Abbas read "uffa" lightly. All of this is indeclinable (binā'), except that the recitation of Nafi' gives indefiniteness, as you say "ayhin" (an interjection of urging). There are dialects in which it was not recited: "uffun" with raf' and tanwin, which Harun related as a recitation; "uffan" with nasb and tanwin; "uffī" with a ya' after the kasra, related by al-Akhfash al-Kabir; "ufā" with an alif after the fatha; "uffa" with the fa' doubled and sukun; "uffu" like "rabb." Among the Arabs there are those who incline "ufā," and among them are those who add the silent hā' and say "ufāhu."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of the word is that it is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), as if one who wants to say "I am annoyed," or "I am disgusted," or "I dislike," or something similar, expresses it concisely with this word, which gives the meaning of the verb mentioned. God the Exalted made this word an example of everything that one might respond to parents with that they dislike. This word is not intended in itself; rather it is an example of what is greater and what is lesser. This is the meaning of the implicit address (mafhum al-khitab), whose ruling is the ruling of what is stated.

"Al-intihār" is the manifestation of anger in the voice and the wording. "Qawl karīm" (a generous word) is that which gathers excellences, of gentleness, goodness of meaning, and the inclusion of kindness, and this is like your saying "thawbun karīm" (a noble garment), meaning it has many excellences. "Al-uff" is the dirt under the fingernails. A group said: this word in the verse is derived from that. Mujahid said regarding His saying the Exalted ﹟so do not say to them "uff"﹟: its meaning is: when you see from them, in the state of old age, the excrement and urine that they saw from you in the state of childhood, do not be disgusted by them, and do not say "uff."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The verse is more general than this statement, and this is included in the totality of what it requires. Abu al-Sarraj al-Tujibi said: I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "Everything in the Qur'an about kindness to parents I have understood, except His saying ﹟And speak to them a generous word﹟. What is this generous word?" Ibn al-Musayyab said: "The word of a sinful servant to a harsh master."

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ is a metaphor, meaning: cut off from yourself the side of humiliation, and make yourself and your character gentle toward them. Mention of humiliation (dhull) is emphasized here, and it is not mentioned in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 215], and this is according to the greatness of the right here. The majority read "al-dhulli" with a damma on the dhal. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr read "al-dhili" with a kasra on the dhal. It is narrated from 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud. "Al-dhilu" (p-464) in animals is the opposite of "difficulty," and from it comes "the tame camel" (al-jamal al-dhalul). The meanings are close. By the ruling of this verse, a person should place himself with his parents in a state of humility in his words, his movements, and his gaze, and not fix his eyes sharply upon them, for that is the look of the angry person. In a hadith: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'May God distance him and destroy him.' They said: 'Who, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'One who reaches his parents, or one of them, and is not forgiven.'"

His saying the Exalted: ﴿from mercy﴾: "min" here is for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins), meaning that this lowering is from the mercy that is hidden within the soul, not that it be mere practice. It is also valid that it be for the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya).

Then God the Exalted commanded His servants to show mercy to their parents and to mention their favors upon them in raising them, so that remembering that state would increase a person in compassion for them and tenderness toward them. All of this concerns believing parents. The Qur'an has forbidden seeking forgiveness for dead polytheists, even if they were close relatives. It is mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas here the term "naskh" (abrogation), but this is not the place of abrogation.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾, meaning: of belief in mercy toward them and tenderness toward them, or other than that, and some make the outward show of their kindness into mere display (riya'). Then He, glorified and exalted, promised at the end of the verse forgiveness together with the condition of righteousness and turning back, after turning back to the obedience of God. The people's expressions differed concerning "al-awwabīn" (those who turn back). A group said: they are the reformers. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they are those who glorify God. He also said: they are the obedient, the doers of good. Ibn al-Munkadir said: they are those who pray the sunset and night prayers, because "the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked about the prayer at that time, and he said: 'That is the prayer of the awwabin.'"

(p-465) It has been said other than that, concerning those who seek forgiveness and the like. 'Awn al-'Uqayli said: they are those who pray the forenoon prayer (ṣalāt al-ḍuḥā). The literal meaning of the word is from "āba yu'awwibu," meaning he returned. All of these have a return to the obedience of God, blessed and exalted, but it is a word whose customary usage became specific to the righteous. Ibn al-Musayyab said: it is the servant who repents, then sins, then repents, then sins, then repents. The majority interpreted "al-awwabīn" as those returning to good. Ibn Jubayr said: by His saying "ghafūran lil-awwabīn" (Forgiving to those who turn back) He meant the slip and the lapse that a man commits toward one of his parents, when he did not persist in it in his heart, and God did not know it from him. A group said: "lowering the wing" is that one should not refuse anything that they desire of him.

A man asked al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, saying: "He divorced his wife three times." Al-Hasan said to him: "You have disobeyed your Lord, and your wife has become irrevocably separated from you by three." The man said: "That was decreed upon me." Al-Hasan said to him, and he was eloquent: "What God decreed is not what God commanded," and he recited this verse. People said: "Al-Hasan has spoken about predestination (qadar)."

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yablughān" (reach), and this is the recitation of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Yahya, Talha, al-A'mash, and al-Jahdari; here the nun is the heavy nun (nun al-tawkid) introduced for emphasis, and it is not the dual nun. "I was like one with two legs: one healthy, and a man whom time struck, so it became paralyzed."

Some grammarians have mentioned this for this verse, but Sibawayh did not consider this dialect to have any place in the Noble Qur'an.

Abu 'Amr read "uffin" with a kasra on the fa' and without tanwin. This is the recitation of Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr. Nafi', al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and 'Isa read "uffin" with a kasra and tanwin. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "uffa" with a fatha on the fa'. Abu al-Sammal read "uffu" with a damma on the fa'. Ibn 'Abbas read "uffa" lightly. All of this is indeclinable (binā'), except that the recitation of Nafi' gives indefiniteness, as you say "ayhin" (an interjection of urging). There are dialects in which it was not recited: "uffun" with raf' and tanwin, which Harun related as a recitation; "uffan" with nasb and tanwin; "uffī" with a ya' after the kasra, related by al-Akhfash al-Kabir; "ufā" with an alif after the fatha; "uffa" with the fa' doubled and sukun; "uffu" like "rabb." Among the Arabs there are those who incline "ufā," and among them are those who add the silent hā' and say "ufāhu."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of the word is that it is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), as if one who wants to say "I am annoyed," or "I am disgusted," or "I dislike," or something similar, expresses it concisely with this word, which gives the meaning of the verb mentioned. God the Exalted made this word an example of everything that one might respond to parents with that they dislike. This word is not intended in itself; rather it is an example of what is greater and what is lesser. This is the meaning of the implicit address (mafhum al-khitab), whose ruling is the ruling of what is stated.

"Al-intihār" is the manifestation of anger in the voice and the wording. "Qawl karīm" (a generous word) is that which gathers excellences, of gentleness, goodness of meaning, and the inclusion of kindness, and this is like your saying "thawbun karīm" (a noble garment), meaning it has many excellences. "Al-uff" is the dirt under the fingernails. A group said: this word in the verse is derived from that. Mujahid said regarding His saying the Exalted ﹟so do not say to them "uff"﹟: its meaning is: when you see from them, in the state of old age, the excrement and urine that they saw from you in the state of childhood, do not be disgusted by them, and do not say "uff."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The verse is more general than this statement, and this is included in the totality of what it requires. Abu al-Sarraj al-Tujibi said: I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "Everything in the Qur'an about kindness to parents I have understood, except His saying ﹟And speak to them a generous word﹟. What is this generous word?" Ibn al-Musayyab said: "The word of a sinful servant to a harsh master."

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ is a metaphor, meaning: cut off from yourself the side of humiliation, and make yourself and your character gentle toward them. Mention of humiliation (dhull) is emphasized here, and it is not mentioned in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And lower your wing to those who follow you among the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 215], and this is according to the greatness of the right here. The majority read "al-dhulli" with a damma on the dhal. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr read "al-dhili" with a kasra on the dhal. It is narrated from 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud. "Al-dhilu" (p-464) in animals is the opposite of "difficulty," and from it comes "the tame camel" (al-jamal al-dhalul). The meanings are close. By the ruling of this verse, a person should place himself with his parents in a state of humility in his words, his movements, and his gaze, and not fix his eyes sharply upon them, for that is the look of the angry person. In a hadith: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'May God distance him and destroy him.' They said: 'Who, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'One who reaches his parents, or one of them, and is not forgiven.'"

His saying the Exalted: ﴿from mercy﴾: "min" here is for specifying the kind (bayan al-jins), meaning that this lowering is from the mercy that is hidden within the soul, not that it be mere practice. It is also valid that it be for the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya).

Then God the Exalted commanded His servants to show mercy to their parents and to mention their favors upon them in raising them, so that remembering that state would increase a person in compassion for them and tenderness toward them. All of this concerns believing parents. The Qur'an has forbidden seeking forgiveness for dead polytheists, even if they were close relatives. It is mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas here the term "naskh" (abrogation), but this is not the place of abrogation.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾, meaning: of belief in mercy toward them and tenderness toward them, or other than that, and some make the outward show of their kindness into mere display (riya'). Then He, glorified and exalted, promised at the end of the verse forgiveness together with the condition of righteousness and turning back, after turning back to the obedience of God. The people's expressions differed concerning "al-awwabīn" (those who turn back). A group said: they are the reformers. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they are those who glorify God. He also said: they are the obedient, the doers of good. Ibn al-Munkadir said: they are those who pray the sunset and night prayers, because "the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked about the prayer at that time, and he said: 'That is the prayer of the awwabin.'"

(p-465) It has been said other than that, concerning those who seek forgiveness and the like. 'Awn al-'Uqayli said: they are those who pray the forenoon prayer (ṣalāt al-ḍuḥā). The literal meaning of the word is from "āba yu'awwibu," meaning he returned. All of these have a return to the obedience of God, blessed and exalted, but it is a word whose customary usage became specific to the righteous. Ibn al-Musayyab said: it is the servant who repents, then sins, then repents, then sins, then repents. The majority interpreted "al-awwabīn" as those returning to good. Ibn Jubayr said: by His saying "ghafūran lil-awwabīn" (Forgiving to those who turn back) He meant the slip and the lapse that a man commits toward one of his parents, when he did not persist in it in his heart, and God did not know it from him. A group said: "lowering the wing" is that one should not refuse anything that they desire of him.

(p-460) The words of the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to your parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "Uff," nor rebuke them, but speak to them a generous word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small." Your Lord knows best what is in your souls; if you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him).﴾

I say: the meaning is, "Your Lord has decreed His command, ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾," and these words contain nothing but a command to restrict worship to God alone. That is the thing decreed, not the act of worship itself. In the speech of the Arabs, "qaḍā" means to complete something and make it firm, and what is decreed here is the command.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 26–30:

The Almighty and Majestic said:

﴿Give the near of kin his due, and the needy and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the wasteful are brothers of the devils, and the devil has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word.﴾ ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is ever Aware of His servants, Seeing.﴾

The commentators differed concerning "dhi al-qurba" (the near of kin). The majority said: the verse is an injunction to all people to maintain the ties of kinship. The Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed with it, and the intended meaning is the community (ummah). "Haqq" (due right) in this verse is what becomes obligatory through maintaining the ties of kinship, meeting needs, and comforting with wealth and help in every way when there is need. Al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Ibn 'Abbas and others said something similar. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn said concerning this: they are the relatives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to give them their rights from the public treasury (bayt al-mal).

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The first opinion is clearer, and it is supported by the conjunction with "the needy and the wayfarer." "Ibn al-sabil" (the wayfarer) here includes both the rich and the poor, since each of them has a right, even if they differ. "Ibn al-sabil" in the verse on charity (zakat) is more specific.

"Tabdhir" (wasteful squandering) is spending wealth in corruption, or in extravagance in what is permissible. It derives from "badhr" (seed-scattering). The word of the Exalted, "the wasteful" (al-mubadhdhirin), may be a generic noun, and it may mean specifically the people of Makkah; al-Naqqash mentioned this. The word of the Exalted "brothers" (ikhwan) means that they are in the same judgment, since the squanderer strives in corruption and the devil always strives in corruption. "Ikhwan" is the plural of "akh" (brother) by means other than lineage, and it may occasionally deviate from this usage. An example is the word of the Exalted in Surah al-Nur: ﴿or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers﴾ [al-Nur 24:31]. "Ikhwah" is the plural of "akh" in lineage, and it too may deviate. An example is the word of the Exalted: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:10]. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "brother of the devil" in the singular (ikhwan al-shaytan written as akhu), and it is likewise established in the codex of Anas ibn Malik. Then the Blessed and Exalted mentioned the disbelief of the devil, so that the warning against imitating him in corruption would be comprehensive and clear.

The word of the Exalted: ﴿And if you turn away﴾, the verse. The pronoun in "from them" refers to those mentioned earlier, namely the needy and the wayfarers. Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) in this verse: if one of them asks him and he does not find anything to give, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would respond with turning away, out of courtesy, so as not to explicitly reject him, and while awaiting provision from Allah the Exalted that would come and from which he would give. [The command is] that he should comfort him with gentle speech, which is that in which there is hope in the bounty of Allah, comfort with a good promise, and supplication for Allah the Exalted's expansion and giving. It is related that he (ﷺ), after the revelation of this verse, when he had nothing to give, would say: "May Allah provide for us and for you from His bounty." So mercy, according to this interpretation, is the awaited provision. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah. Ibn Zayd said: mercy is reward and recompense. The verse was revealed concerning people who used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he would refuse to give them, because he knew they would spend wealth in corruption. So he would turn away from them, desiring reward in withholding from them, lest he assist them in their corruption. Then Allah the Blessed and Exalted commanded him to say to them a gentle word that includes supplication for their opening (of provision) and their reform.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Some of the people of the first interpretation said: the verse was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir and his category. "Al-maysur" (the gentle) is a passive participle from the word "yusr" (ease). You say: "yassartu laka kadha" (I prepared such-and-such for you) when you have readied it.

The word of the Exalted: ﴿And do not make your hand chained﴾, the verse. It is related from Qaloon: "kalla al-busti" with the sad (ص) letter, and al-A'sha narrated it from Abu Bakr. "Al-ghull ila al-'unuq" (the chain to the neck) is borrowed for a hand that is withheld from spending, characterized by miserliness. And the hand that exhausts all that it has, reaching the utmost extension, is the opposite of the chain, and all this concerns spending on good. As for spending on corruption, its little and its much are forbidden.

This verse is connected to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The example of the miser and the one who gives charity..." the hadith in its entirety. The blame here applies to one who asks from those who deserve but finds nothing to give. "Al-mahsur" is the one who has been made incapable, whose strength has been exhausted. You say: "hasartu al-ba'ir" (I wearied the camel) when you tire it until it has no strength left, so it is "hasir" (exhausted). From this is the verse of the poet:

*Their trotting has exhausted them in the travel by night, and among them one that rises and is still exhausted.*

From this also: "al-basar al-hasir," meaning the weary sight, which is fatigued. Ibn Jurayj and others said regarding the meaning of this verse: do not withhold from spending in what I have commanded you of the right, and do not extend it fully in what I have forbidden you from. Qatadah said: "tabdhir" is spending in disobedience. Mujahid said: if a person spends all his wealth on a right matter, it is not tabdhir; and if he spends a mudd (a small measure) in falsehood, it is tabdhir.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This requires consideration. "Al-bast" (extension) does not imply a meaning that has not been permitted in that which is forbidden, and it is not said about disobedience: "and do not squander," but rather it is said: "and do not spend, even with moderation and balance." How excellent is the understanding of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them both), for they said: "Tabdhir is spending in other than what is right." This expression encompasses disobedience and permissible extravagance. This verse only alerts to exerting full effort in what first arises from the requests of believers, lest there remain after that one who comes with nothing, and lest the spender neglect his dependents, and the like. From the words of wisdom: "I have never seen extravagance except that with it there was a neglected right." These are verses of "fiqh al-hal" (understanding of circumstances), and their ruling is not clarified except by considering the particular person among people.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills﴾, the meaning is: O Muhammad, be upon what has been prescribed for you of moderation and spending with balance, and let not the poverty of those you see like that concern you, for they are under the sight of Allah, His hearing, and His will. "Yaqdiru" (restricts) means: He straitens.

Some of the people of the first interpretation said: the verse was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir and his category. "Al-maysur" (the gentle) is a passive participle from the word "yusr" (ease). You say: "yassartu laka kadha" (I prepared such-and-such for you) when you have readied it.

The word of the Exalted: ﴿And do not make your hand chained﴾, the verse. It is related from Qaloon: "kalla al-busti" with the sad (ص) letter, and al-A'sha narrated it from Abu Bakr. "Al-ghull ila al-'unuq" (the chain to the neck) is borrowed for a hand that is withheld from spending, characterized by miserliness. And the hand that exhausts all that it has, reaching the utmost extension, is the opposite of the chain, and all this concerns spending on good. As for spending on corruption, its little and its much are forbidden.

This verse is connected to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The example of the miser and the one who gives charity..." the hadith in its entirety. The blame here applies to one who asks from those who deserve but finds nothing to give. "Al-mahsur" is the one who has been made incapable, whose strength has been exhausted. You say: "hasartu al-ba'ir" (I wearied the camel) when you tire it until it has no strength left, so it is "hasir" (exhausted). From this is the verse of the poet:

*Their trotting has exhausted them in the travel by night, and among them one that rises and is still exhausted.*

From this also: "al-basar al-hasir," meaning the weary sight, which is fatigued. Ibn Jurayj and others said regarding the meaning of this verse: do not withhold from spending in what I have commanded you of the right, and do not extend it fully in what I have forbidden you from. Qatadah said: "tabdhir" is spending in disobedience. Mujahid said: if a person spends all his wealth on a right matter, it is not tabdhir; and if he spends a mudd (a small measure) in falsehood, it is tabdhir.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This requires consideration. "Al-bast" (extension) does not imply a meaning that has not been permitted in that which is forbidden, and it is not said about disobedience: "and do not squander," but rather it is said: "and do not spend, even with moderation and balance." How excellent is the understanding of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them both), for they said: "Tabdhir is spending in other than what is right." This expression encompasses disobedience and permissible extravagance. This verse only alerts to exerting full effort in what first arises from the requests of believers, lest there remain after that one who comes with nothing, and lest the spender neglect his dependents, and the like. From the words of wisdom: "I have never seen extravagance except that with it there was a neglected right." These are verses of "fiqh al-hal" (understanding of circumstances), and their ruling is not clarified except by considering the particular person among people.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills﴾, the meaning is: O Muhammad, be upon what has been prescribed for you of moderation and spending with balance, and let not the poverty of those you see like that concern you, for they are under the sight of Allah, His hearing, and His will. "Yaqdiru" (restricts) means: He straitens.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Aware of His servants, Seeing﴾, that is: He knows the benefit of one people in poverty, and He knows the benefit of others in wealth. Some exegetes, and al-Tabari related it, said: the verse is an allusion to the state of the Arabs, whom poverty would reform, and when they were satisfied they would transgress, kill others, and raid; and when hunger and famine occurred, it occupied them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 31–33:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is ever a great sin.﴾ ﴿And do not approach fornication. Indeed, it is an abomination and an evil way.﴾ ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing. Indeed, he is ever supported.﴾

al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read: "wa-la tuqattilu" with the verb doubled (intensive form).

This verse is a prohibition against wa'd (burying infant daughters alive), which the Arabs used to practise, as in His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And when the buried infant girl is asked﴾ [al-Takwir: 8]. It is said that their ignorance reached the point that one of them would starve his dog and kill his child. "Khashyata" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). "Al-imlaq" means poverty and lack of wealth; amlaqa al-rajul means the man has nothing left except the malaqat, which are large, smooth, black stones.

al-Jumhur read: "khit'an" with a kasra on the kha' and a sukun on the ta', with hamza and qasr (short vowel). Ibn 'Amir read: "khata'an" with a fatha on the kha' and the ta', with the hamza short (maqsurah). This is the reading of Abu Ja'far. These two readings are derived from khati'a (to commit a sin deliberately), so it is like hidhr/hadhar, mithl/mathal, shibh/shabah, which are both noun and verbal noun. From this is the poet's saying:

"Error is an abomination, and righteousness is a supererogatory act, like a date-cluster planted in the ground that is grafted."

al-Zajjaj said: khati'a al-rajul yakhta'u khit'an, like atham yata'thamu ith'man; this is the verbal noun, and khata'a is a noun derived from it. Some scholars said: khati'a means to commit the sin with intent, while akhta'a means to commit it without intent, and from it is His the Exalted's saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget or make mistake﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this may take the place of that and that the place of this, so akhta'a is used in the sense of ta'ammada (to intend), in the poet's saying:

"Your servants err, and You are a Lord, generous; reproach does not befit You."

And khuti'a is used in the sense of not intending, in the saying of another:

"People blame the commander when they err in what is right, and the guide is not blamed."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, the reading "khat'an" with a fatha on the kha', sukun on the ta', and hamza. Ibn Kathir read: "khita'an" with a kasra on the kha', fatha on the ta', and extended hamza. This is the reading of al-A'raj in one narration, and Talhah, Shibl, al-A'mash, 'Isa, Khalid ibn Ilyas, Qatadah, and al-Hasan in one narration. al-Nahhas said: I do not know a valid basis for this reading, and Abu Hatim likewise considered it an error. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is a verbal noun of khata'a yukhati'u, although we have not found khata'a, but we have found takhata'a, which is the intransitive form of khata'a, and it points to it. From it is the poet's saying:

"The arrows missed his insides, and delayed my day, so I was not hasty."

And another's saying describing a truffle:

"The hunter missed it until I found it, and its snout was sunk in the water's pool."

It is as if those who kill their children are missing the truth and justice. al-Hasan, as is narrated from him, read: "khata'an" with fatha on the kha' and ta', and extension on the hamza. Abu Hatim said: this is not known in the language, it is an unacceptable error, and it is not as Abu Hatim said. Abu al-Fath said: al-khata' from "akhta'at" is like al-ata' from "a'tayt"; it is a noun in the sense of the verbal noun. al-Hasan (in one narration) read: "khata'an" with fatha on the kha' and ta', tanwin, without hamza. Abu Raja' and al-Zuhri read: "khita'an" with kasra on the kha' and fatha on the ta', like the one before it; these two are abbreviated forms of khata'an and khit'a'.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ is a prohibition. Al-zina may be pronounced with a long or short vowel; the short form is the Qur'anic usage and the language of the whole Book of Allah. From the long form is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Abu Hazim, whoever commits zina is known by his zina, and whoever drinks the intoxicant wakes up drunk."

It is also narrated as "Abu Khalid." Al-fahisha is that which is hidden from among the sins because of its ugliness.

"Sabilan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz); the implied meaning is: "and evil is its way as a way," i.e., because it leads to the Fire.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And do not kill﴾ and the verbs before it are in the jussive mood by way of prohibition.

al-Tabari held that these are coordinated with His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. The first view is more correct and more eloquent in meaning.

The alif and lam in "al-nafs" are for the genus. The "haqq" by which a soul is killed is what the Prophet ﷺ explained in his saying: "The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, zina after marriage, or killing a soul."

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Connected to these are matters that return to them. Among them is highway robbery, since it has the meaning of killing a soul, and it is hirabah. Among them is zandaqah. Among them is the question of abandoning prayer, since it has the meaning of disbelief after faith. Among them is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, killing those who withheld zakat, and the killing of those in cities who refuse communal obligations (fard al-kifayah).

His the Exalted's saying: "mazluman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and its meaning is: other than these mentioned aspects.

"Al-wali" is the one who holds the right to the blood, and it is the one who is the son of the deceased, or whose son is the deceased, or who shares with him a common father. According to a group of scholars, women have no part in guardianship of blood, while others hold that they do. "Al-sultan" means the proof, and the authority given to him to choose between accepting blood-money (diyah) or pardoning, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. Qatadah said: "al-sultan" is retaliation (qawd).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read: "fa-la yusrif" with the yā', and this is the reading of the majority, meaning the wali does not transgress God's command. Transgression is that he kills someone other than the killer from among the rest of the tribe, or kills two for one, and other forms of transgression. All of this the Arabs used to do, therefore the warning against it occurred. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the most rebellious of people against Allah are three: a man who kills someone other than his killer, or kills in the manner of the Jahiliyyah (dahan al-jahiliyyah), or kills in the sanctuary of Allah." Another group said: the meaning of His saying: ﴿fa-la yusrif﴾ is the killer whom the speech implies, and the meaning is: let none of the transgressors be one who kills a soul, for it falls within the context of this ruling. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-la tusrif" with the tā' from above, and this is the reading of Hudhayfah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Mujahid (in one narration), and al-A'mash and a group. al-Tabari said: in the sense of address to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and to his community after him, meaning: do not kill other than the killer.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also valid that it refers to the wali, meaning: do not transgress, O wali, in killing anyone within the scope of this ruling. Abu Muslim al-Sarraj, companion of the Abbasid call, read: "fa-la yusrifu" with a damma on the fa', as a statement of fact rather than a prohibition. According to this interpretation, the intended person is the wali alone.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is scrutiny in citing Abu Muslim as a source for this reading. In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "fa-la tusrifu fi al-qatl, inna wali al-maqtul kana mansuran" (do not transgress in killing; indeed the guardian of the one slain was supported). The pronoun in His saying: "innahu" refers to the wali, and it was said: to the one slain. This is, in my view, the most preferred of the opinions, because he is the wronged party, and the word "nasr" (support) always stands opposite to "zulm" (oppression), as in His, upon Him be blessings and peace, saying: "Support of the oppressed and fulfilment of oaths," and his saying ﷺ: "Support your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed," along with many other examples. It was also said: it refers to the killing; and Abu 'Ubayd said: it refers to the killer, since if he is killed in this world and thereby saved from the punishment of the Hereafter, then he has been supported.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak and far from the intended meaning.

al-Dahhak said: this is the first thing revealed in the Qur'an concerning killing, and it is Meccan.

al-Tabari held that these are coordinated with His saying: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. The first view is more correct and more eloquent in meaning.

The alif and lam in "al-nafs" are for the genus. The "haqq" by which a soul is killed is what the Prophet ﷺ explained in his saying: "The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, zina after marriage, or killing a soul."

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Connected to these are matters that return to them. Among them is highway robbery, since it has the meaning of killing a soul, and it is hirabah. Among them is zandaqah. Among them is the question of abandoning prayer, since it has the meaning of disbelief after faith. Among them is Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, killing those who withheld zakat, and the killing of those in cities who refuse communal obligations (fard al-kifayah).

His the Exalted's saying: "mazluman" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and its meaning is: other than these mentioned aspects.

"Al-wali" is the one who holds the right to the blood, and it is the one who is the son of the deceased, or whose son is the deceased, or who shares with him a common father. According to a group of scholars, women have no part in guardianship of blood, while others hold that they do. "Al-sultan" means the proof, and the authority given to him to choose between accepting blood-money (diyah) or pardoning, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. Qatadah said: "al-sultan" is retaliation (qawd).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim read: "fa-la yusrif" with the yā', and this is the reading of the majority, meaning the wali does not transgress God's command. Transgression is that he kills someone other than the killer from among the rest of the tribe, or kills two for one, and other forms of transgression. All of this the Arabs used to do, therefore the warning against it occurred. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the most rebellious of people against Allah are three: a man who kills someone other than his killer, or kills in the manner of the Jahiliyyah (dahan al-jahiliyyah), or kills in the sanctuary of Allah." Another group said: the meaning of His saying: ﴿fa-la yusrif﴾ is the killer whom the speech implies, and the meaning is: let none of the transgressors be one who kills a soul, for it falls within the context of this ruling. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-la tusrif" with the tā' from above, and this is the reading of Hudhayfah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Mujahid (in one narration), and al-A'mash and a group. al-Tabari said: in the sense of address to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and to his community after him, meaning: do not kill other than the killer.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also valid that it refers to the wali, meaning: do not transgress, O wali, in killing anyone within the scope of this ruling. Abu Muslim al-Sarraj, companion of the Abbasid call, read: "fa-la yusrifu" with a damma on the fa', as a statement of fact rather than a prohibition. According to this interpretation, the intended person is the wali alone.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is scrutiny in citing Abu Muslim as a source for this reading. In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "fa-la tusrifu fi al-qatl, inna wali al-maqtul kana mansuran" (do not transgress in killing; indeed the guardian of the one slain was supported). The pronoun in His saying: "innahu" refers to the wali, and it was said: to the one slain. This is, in my view, the most preferred of the opinions, because he is the wronged party, and the word "nasr" (support) always stands opposite to "zulm" (oppression), as in His, upon Him be blessings and peace, saying: "Support of the oppressed and fulfilment of oaths," and his saying ﷺ: "Support your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed," along with many other examples. It was also said: it refers to the killing; and Abu 'Ubayd said: it refers to the killer, since if he is killed in this world and thereby saved from the punishment of the Hereafter, then he has been supported.

al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak and far from the intended meaning.

al-Dahhak said: this is the first thing revealed in the Qur'an concerning killing, and it is Meccan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 34–36:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches his maturity. And fulfil the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned.﴾ ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true balance. That is better and more suitable in outcome.﴾ ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned.﴾

The address in this verse is to the guardians (awsiya', plural of wasi) who are appointed to be near the property of the orphan. Then it also applies to whoever becomes involved in some matter of theirs without being a guardian. "Yatim" (orphan) means a child who is alone among his parents; al-yutm means solitariness. It is said: "yatima al-sabiyy yaytamu" when a child loses his father. Ibn al-Sikkit said: orphanhood among humans is from the father's side, and among animals from the mother's side. In the book of al-Mawardi: orphanhood among humans is also from the mother's side. The plural of yatim is aytam, like sharif and ashraf, and shahid and ashhad. It is also pluralised as yatama, like asir and asara, as if they are in the disliked matters that overcome a person. Ibn Sida said: Ibn al-A'rabi related "yatman" as a form of "yatim", and cited in this regard:

؎ So I spent the night roasting my little child and my wife, tender, while the wolf's cub, an orphan, was hungry.

It is possible that "yatama" is the plural of "yatman". In a hadith: "There is no orphanhood after puberty (hulm)." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except in the best manner﴾ means: except in the best of conditions.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That applies to a wealthy guardian: that he should develop the wealth and safeguard it, and not withhold any of it for the purpose of benefiting from it. This is the ideal of scrupulousness (wara'), and the better course is that he should not be occupied with the orphan's property and be stingy with it; the jurisprudential ruling is that you assign him a wage. As for the poor guardian whose occupation with the orphan's property keeps him from his livelihood, the people differed (p-475) about how he may eat from it in a reasonable manner. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he may borrow from it, and when he becomes well-off he repays it. Ibn al-Musayyab said: he should not drink water from the orphan's property. It was said: then what is the meaning of ﴿let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [an-Nisa: 6]? He said: that is only for his service and washing his garment. Mujahid said: he should not approach it except through trade, and should not borrow from it. He said: the Exalted's saying ﴿let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [an-Nisa: 6] refers to his own property. Abu Yusuf said: perhaps His saying ﴿let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [an-Nisa: 6] has been abrogated by His saying ﴿Do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [an-Nisa: 29]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he may eat from it a sip of milk, a taste of fruit, and the like of what serves him, and he may repair the pond, pick the dates, and search for a lost animal, and he eats without harming the offspring or excessively milking. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he eats from it with the tips of his fingers, a sustenance from his labour.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a metaphor for minimal use. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others said: he takes a wage from it according to the measure of his labour, and all of these fall within what is "best." The full explanation of these meanings is in Surat an-Nisa according to the wording of those verses. It is reported from Qatada that when this verse was revealed it was difficult for the Muslims, and they avoided eating with orphans in the same dish, so there was revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers; and Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqara: 220].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾ is the limit of withholding from the orphan's property. Then, beyond this limit, another verse has laid down the ruling. What lies beyond these limits always remains suspended until a legal proof is established regarding it, or equity in the particular case requires otherwise. A similar case is the saying of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "I myself twisted the garlands for the offering of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with my own hand, and sent them off, and nothing became forbidden to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Allah had made lawful for him until he sacrificed the offering."

And "al-ashudd": according to Sibawayh it is the plural of (shadd); Abu 'Ubayda said: it has no singular from its own form. Its meaning is his strength in intellect, experience, and judgement for himself, and that does not occur except with puberty. So "al-ashudd" in the school of Malik is the coupling of puberty with wet dreams or what stands in their place, according to the difference of opinion on this, and "rushd" refers to property. It has been disputed whether soundness of religion is among the conditions of that rushd, on two views: Ibn al-Qasim does not take it into account if he is competent with his property, while some of Malik's companions took it into account. The school of Abu Hanifa holds that al-ashudd is puberty alone, so there is no restriction on a mature person unless he is known for foolishness.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I am not confident in this restriction in His saying.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: al-ashudd in His saying is that the child reaches eighteen years.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He meant that this is one of what has been said regarding the limit of puberty for one who does not experience wet dreams. As for his being mature and sound of judgement so that his property is not handed to him until he reaches this period, that is a thing I do not know anyone saying.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾ is a general term for every covenant and contract between a person and his Lord, or between him and the created beings in obedience. His saying: ﴿indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾ means: it will be demanded from the one to whom it was entrusted or with whom it was made, whether he fulfilled it or not.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾, the verse. In this verse Allah commands the people of trade of weighing and measuring to give the right in their measuring and weighing. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he would stand in the market and say: "O assembly of clients, you have been entrusted with two matters by which the people before you were destroyed: this measure and this balance."

(p-477) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse implies that the measuring is the duty of the seller, since the buyer is not told "give full measure"; this is the apparent meaning of the wording and what is foremost from it. "Qistas": al-Hasan said it is the qabban (steelyard balance). It is also said qaffan, and it is al-qasitun, and it is said qartasun. It was said: al-qistas is a balance, small or large. Mujahid said: al-qistas is justice, and he used to say: it is a Roman word, as if the people were told: weigh with justice in your weighing. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr) read "al-qusṭas" with a ḍamma on the qaf; Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "al-qistas" with a kasra; both are dialects, and the word, from qist, is an intensive form, and what is meant in the verse is the class of just balances in whatever form they may be.

Abu Hatim said: "Only the people of Kufa read with a kasra on the qaf, and any reading that does not go beyond Kufa to the two Harams and Basra, then do not read it." And a group read "al-qisṭas" with a ṣad.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Mujahid's view on this, and on the Scale of the Resurrection, and on all of that, was that they are metaphors for justice; but his saying "the Scale of the Resurrection" is rejected, and the creed of the People of the Sunna is that it is a scale with a pillar and two pans. I heard my father, may Allah be pleased with him, say: I saw the preacher Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari in the mosque of 'Amr ibn al-'As preaching to the people about weighing, and he said in the course of his speech: the shape of the hand with the balance is an admonition, for the fingers form the shape of the written letters: alif, lam, mim, ha', so it is as if the balance says: Allah, Allah.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a beautiful admonition.

"Ta'wil" in this verse means outcome (ma'al), said by Qatada, and it is possible that "ta'wil" is a verbal noun of ta'awwala, meaning: good will be made to come about for you (yata'awwalu 'alaykum al-khayr) in all your affairs when you act well in measuring and weighing.

(p-478) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The purpose of measuring and weighing is to seek out the truth. If a person, after seeking it, is overcome by a slight, unintended, rare deficiency, then that is a trifle whose sin is lifted from him, since avoiding it is not within one's capacity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not pursue (laa taqfu)﴾ means: do not say and do not follow.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Yet it is a word used for slander and for admonition. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We are the sons of an-Nadr; we do not defame our mother nor disown our father." And you say: "so-and-so is my qifwa", meaning the object of my accusation. And you say: "Many a listener has heard my excuse but has not heard my qifwa", meaning what I was accused of; this is a proverb for one who divulges his secret and then apologises for a wrong that the one he apologises to did not hear of. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Mujahid: ﴿laa taqfu﴾ means: do not throw (accusation). From this word is the saying of the poet:

؎ Like dolls, lofty of noble bearing, they dwell, modesty among them; they do not stir up accusations.

(p-479) And al-Kumayt said:

؎ I do not hurl at the innocent without fault, nor do I follow the traces of the women who are guarded, if they are guarded.

The root of this word is from following a trace; you say: "qafawtu al-athar" (I followed the trace). It seems that this is from "al-qafa" (the back of the head/neck), and from it comes qafiyat al-shi'r (the rhyme of poetry), because it follows the verse (taqfu al-bayt). You also say: "quftu al-athar", and from this is al-qa'if (the tracker). And you say: "fuqtu al-athar" with the fa' placed before the qaf; it seems that this is one of the Arabs' playfulness with some words, as they said "ra'mli" for "la'amri". Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: qafa and qaf, like 'ata and 'at. So the meaning of the verse is: do not let your tongue follow what you have no knowledge of in speech. Mundhir ibn Sa'id held that qafa and qaf are like jadhaba and jabadha. So this verse, in sum, forbids false speech, slander, and what resembles that of corrupt and lying words.

The majority read: "wa-laa taqfu". Some people, as related by al-Kisa'i, read: "wa-laa taqufu" with a ḍamma on the qaf and a sukun on the fa'.

Al-Jarrah read "wal-fawad" with a fatha on the fa', which is a dialect; Abu Hatim and others denied it. He expressed "the hearing, the sight, and the heart" with "ulaika" because they are senses that have perception, and He made them questioned in this verse, so they have the state of one who understands; therefore He expressed them with "ulaika". Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding the Exalted's saying ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]: he said "ra'aytuhum" for the stars because when He described them with prostration, which is an act of one who understands, He referred to them with the pronoun of one who understands. Al-Zajjaj related that the Arabs express what is understood and what is not understood with the verb of perception, and he and al-Tabari cited:

؎ He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and the life after those days.

As for Abu Ishaq's report about the language, it is a matter to be held in suspense. As for the verse, the transmitted reading is "al-aqwam" (the peoples). The pronoun in "'anhu" returns to what a person has no knowledge of, and the meaning is: Allah the Exalted questions a person's hearing, sight, and heart about what he uttered of what he had no knowledge of, so his denial comes from his own limbs, and that is the utmost disgrace. It is also possible that the pronoun in "'anhu" returns to "kullu", which refers to the hearing, sight, and heart, and the meaning is: Allah the Exalted questions the person about what his hearing, sight, and heart contained, as if He said: all of these, the person will be questioned about them, that is, about what these faculties perceived and what sins occurred through them. So the implied phrase is "about their deeds", and it is by elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf).

؎ He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and the life after those days.

So the implied phrase is "about their deeds", and it is by elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 34–36:

The Almighty's saying:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches his maturity. And fulfil the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned.﴾ ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true balance. That is better and more suitable in outcome.﴾ ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned.﴾

The address in this verse is to the guardians (awsiya', plural of wasi) who are appointed to be near the property of the orphan. Then it also applies to whoever becomes involved in some matter of theirs without being a guardian. "Yatim" (orphan) means a child who is alone among his parents; al-yutm means solitariness. It is said: "yatima al-sabiyy yaytamu" when a child loses his father. Ibn al-Sikkit said: orphanhood among humans is from the father's side, and among animals from the mother's side. In the book of al-Mawardi: orphanhood among humans is also from the mother's side. The plural of yatim is aytam, like sharif and ashraf, and shahid and ashhad. It is also pluralised as yatama, like asir and asara, as if they are in the disliked matters that overcome a person. Ibn Sida said: Ibn al-A'rabi related "yatman" as a form of "yatim", and cited in this regard:

؎ So I spent the night roasting my little child and my wife, tender, while the wolf's cub, an orphan, was hungry.

It is possible that "yatama" is the plural of "yatman". In a hadith: "There is no orphanhood after puberty (hulm)." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except in the best manner﴾ means: except in the best of conditions.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That applies to a wealthy guardian: that he should develop the wealth and safeguard it, and not withhold any of it for the purpose of benefiting from it. This is the ideal of scrupulousness (wara'), and the better course is that he should not be occupied with the orphan's property and be stingy with it; the jurisprudential ruling is that you assign him a wage. As for the poor guardian whose occupation with the orphan's property keeps him from his livelihood, the people differed (p-475) about how he may eat from it in a reasonable manner. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he may borrow from it, and when he becomes well-off he repays it. Ibn al-Musayyab said: he should not drink water from the orphan's property. It was said: then what is the meaning of ﴿let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [an-Nisa: 6]? He said: that is only for his service and washing his garment. Mujahid said: he should not approach it except through trade, and should not borrow from it. He said: the Exalted's saying ﴿let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [an-Nisa: 6] refers to his own property. Abu Yusuf said: perhaps His saying ﴿let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [an-Nisa: 6] has been abrogated by His saying ﴿Do not consume your properties among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [an-Nisa: 29]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he may eat from it a sip of milk, a taste of fruit, and the like of what serves him, and he may repair the pond, pick the dates, and search for a lost animal, and he eats without harming the offspring or excessively milking. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he eats from it with the tips of his fingers, a sustenance from his labour.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a metaphor for minimal use. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and others said: he takes a wage from it according to the measure of his labour, and all of these fall within what is "best." The full explanation of these meanings is in Surat an-Nisa according to the wording of those verses. It is reported from Qatada that when this verse was revealed it was difficult for the Muslims, and they avoided eating with orphans in the same dish, so there was revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers; and Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqara: 220].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾ is the limit of withholding from the orphan's property. Then, beyond this limit, another verse has laid down the ruling. What lies beyond these limits always remains suspended until a legal proof is established regarding it, or equity in the particular case requires otherwise. A similar case is the saying of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "I myself twisted the garlands for the offering of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with my own hand, and sent them off, and nothing became forbidden to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Allah had made lawful for him until he sacrificed the offering."

And "al-ashudd": according to Sibawayh it is the plural of (shadd); Abu 'Ubayda said: it has no singular from its own form. Its meaning is his strength in intellect, experience, and judgement for himself, and that does not occur except with puberty. So "al-ashudd" in the school of Malik is the coupling of puberty with wet dreams or what stands in their place, according to the difference of opinion on this, and "rushd" refers to property. It has been disputed whether soundness of religion is among the conditions of that rushd, on two views: Ibn al-Qasim does not take it into account if he is competent with his property, while some of Malik's companions took it into account. The school of Abu Hanifa holds that al-ashudd is puberty alone, so there is no restriction on a mature person unless he is known for foolishness.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I am not confident in this restriction in His saying.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: al-ashudd in His saying is that the child reaches eighteen years.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He meant that this is one of what has been said regarding the limit of puberty for one who does not experience wet dreams. As for his being mature and sound of judgement so that his property is not handed to him until he reaches this period, that is a thing I do not know anyone saying.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾ is a general term for every covenant and contract between a person and his Lord, or between him and the created beings in obedience. His saying: ﴿indeed, the covenant will be questioned﴾ means: it will be demanded from the one to whom it was entrusted or with whom it was made, whether he fulfilled it or not.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾, the verse. In this verse Allah commands the people of trade of weighing and measuring to give the right in their measuring and weighing. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he would stand in the market and say: "O assembly of clients, you have been entrusted with two matters by which the people before you were destroyed: this measure and this balance."

(p-477) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse implies that the measuring is the duty of the seller, since the buyer is not told "give full measure"; this is the apparent meaning of the wording and what is foremost from it. "Qistas": al-Hasan said it is the qabban (steelyard balance). It is also said qaffan, and it is al-qasitun, and it is said qartasun. It was said: al-qistas is a balance, small or large. Mujahid said: al-qistas is justice, and he used to say: it is a Roman word, as if the people were told: weigh with justice in your weighing. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr) read "al-qusṭas" with a ḍamma on the qaf; Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "al-qistas" with a kasra; both are dialects, and the word, from qist, is an intensive form, and what is meant in the verse is the class of just balances in whatever form they may be.

Abu Hatim said: "Only the people of Kufa read with a kasra on the qaf, and any reading that does not go beyond Kufa to the two Harams and Basra, then do not read it." And a group read "al-qisṭas" with a ṣad.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Mujahid's view on this, and on the Scale of the Resurrection, and on all of that, was that they are metaphors for justice; but his saying "the Scale of the Resurrection" is rejected, and the creed of the People of the Sunna is that it is a scale with a pillar and two pans. I heard my father, may Allah be pleased with him, say: I saw the preacher Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari in the mosque of 'Amr ibn al-'As preaching to the people about weighing, and he said in the course of his speech: the shape of the hand with the balance is an admonition, for the fingers form the shape of the written letters: alif, lam, mim, ha', so it is as if the balance says: Allah, Allah.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a beautiful admonition.

"Ta'wil" in this verse means outcome (ma'al), said by Qatada, and it is possible that "ta'wil" is a verbal noun of ta'awwala, meaning: good will be made to come about for you (yata'awwalu 'alaykum al-khayr) in all your affairs when you act well in measuring and weighing.

(p-478) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The purpose of measuring and weighing is to seek out the truth. If a person, after seeking it, is overcome by a slight, unintended, rare deficiency, then that is a trifle whose sin is lifted from him, since avoiding it is not within one's capacity.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not pursue (laa taqfu)﴾ means: do not say and do not follow.
