Yet it is a word used for slander and for admonition. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We are the sons of an-Nadr; we do not defame our mother nor disown our father." And you say: "so-and-so is my qifwa", meaning the object of my accusation. And you say: "Many a listener has heard my excuse but has not heard my qifwa", meaning what I was accused of; this is a proverb for one who divulges his secret and then apologises for a wrong that the one he apologises to did not hear of. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Mujahid: ﴿laa taqfu﴾ means: do not throw (accusation). From this word is the saying of the poet:

؎ Like dolls, lofty of noble bearing, they dwell, modesty among them; they do not stir up accusations.

(p-479) And al-Kumayt said:

؎ I do not hurl at the innocent without fault, nor do I follow the traces of the women who are guarded, if they are guarded.

The root of this word is from following a trace; you say: "qafawtu al-athar" (I followed the trace). It seems that this is from "al-qafa" (the back of the head/neck), and from it comes qafiyat al-shi'r (the rhyme of poetry), because it follows the verse (taqfu al-bayt). You also say: "quftu al-athar", and from this is al-qa'if (the tracker). وقوله عزّ وجلّ:

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height.﴾ ﴿All of that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord.﴾ ﴿That is from what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom (al-hikmah). And do not set up with Allah another god, lest you be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and banished.﴾ ﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons and taken for Himself females from the angels? Indeed, you say a grave saying.﴾

The majority of readers read "maraḥan" with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, as a verbal noun from "marika yamraḥu," meaning to strut proudly, exulting in one's worldly possessions and devoted to one's ease. This is the (true) maraḥ, and the person in this verse is forbidden to walk the earth in this manner. Then it is said to him: "Indeed, you will never cross the earth and sweep it with your walking, nor will you reach the lengths of the mountains so as to attain their height." So if you cannot make yourself level with the earth by your walking, then restricting yourself to what truth requires of walking and conduct is more fitting and more deserving. The Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed with this verse, while the intended meaning is all people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Turning toward hunting and the like for recreation, without any need for it, falls within this verse. As for a man who takes rest on a rare day or at an hour of his day, and gives himself over to leisure and rest in order to strengthen himself for a task of righteousness, such as studying knowledge or prayer, that is not included in this verse, may God be pleased with them both.

A group — according to what Ya'qub has reported — read "marihan" with a kasrah on the rāʾ, in the form of the active participle. This meaning follows from this reading, but another meaning also fits it well, which al-Tabari mentioned alongside the first reading, and which is more suitable with this reading. It is that His saying, "Indeed, you will never tear through the earth, nor will you reach the mountains in height," means: O you who are exultant, arrogant, and boastful, do not tear through the earth, and do not overstep the mountains with your pride and haughtiness. The words are taken in this sense. This fits the reading with a kasrah on the rāʾ of maraḥ, because the person is then forbidden to adopt exultation as a character trait at all times, since walking on the earth never leaves him. So he is only forbidden from being exultant. But according to the other reading, the one who is not exultant is forbidden from walking exultantly at some times. Thus, with the rāʾ kasrah, maraḥ is understood to mean the proud and arrogant one.

Kharq al-ard means cutting through it. Al-kharq is the wide expanse of land, and from it is the poet's saying:

"And a wide expanse whose far side I crossed, / on a strong she-camel that complained of exhaustion."

It is also said of a hole in the earth, "kharq," but this meaning is not in the verse. From it is the saying of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

"And the dark depths, empty of what is pierced."

Al-Jarrah and al-A'rabi read "lan takhruqa al-ard" with a ḍammah on the rāʾ. Abu Hatim said: this dialect is not known.

As for His exalted saying, "All of that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord": Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, and al-A'raj read "sayyi'atan" (with a fatḥah). 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, and Masruq read "sayyi'uhu" with the adjective "sayyi'" annexed to the pronoun. The demonstrative in the first reading refers to what was previously forbidden, such as saying "uff," slandering people, exultant walking, and other things. In the second reading, the demonstrative refers to everything mentioned in these verses of righteousness and disobedience. Then the mention of the evil among them is singled out, as being hateful in the sight of God, the Exalted. As for the one who reads "sayyi'uhu" with the annexation to the pronoun, the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of his reading is clear: "sayyi'" is the subject of "kana," and "makruhan" is its predicate. As for the one who reads "sayyi'atan," it is the predicate of "kana." People differ regarding the i'rab of "makruhan." One group said: it is a second predicate of "kana," treating it according to the wording of "kull" (all). "Sayyi'atan" is treated according to the meaning, concerning all the things mentioned before. Others said: it is an adjective of "sayyi'atan," because its feminine marker is not real, so it is permissible to describe it with a masculine word.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi regarded this as weak, and said: when a feminine noun is made masculine, what follows it should only agree with it. The leniency is only that a verb attributed to a feminine noun may come in the form used for a masculine one. Do you not see that the poet's saying:

"Scarcely did a rain cloud pour its pouring, / nor was there a land that sprouted its sprouting more"

is considered objectionable by them? And if someone said, "absta arḍun" (a land sprouted), it would not be ugly. Abu 'Ali said: However, in His saying, "makruhan," it is permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for His saying, "sayyi'uhu." He said: It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial state (ḥal) of the masculine pronoun in His saying, "'inda rabbika," and His saying, "'inda rabbika," would be in the position of a qualifier of "sayyi'uhu." 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read, "kana sayyi'atuhu," and it is narrated from him, "kana sayyi'at" without the pronoun, and it is narrated from him, "kana khabithuhu" (its foulness). Al-Tabari held that all these prohibitions are conjoined to His earlier saying: "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him" [al-Isra': 23]. But that is not clear.

His exalted saying, "That is from what your Lord has revealed to you," and the rest of the verse: the demonstrative "that" refers to these ethical duties contained in the preceding verses, meaning: these are from the well-ordered acts required by the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted, regarding His servants and His creation, and they are the excellent virtues for them. "Al-hikmah" (wisdom) means the principles of well-ordered meanings and virtuous acts. Then His exalted saying, "And do not set up," is conjoined to the prohibitions mentioned earlier. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is everyone among mankind who hears the verse. "Al-madhur" means the humiliated, the distanced.

His exalted saying, "Has your Lord then favored you with sons," and the rest of the verse, is an address to the Arabs who used to say, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So Allah, the Exalted, established against them this argument: You, O humans, have the more excellent offspring, while for Allah there are daughters? When this incongruity in their saying became apparent, Allah magnified against them the corruption and the ugliness of what they say. Its meaning: great in its reprehensibility and its repulsiveness. "Asfakum" means He made you the possessors of the choicest. Al-Tabari related from Qatadah, from some people of knowledge, that he said: this verse was revealed concerning the Jews, because they made this statement, that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The first (view) is the one held by the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 41–44:

(p-484) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And We have certainly varied [the lessons] in this Qur'an that they may be reminded, but it increases them only in aversion.﴾ ﴿Say: "If there were with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne."﴾ ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they say, [exalted] greatly.﴾ ﴿The seven heavens and the earth exalt Him, and whatever is in them. And there is not a thing except that it exalts [Him] with His praise, but you do not understand their exaltation. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾

The majority read "ṣarrafnā" with a doubled rāʾ, meaning: We varied in it the wisdoms and the admonitions. Al-Ḥasan read "ṣarafnā" with a single rāʾ, meaning: We turned people in it toward guidance through calling to God. Some of those who read it with a doubled rāʾ said that His saying "fī" (in) is superfluous, and the sense is: We varied this Qur'an.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is weak.

The majority read "li-yadhdhakarū," while Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "li-yadhkurū" with a sukūn on the dhāl and a ḍammah on the kāf. This is the reading of Ṭalḥa, Yaḥyā, and al-A'mash. Whatever in the verse conveys hope and expectation, it is with respect to humans and according to their assumption concerning one with whom God does this.

"Nufūr" is an expression for intensity of turning away, likened to the fleeing of a beast, and in this verse it is a verbal noun only.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is related that in the Gospel, regarding the meaning of this verse: "O Children of Israel, We longed for you, but you did not long; We wailed for you, but you did not weep."

His saying, Exalted: ﴿Say: "If there were with Him other gods"﴾ — the verse is an informing with the argument. People differed regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne﴾. Al-Ṭabarī and other exegetes related that its meaning is: they would have sought, through these gods, nearness to the Owner of the Throne and drawing close to Him by obedience to Him, so "the way" in this interpretation has the same meaning as in His saying: ﴿Whoever wills takes a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]. Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, al-Naqqāsh, and the theologians (Abū Manṣūr and others) said: the meaning of the speech is: they would have sought a way to Him to corrupt His dominion and to rival Him in His power.

(p-485) The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation the verse is an explanation of mutual opposition, running in line with His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 22]. It touches briefly on some of the proof that it is not permissible for there to be with God, Blessed and Exalted, anyone other than Him. This is according to what Abū al-Maʿālī and others said: if we supposed it, let us suppose that one of them wills to still a body and the other wills to move it; it is impossible for both wills to be executed, and impossible for neither to be executed, so the body would be neither moving nor still. Thus when the will of one is accomplished and not the other's, the one whose will is not accomplished is not a god. If we say, "Let us suppose they do not differ," we say: their differing is permissible, not rationally impossible, and the permissible, in judgment, is the actual. Another proof: if there were two, it would not be impossible for them to be three, and so on without end. Another proof: the indivisible part of created things is connected only to one power, in which no sharing is valid; the next is likewise, and the one after that likewise, perpetually; so every part is brought into being by one. Explaining this in full detail would be lengthy.

Ibn Kathīr and Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim read "kamā yaqūlūn" with the yā' from beneath, while the majority read "kamā taqūlūn" with the tā'.

"Subḥānahu" is a verbal noun for a verb whose manifest form is omitted, so it has the sense of "tanzīh" (declaring Him far removed from imperfection). Its position here is the position of "tanazzaha" (He is exalted), and therefore the verb "wa-taʿālā" is conjoined to it. "Taʿālī" is of the form "tafāʿul"; in the case of visible bodies it is from two parties, because when a person ascends in his dwelling or on a mountain, it is as though that raises him up, and he rises and ascends. But regarding God, Mighty and Majestic, "taʿālī" is by His power, not by comparison to anything else. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Abū ʿAmr read "ʿammā yaqūlūn" with the yā', while Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "ʿammā taqūlūn" with the tā' from above. "ʿUluwwan" is a verbal noun not from the verb's own root, like His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nūḥ: 17], and this is common.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth exalt Him﴾ — the verse. The meaning: He is declared far above this statement of yours and the association you are pursuing; the seven heavens and the earth [exalt Him]. Then he returned to the heavens and the earth the pronoun of those who understand, when he ascribed to them the act of the rational, which is exalting. And His saying: (p-486) ﴿and whatever is in them﴾ means the angels, humans, and jinn. Then he generalized afterward to all things in His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing except that it exalts [Him] with His praise﴾, i.e., it declares God far removed, praises Him, and glorifies Him.

The people of knowledge differed regarding tasbīḥ. One group said: it is a figure of speech, and its meaning is that everything in which the craftsmanship of the craftsman that indicates Him appears, the sight of that calls to exaltation by one who reflects. Among the proofs of this interpretation is His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] with Him at evening﴾ [Ṣād: 18].

Another group said: "min shay'" is a general term whose meaning is specific to every living and sleeping thing, and that does not apply to pure inanimate matter. From this is the saying of ʿIkrimah: "The tree glorifies, but the pillar does not glorify." Yazīd al-Raqqāshī said to al-Ḥasan, while they were at a meal and the tablecloth had been brought: "Does this tablecloth glorify, Abū Saʿīd?" He said: "It used to glorify once," meaning that the tree, in the time of its growth and uprightness, was glorifying; once it became an oiled table or the like, it became inanimate.

Another group said: this tasbīḥ is literal, and everything in general glorifies with a glorification that humans do not hear and do not comprehend. Had tasbīḥ been what the others said, that it is the trace of the craftsmanship, it would be a matter understood, whereas the verse speaks that this glorification is not comprehended.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This objection may be answered by understanding by His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿you do not understand﴾ the disbelievers and the heedless, i.e., that they turn away from reflection, so they do not comprehend God's wisdom, Blessed and Exalted, in things.

Al-Ḥasan said: "It has reached me that the meaning of this verse is in the Torah, which mentions a thousand things that glorify: the heavens glorified Him, the earth glorified Him, such-and-such glorified, such-and-such glorified."

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim (in the narration of Abū Bakr), and Ibn ʿĀmir read "yusabbiḥu lahu" with the yā'; Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim (in the narration of Ḥafṣ), Ḥamzah, and al-Kisā'ī read "tusabbiḥu lahu" with the tā'. Both readings are good. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, Ṭalḥa, and al-Aʿmash read "sabbaḥat lahu al-samāwāt."

His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ contains an alert to His giving them respite, His pardoning them in this world, and His granting them time despite the abominable nature of this statement. That is: you say a saying from which every created thing declares Him far removed, yet He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving; therefore He has granted you respite.

[p. 487]

The words of the Exalted:

﴿When you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a concealed barrier.﴾ ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness. And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn back on their backs in aversion.﴾ ﴿We know best how they listen when they listen to you, and when they confer privately, when the wrongdoers say, "You follow not but a man affected by magic."﴾

This verse admits of two meanings. The first is that God Most High informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that He would protect him from the disbelievers, the people of Makkah, who used to harm him while he recited the Qur'an and prayed in the Masjid, and who wanted to stretch out their hands against him. Their circumstances in this regard are well known. The second meaning is that God informed him that He places a barrier between the disbelievers and understanding what Muhammad (ﷺ) recites. On this interpretation, the verse has the same meaning as the one after it. On the first interpretation, they are two verses for two meanings.

His words "mastur" (concealed): its most apparent function is that it is an attribute of the barrier, meaning concealed from the eyes of creation, so that no one perceives it by sight as with other barriers. It is from God's power, His sufficiency, and His causing them to go astray, according to the two interpretations mentioned. It has also been said that the implied sense is "concealed by it," with the returning pronoun omitted. Al-Akhfash said that "mastur" means "concealing" (satir), like "mash'um" and "maymun," meaning "shā'im" (one who is ill-omened) and "ya'man" (one who is blessed).

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This, without a compelling reason for it, is far-fetched, and its example is not accepted. It has also been said that it is meant as an intensive, as they said: "poetry, a poet" (shi'r sha'ir). This is objected to on the grounds that intensification is always expressed through the active participle and from the same root word. Had he said "hijaban hajiban" (a barrier, a blocking one), the comparison would have been valid.

His words, "And We have placed over their hearts coverings" (verse), "al-akinna" is the plural of "kinan," which is whatever covers a thing, and from it comes "kinanat al-nabl" (the quiver of arrows). "Al-waqr" is the heaviness in the ear that prevents hearing, which is deafness. All of these are metaphors for the misguidance with which God has surrounded them. He expressed the abundance and magnitude of this by saying that they are like one whose heart is covered and whose ear is deafened.

His words, "And when you mention your Lord" (verse), he means: when the passages of tawhid (monotheism) come in the Qur'an during your recitation, the disbelievers of Makkah flee from hearing them, denying and loathing them, because they contain a rejection of their gods and a casting them aside. Some scholars said: "The chiefs of Quraysh entered upon Abu Talib to visit him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon them, recited, and passed over the tawhid. Then he said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, say: "There is no god but God" (la ilaha illa Allah), by which you will rule the Arabs, and the non-Arabs will submit to you.' They turned away and fled, and the verse was revealed."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

That the verse describes the state of those who fled from him at the time of his proclamation of tawhid during his recitation is clearer and more consistent with the wording.

His words, "nufuran" (in aversion), may be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), and it may be the plural of "nafir," like "shahid" and "shuhud," since "fa'ul" is among the patterns of the active participle in attributes. Its accusative status is as a circumstantial state, meaning "fleeing" (nafirin). His words, "lest they understand it" (verse): "an" is in the accusative as an object, meaning "out of dislike that" or "prevented that," and the pronoun in "yafqahuhu" refers to the Qur'an. Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: "By His words, 'they turn back on their backs in aversion,' He meant only the devils, who flee from the recitation of the Qur'an."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

He means that the meaning indicates them, even though they are not mentioned in the wording. This is similar to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the call to prayer is given, Satan turns and runs away, passing wind" (lahu khusas).

His words, "We know best how they listen when they listen" (verse): this is like your saying: "So-and-so listens eagerly and attentively, or with disregard, heedlessness, and contempt." The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "ma," which here means "alladhi" (that which). What is meant by "that which" is the contempt and disregard we have mentioned. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 48–51:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Look how they strike for you the similitudes, so they have gone astray, and they cannot find a way.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Be you stones or iron,﴾ ﴿or some creation that is greater in your breasts." Then they will say, "Who will bring us back?" Say, "The One who originated you the first time." Then they will shake their heads toward you and say, "When will that be?" Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾

Striking the similitude for him (the Prophet) was their saying: "Bewitched," "a sorcerer," "a madman," "a soothsayer," because none of them was certain of any of these; rather, they were said by them by way of comparison. Then al-Walid ibn al-Mughira judged that the closest of these matters, according to the imagination of those who came upon them, was that he was a sorcerer. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, passed judgment on them as being in error.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿so they cannot find a way﴾ admits of two meanings. One of them: they cannot find a way to guidance and to the reflection that leads to faith, so the verse runs in the manner of His saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ [al-Isra: 46] and the like of this. The other: they cannot find a way to corrupt your affair and to extinguish the light of Allah by their striking similitudes for you, and their pursuing every stratagem against you.

al-Tabari related that this verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and his companions.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust?"﴾ This verse concerns their denial of resurrection, and this from them is amazement, denial, and deeming it remote. And "al-rufat" of things is that which time has passed over until it reached the utmost of decay and brought it close to the state of dust. It is said: "rufita rafatan, fahuwa marfut," and the pattern fu'al is its form for this meaning, like al-hutam, al-futat, al-rudad, and al-diqaq. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "rufatan" means dust (ghubaran), and Mujahid said: dirt (turaban).

The readers differed concerning these two interrogatives. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "a-idha, a-inna" both with interrogation, except that Abu 'Amr prolongs the hamza, then brings the ya' sukun, while Ibn Kathir brings a sukun ya' after the hamza without prolongation. Nafi' read the first like Abu 'Amr, with differing reports from him concerning the prolongation, and he read the second: "inna" with a kasra, as a statement. Al-Kisa'i agreed with him in dispensing with the interrogative of the second because of the first, except that he would pronounce the hamza with two hamzas. 'Asim and Hamza read: "a-idha kunna, a-inna" with two hamzas in them both. Ibn 'Amir read: "idha kunna" with a kasra on the alif without interrogation, "a-inna," pronouncing the hamza, then prolonging, then pronouncing the hamza again, and a report from him is like Hamza's reading.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The explanation of these readings is in the commentary on Surat al-Ra'd.

"Jadid" is an adjective for what has recently come into being among things, and it is thus applied to the masculine and feminine alike; it is said: "milhafa jadid." Their saying "jadida" is a weak dialect, so said Sibawayh.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Say, "Be you stones or iron"﴾ and the verse. The meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad: "Be these difficult, impossible things, if you are able, you must still be resurrected." His saying "Be" is what the speakers call taʻjiz (challenge to impotence), among the types of the form "fa'al" (imperative). Some have used this verse as an example, and in this I have a reservation; rather, taʻjiz is where the command entails doing what the addressee cannot do, like His saying: ﴿Then avert from yourselves death﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168] and the like. As for this verse, its meaning is: "Be, through supposition and estimation, such and such; He who originated you thus will restore you." Mujahid said: by the creation that is greater in the breasts he meant the heavens, the earth, and the mountains. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak said: he meant death. Qatada and Mujahid said: rather, He referred them to their nature (fitra) in general, and al-Tabari preferred this.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the most sound, because He began with something solid, then the speech progressed to something stronger than it, then He referred them to their nature if He wills; and [there is nothing harder] than iron, so there is no basis for restricting it to one thing over another. Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, argued against them concerning the return through the first origination, from the point that He created them and brought them into being from dust, and likewise He will restore them when He wills; there is no lord but Him. Al-Zajjaj said: moving the head of one who disparages a thing and finds it slow, and from it is the poet's saying:

He shook his head toward me and raised it, as if he had seen something that made him covet.

It is said: "nagha al-sinn" when the tooth moved. Dhu al-Rumma said:

Caravans which did not dwell on the sides of a town, with a sword, and the bridges did not shake with them.

al-Tabari and Ibn Sallam said: "'asa" from Allah is binding, so the meaning is: and He is near.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is only from the Prophet ﷺ, but it is by the command of Allah, the Exalted, to him, so that brings it close to being obligatory. For this reason, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "I was sent, and the Hour is like these two," and within the wording there is a warning to them.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust?"﴾ This verse concerns their denial of resurrection, and this from them is amazement, denial, and deeming it remote. And "al-rufat" of things is that which time has passed over until it reached the utmost of decay and brought it close to the state of dust. It is said: "rufita rafatan, fahuwa marfut," and the pattern fu'al is its form for this meaning, like al-hutam, al-futat, al-rudad, and al-diqaq. The explanation of these readings is in the commentary on Surat al-Ra'd.

He shook his head toward me and raised it, as if he had seen something that made him covet.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 52–55:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿On the Day He calls you, and you respond with His praise, and you will think that you tarried only a little.﴾ ﴿And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan incites discord among them. Indeed, Satan has ever been to mankind a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you; or if He wills, He will punish you. And We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ ﴿And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others, and We gave David the Zabur.﴾

"Yawma" (on the Day): it is a substitute (badal) for His words "qariban" (near). It appears that the meaning is: "It is a Day," as an answer to their words: ﴿When is it?﴾ [al-Isra': 51]. The meaning is: He calls you from your graves by the blowing of the trumpet (al-Sur) so that the Hour is established. His words "fa-tastajibuna" (and you respond) mean: by rising, returning and getting up towards the call. As for His words "bihamdihi" (with His praise), al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: its meaning is "by His command." Ibn Jurayj also said likewise, and Qatadah said: its meaning is "by His obedience and His recognition."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is an interpretation that the wording does not give, and there is no doubt that all of that is by the command of Allah the Exalted. Rather, the meaning of "bihamdihi" is either that all the worlds, as Ibn Jubayr said, rise while praising Allah the Exalted and glorifying Him for what becomes manifest to them of His power; or that His words "bihamdihi" are like when you say to a man, when you dispute with him or debate with him about knowledge: "You have erred, by the praise of Allah." The Prophet ﷺ used to say to them concerning (p-494) these verses: "Perhaps the Hour is near, the Day you are called you will stand up, contrary to what you believe now, and that is by the praise of Allah for the truth of my report." al-Tabari went in this direction but did not make it clear.

His Exalted words: ﴿And you think that you tarried only a little﴾ may carry two meanings. One of them is that He informs that when they returned to the state of life and the movement of bodies, there occurred to them a thought that they had not been separated from the state of the world except a little, because the knowledge of the measure of time was hidden from them; for whoever is in the Hereafter does not measure the time of the world, since they are without doubt far more separated from it than sleepers. On this interpretation al-Tabari relied, and he argued with His words: ﴿How many years did you remain on earth?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 112] ﴿They said: We remained a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. The other meaning is that "zann" (thinking) is in the sense of "yaqin" (certainty), as if He said to them: On the Day you are called and you respond with the praise of Allah, and you are certain that you only tarried a little, in view of how it has passed and ended. This is like when it is said of the whole world: "a passing enjoyment" (mata' qil), as if it were of small worth. However, "zann" in the sense of "yaqin" is troubling here, because it concerns something that has already occurred. "Zann" in the sense of "yaqin" comes only regarding what has not yet come out into existence and being. In the speech there is a strengthening of the resurrection, as if He says: O you who deny the gathering, who believe that you will never be resurrected, you must be called to the resurrection, and you will stand and see that you only remained a little, passed and gone. al-Tabari reported from Qatadah that when they see the terror of the Day of Resurrection they will belittle the world, and so they will think that they remained in it only a little.

His Exalted words: ﴿And tell My servants to say that which is best.﴾ The grammarians differed concerning His words "yaqulu" (they say). The view of Sibawayh is that it is the answer to an implied conditional, its estimate being: "And tell My servants, if you tell them, they will say," and this is according to his principle that the imperative is not answered directly, but rather a implied condition is answered with it. The view of al-Akhfash is that the imperative is answered, and that His words here "yaqulu" are the answer to "qul" (say).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is not sound on this view by making "qul" specific to these words, in the sense that (p-495) the Prophet ﷺ would say to them: "Say that which is best." Rather, it is sound only if "qul" is an imperative to dialogue in this meaning with whatever words are possible, as if He said: "Make clear to My servants," so that the fruit of that speech and clarification is their saying that which is best. This meaning is permitted by the view of Sibawayh which we mentioned earlier. The view of Abu al-'Abbas is that "yaqulu" is an answer to an omitted imperative, its estimate being: "And tell My servants: Say that which is best, they will say," so the words were omitted and the speech folded. The view of al-Zajjaj is that "yaqulu" is in the jussive by the imperative, with the estimate: "Tell My servants that they may say," so the lam was omitted because the imperative preceded. Abu 'Ali related in "al-Halabiyyat," among the scattered parts of his speech, that the view of Abu 'Uthman al-Mazini concerning "yaqulu" is that it is a built (mabni) verb, because it is an imperfect that took the place of the built form which is the imperative verb, since the meaning is: "Say to My servants: Say."

People differed concerning ﴿that which is best﴾. One group said: it is "There is no god but Allah." It follows on this view that His words "to My servants" intend all creation, since all of them are invited to "There is no god but Allah." His words after that, ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾, would not fit the meaning except with reluctance, by taking "baynahum" to mean "in their midst and among them," and taking "nazgh" to mean whispering and misguidance. The majority said: "that which is best" is the good manner of dialogue, according to the meaning, a meaning. al-Hasan said: "He says: May Allah forgive you, may Allah have mercy on you."

His Exalted words "to My servants" are specific to the believers, so the verse is as if in the sense of His saying ﷺ: "Be servants of Allah, brothers." Then they differed. One group said: Allah commanded the believers among themselves with good manners, lowering the wing, softness of speech, and casting aside the incitements of Satan. Another group said: Allah, blessed and exalted, commanded the believers in this verse to speak gently to the polytheists in Makkah during the days of truce.

The occasion of the verse: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was insulted by some of the disbelievers, so 'Umar reviled him and intended to kill him, and it nearly stirred up strife, so the verse was revealed. It is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

al-Jumhur read "yanzaghu" with a fatha on the za'. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "yanzighu" with a kasra on the za', according to the original form. Abu Hatim said: "Perhaps it is a dialect, and the recitation is with the fatha." The meaning of nazgh is the swift movement of Satan to cause corruption. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Let none of you point a weapon at his brother, for Satan may incite (yanzagh) in his hand," so this takes the word out of the sense of whispering. The clear enmity of Satan is his story with Adam, peace be upon him, which comes later.

His Exalted words: ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of you﴾, the verse. This verse strengthens that the preceding one concerns what is between the believing servants and the disbelievers of Makkah, because this address in His words: ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of you﴾ is to the disbelievers of Makkah, by the evidence of His words: ﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾. So it is as if Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded the believers not to be harsh with the disbelievers in religion, then He said to the disbelievers: He knows them best, and He gave them hope and frightened them. The meaning of "He will have mercy upon you" is by turning to you in repentance from disbelief, as Ibn Jurayj and others said. Then the Prophet ﷺ was told: "Your duty is only to convey," and you are not a guardian over their faith in any case, so the verses fit together by this interpretation.

Then the Blessed and Exalted said to His Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿And your Lord is most knowing of whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, and He is the One who preferred some prophets over others according to His knowledge of them. This is a reference to Muhammad ﷺ, and to the Quraysh's deeming it unlikely that the Messenger should be a human. The meaning: Do not deny the matter of Muhammad and that he was given a Qur'an, for the prophets were preferred, and David was given the Zabur; Allah knows best where to place His message.

The preference of some messengers over others is either by this general report without naming the one who is preferred less, and on this basis it is correct for us to say: Muhammad is the best of mankind, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade specifying any one of them in the story of Musa and Yunus; or the preference is distributed among them: (p-497) this one was given speech, that one was given friendship, Muhammad the five (prayers / the five things), and 'Isa the raising of the dead, so each of them is preferred in one respect and absolutely excellent.

His Exalted words: ﴿Concerning whoever is in the heavens﴾. The ba' is connected to a verb whose estimate is "He knows of whoever is in the heavens." Abu 'Ali held this view, because if it were connected to "a'lamu" it would imply that He is not more knowing in other than that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This does not follow, and it is valid for it to be connected to "a'lamu," and one does not turn to the argument of the implicature (dalil al-khitab).

al-Jumhur read "Zabura" with a fatha on the za'; it is fa'ul in the sense of maf'ul, and it is rare, appearing only in qaruʿ, rukub, and halub. Hamzah, Yahya, and al-A'mash read "zubura" with a damma on the za'. It has two possibilities: one is that it is the plural of zabur by dropping the added letter, as they said in the plural of tariq: turuq; the other is that it is the plural of zabr, as if what David brought was divided into parts, each part of which is a zabr, named by the verbal noun of zabara yazbur, then those parts were collected into zubur, as if He said: "We gave David a book." It may also be the plural of "zabr," which is intellect and soundness of judgment, since David was given many admonitions and counsels. From this word is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ at the end of the Book of Muslim: "And the people of the Fire are five: the weak one who has no zabr (discernment)." Qatadah said: the Zabur of David consists of admonitions, wisdom and supplication, and there is nothing in it of lawful or unlawful.

Ibn Fawrak and others said: the statement from His words, blessed and exalted, "Those whom they call upon" refers to the prophets mentioned earlier, and "yad'una," on this view, is from supplication in the sense of seeking to Allah the Exalted; the pronouns in "yad'una" and "yabtaghuna" refer to them. The rest of the verse is clear.

As for His words, "And there is no town": this verse informs us that there is no city among the cities but that it will be destroyed before the Day of Resurrection by death and annihilation, whether it is spared and only a part of it is taken, or it is punished and seized once. This is general for every city. "Min" is for specifying the kind. It has been said that the intended meaning is particular: "And there is no unjust town." Al-Naqqash related that in the book of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, in his tafsir of this verse, there was a survey of the well-known lands of today, mentioning for the destruction of each region a characteristic; then he mentioned something similar from Wahb ibn Munabbih, in which he stated that the destruction and ruin of al-Andalus would be by the hooves of horses and the clashing of armies in it. (These reports) were left aside, as the others are of no soundness in this regard. What is known is that every town perishes either through famine, sinking, or drowning, or through strife, or through both. The forms of this are many, which none knows but Allah the Exalted. As for what perishes by strife, it is necessarily due to wrongdoing, whether in disbelief, sins, or negligence in defence. As for famine, Allah afflicts with it whom He wills, and likewise sinking. His words "muhlikuha" (its destroyers): the pronoun refers to the town, and within that is implied its people. His words, "or punish it" (muʻadhdhibuha): it is by omission of a modifier, for only the people are punished. His words, "in the Book" (fi al-kitab), mean: in the prior decree and what the pen inscribed on the Preserved Tablet. "Al-mastur" means: written in lines.

As for His words, "And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs": this expression, "prevented Us," is according to the apparent sense understood by the Arabs; He named the prior decree of His regarding the denial of those who denied and their punishment as "prevention." The first "an" is in the accusative position, and the second is in the nominative position; the implied meaning is: nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except denial.

The reason for this verse is that the Quraysh proposed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that Safa be turned into gold for them, and some of them proposed that he remove the mountains from them so that they could farm the land. Allah then revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ): "If you wish, I will do that for them; but if they are late in believing, the punishment will hasten upon them. And if you wish, I will give them respite, perhaps I will choose believers from among them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rather, grant them respite, O Lord." So Allah the Exalted informed in this verse that nothing prevented Him from sending the proposed signs except the granting of respite, since His custom had already passed of hastening punishment upon the nations to whom the proposed sign came and who did not believe. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah the Exalted informed that the appointed time for the disbelievers of this nation is the Hour, due to His words, "Nay, the Hour is their appointed time" [al-Qamar: 46]; so this verse looks toward that.

Then Allah the Exalted mentioned the matter of Thamud as an argument, in case one of them said: "We would have believed if a sign we proposed had come to us, and we would not disbelieve in any way." So Allah the Exalted mentioned Thamud, meaning: you are not safe from wronging yourselves with the sign as Thamud wronged itself with the she-camel. The majority read "Thamud" without tanwin. Harun said: the people of Kufa read "Thamudan" with tanwin in every case. Abu Hatim said: the common readers and the scholars of the readings do not put tanwin on "Thamud" in any way, and in four places there is a written alif, but we read it without alif.

His words, "mubsiratan" (visible), are in the sense of attribution (nisbah): i.e., it has sight with it, as He said, "And We made the sign of the day visible" [al-Isra: 12], i.e., it has sight for the one who looks; this is an expression for clarifying its matter and the clarity of its miraculousness. Some read "mubsarah" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the sad, related by al-Zajjaj, meaning: clearly manifest. Qatadah read "mabsarah" with a fatha on the mim and the sad; it is a noun of place from "basar" (sight). From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

Disbelief is a corruption (makhbathah) for the soul of the benefactor.

His words, "But they wronged it" (fa-zalamu biha): i.e., they placed the act in other than its proper place, namely by slaughtering her; it has been said: by disbelief concerning her matter. Then Allah the Exalted informed that He sends signs other than those proposed only as a warning to the servants, and these are signs accompanied by respite, not immediate punishment; among them are eclipses, thunder, earthquakes, the rainbow, and other things. Al-Hasan said: and sudden deadly plague. It is related that Kufa shook during the time of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and he said: "O people, your Lord is asking you to make amends, so make amends to Him." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning eclipses: "Then hasten to prayer," the hadith. The signs of Allah by which one takes heed are of three kinds: one kind is general in everything, for wherever you cast your gaze you find a sign, and this is the reflection of the scholars; another kind is customary and recurring periodically, like thunder, eclipses and the like, and this is the reflection of the ignorant only; and another kind is extraordinary, breaking custom, and it has ended with the ending of prophethood; it is only taken as a lesson by way of conjecture regarding what has passed from it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 60:**

The Most High said:

﴿And [remember] when We said to you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people. And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people, and [also] the accursed tree in the Qur'an. And We warn them, but it increases them only in great transgression."﴾

Al-Ṭabarī said: The meaning of His words, ﴿And [remember] when We said to you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people"﴾, is: in Your protection, O Muḥammad, and Your enclosure and preservation. The verse is therefore a report to him that he is protected from the disbelievers, safe from being killed or from suffering a great harm. That is, "Let him convey the message of your Lord, and do not fear any of the created beings."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a clear interpretation that accords with the wording, and something similar has been transmitted from al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī. However, it does not fit what follows it very closely. It may be possible to make the statement fit what follows it, as a preparation for it. I say: People have differed about the vision (al-ru'yā). The majority (al-jumhūr) said: it is a vision of the eye and of wakefulness, and it is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw on the night of the Isrā' (the Night Journey). They said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed them, on the morning after the Isrā', of what he had seen that night of wonders, the disbelievers said, "Indeed, this is astonishing! Caravans take two months to reach Bayt al-Maqdis going and returning, and Muḥammad says that he went there and came back in a single night?" They were tempted by this deception, and some of the weak among the Muslims were led astray and apostatized. This distressed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and so these verses were revealed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this view, it is good that the meaning of His words, ﴿And [remember] when We said to you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people"﴾, is: in their misguidance and their guidance, and that each one is made easy for what he was created for. That is, do not be preoccupied with the disbelief of those who disbelieve, and do not grieve over them. It has been said to you: "Do not grieve over them." Indeed, Allah encompasses them and possesses their affairs, and He has made this a trial so that whoever was already destined for disbelief might disbelieve. The vision is called ruʾyā in this interpretation because both (ru'yā and ru'yah) are verbal nouns from ra'ā (to see).

Al-Naqqāsh said: This came in accordance with the belief of those who thought it was a dream, although the reality was otherwise.

ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her and her father, said: The vision in the Isrā' was a vision of sleep (ru'yā manām). This is the view of the majority, contrary to it. This verse argues against it, because a dream of sleep contains no trial, and no one would have denied it. This has been treated comprehensively at the beginning of the surah.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: The vision in this verse is the vision of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he would enter Makkah. He hastened in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyya, but was turned back, and the Muslims were tempted by this. So these verses were revealed.

Sahl ibn Saʿd said: This vision was only that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw the Banū Umayya leaping upon his minbar like monkeys leaping. He was grieved by this, and from that day onward he was never seen laughing until he died. So the verse was revealed to inform that this was from their gaining power and ascending the pulpits, which Allah makes only a trial and a test for the people.

His words, Most High, ﴿encompassed the people﴾, may also mean: by His decree, and that everything He has decreed is executed. So do not be concerned with what will happen after you because of that. Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī said in his speech concerning his giving of allegiance to Muʿāwiya: ﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial for you and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 111].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is room for doubt about this interpretation, and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him, is not included in this vision, nor ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, nor Muʿāwiya.

His words, Most High, ﴿and the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾, are conjoined to His words, glorified is He, "the vision." That is, We made the vision and the tree a trial. The "tree" (al-shajara) here, according to the majority, is the tree of al-Zaqqūm. When its matter was revealed in the surah of al-Ṣāffāt, Abū Jahl and others said: "This Muḥammad threatens you with a fire that burns stones, then claims that it will make trees grow? We know nothing of al-Zaqqūm except dates with butter." Then Abū Jahl ordered a slave-girl of his to bring dates and butter, and said to his companions: "Eat your zaqqūm!" Some of the weak were also tempted by this statement. So Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ that He had made the Isrā' and the mention of the tree of al-Zaqqūm a test, so that whoever was destined for disbelief might disbelieve, and whoever had already been destined for faith might affirm it. It is also reported that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, was told on the morning after the Isrā': "Your companion claims that he went last night to Bayt al-Maqdis and returned from it." He said: "If he said that, then he has spoken the truth." He was asked: "Do you affirm it before you have heard it from him?" He said: "Where are your minds? I affirm him concerning the news of the heaven, so how should I not affirm him concerning the news of Bayt al-Maqdis, when heaven is far more distant than it?"

A group said: The tree refers to the people mentioned earlier in the vision.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak and novel view, and it is not transmitted from Sahl ibn Saʿd or anyone like him. Al-Ṭabarī said, citing Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: The accursed tree means: the one who eats it is accursed, because no prior mention of it has occurred.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that "the accursed" here means: He emphasized the matter by His words, ﴿in the Qur'an﴾. A group said: "The accursed" means: the one far removed, the detested. This is what is meant, because He cursed it with the well-known term of cursing. This is close in meaning to what came before. Also, what grows at the root of the Hellfire is at the utmost distance from the mercy of Allah.

His words, Most High, ﴿And We warn them﴾, mean either the disbelievers of Makkah, or the kings of the Banū Umayya after the caliphate about which the Prophet ﷺ said: "The caliphate after me will be thirty years, then it will become a biting kingship." The first of these two is more correct, as we said before.

His words, Most High, ﴿but it increases them only in great transgression﴾, mean their disbelief and their violation of it, like the words of Abū Jahl about the zaqqūm and the eating of it. Al-Naqqāsh said that this is what was revealed concerning it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And similar to it. Al-Aʿmash recited ﴿wa-yukhawwifuhum﴾ with the yāʾ (a third-person form), while the majority (al-jumhūr) recited ﴿wa-nukhawwifuhum﴾ with the nūn (a first-person plural form).

(p-506) Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He said, "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Tell me, is this the one You have honored above me? If You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely take control of his descendants, except for a few."﴾ ﴿He said, "Go, and whoever among them follows you, then indeed Hell is your recompense, a full recompense.﴾ ﴿And incite whomever you can among them with your voice, and attack them with your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and make promises to them." But Satan promises them nothing except delusion.﴾ ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, and your Lord is sufficient as a Guardian.﴾

The meaning: "Remember when We said." Likewise, "idh" (when) in the preceding verse is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb. The creation of Adam and the command to prostrate to him have already been mentioned in other places.

Scholars differ regarding the phrase ﴿except Iblis﴾. It is said that it is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category), because Iblis was not among the angels. It is also said that it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), because Iblis was among the angels. The phrase "clay" (ṭīnan) may be a specification (tamyīz) or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), both of which are grammatically sound.

In this matter Iblis analogized and erred. He saw superiority for himself because he saw fire as better than clay, and he was ignorant of the fact that excellences in things lie in where Allah the Blessed and Exalted specifies them, and one does not look to their origins.

Al-Ṭabarī reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Iblis was the one whom Allah commanded, so he took a clay of the earth's surface and created Adam from it. The well-known view, however, is that he was the Angel of Death. Iblis's disbelief lay in his ignorance of the attribute of justice of Allah the Exalted, when pride and arrogance seized him. The root of this was envy, and for this reason it was said: "The first thing with which Allah the Exalted was disobeyed was envy." This appeared from Iblis in his saying: ﴿Tell me, is this the one You have honored?﴾ and ﴿I am better than him﴾ [Ṣād 38:76], as Allah the Exalted mentioned in another verse. This is the clear text that his action was not upright.

The "ka" in his saying "arā'aytaka" is the particle of address and emphasis for alerting, having no place in i'rab (grammatical case analysis); it is therefore superfluous. The meaning of "ara'ayt" is like "a-ta'ammalt" (have you considered?). It is as if the speaker is alerting the addressee so that he gathers his attention for what is stated after it. Sibawayh said it means "akhbirnī" (tell me), and he gave the example: "Arā'aytaka Zayd, a-yu'minu huwa?" (Tell me about Zayd, does he believe?)

(p-507) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Zajjaj said it regarding "āyātinā" (Our signs) and did not give an example. Sibawayh's statement is correct where a question follows it, as in his example. The "ka" in this verse is as I have said, and it is not the one Sibawayh mentioned, may Allah have mercy on him.

Ibn Kathir read "akhkharta-nī" with a yā' in both pause and connection, and this is the original form. This position is not like a rhyme where omission is good, as in the verse of al-A'sha:

"Will my wandering in the wilderness, from fear of death, prevent it from coming to me?"

Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read with a yā' in connection and omit it in pause. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "akhkharta-n" with the yā' omitted in both connection and pause. This is an assimilation to the yā' of "qāḍin" and similar words, because it is a final yā' preceded by a kasra. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ [Hud 11:105].

His saying "la-aḥtanikanna" means "la-umīlanna" (I will surely incline them) and "la-ajurrannna" (I will surely lead them). It is derived from "taḥnīk al-dābba" (bridling the animal), which is to tie a rope or something else around its jaw so that it becomes docile. The year "taḥtanik al-māl" means it devours the wealth, that is, it chews it up. From this is the poet's saying:

"We complain to You of a year that has crushed us, hardship upon hardship, and weakened us, and has devoured our wealth and oppressed us."

(p-508) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

From this poetry al-Ṭabarī said regarding "la-aḥtanikanna": "la-astaʾṣilanna" (I will surely uproot). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, expressed it as "la-astawliyanna" (I will surely take control). Ibn Zayd said: "la-uḍillanna" (I will surely lead astray).

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a substitution of the word, not an explanation of it.

Iblis passed this judgment on the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, because he saw the creation as hollow, with differing parts, combined with desires and accidents such as anger and the like. Then he made an exception of the few, because he knew that among his descendants there would be some who would be steadfast in obedience to Allah the Exalted.

His saying, Exalted is He, "Go," and what follows it of commands, is in the form of "if'al" (imperative) used for threat, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:40]. "Tabi'aka" (follows you) means: in the path of disbelief to which you call. So the verse concerns the disbelievers and those among the disobedient upon whom the threat is executed. His saying, Exalted is He, "jazā'an" (as a recompense) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and "al-mawfūr" means "complete."

"Istafziz" means: deceive and trick until he falls into your will. You say: "Istafazzanī fulān fī kadhā" (So-and-so provoked me into such-and-such) when he tricked you until you fell into a matter he intended. From lightness (khiffa) the calf of a cow is called "fazz." From this is Zuhayr's saying:

"As a wild ass calf flees from a predator, having feared the eyes, so it is not seen by the sharp-eyed."

(p-509) As for "al-ṣawt" (voice) here, it has been said that it means singing, flutes and entertainments, because these are all sounds specific to disobedience, and so they are attributed to Satan. This was said by Mujahid. It has also been said that it means: by your calling them to your obedience. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "His voice is the call of every sinner to the disobedience of Allah the Exalted."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that "al-ṣawt" encompasses all of that.

His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-ajlib" means "hawwil" (frighten), and "al-jalaba" is a loud, mixed, terrifying sound. Al-Ḥasan read "wa-ijlub" with a connecting alif and a ḍamma on the lām. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿with your cavalry and your infantry﴾ has been said to be a metaphor and figurative expression meaning: "Exert your effort and exhaust your utmost." It has also been said that it means he has cavalry and infantry from among the jinn, as said by Qatada. It has also been said that the meaning is the horsemen and foot soldiers of mankind who act in falsehood, for they are all helpers of Iblis against others, as said by Mujahid. The majority read "wa-rajlika" with a sukun on the jīm, which is the plural of rājil (foot soldier), like tājir and tajr (merchant and merchants), ṣāḥib and ṣaḥb (companion and companions), shārib and sharb (drinker and drinkers). Ḥafs from 'Asim read "wa-rajilika" with a kasra on the jīm, on the pattern fa'il, and likewise al-Ḥasan and Abu 'Amr (in one transmission) read it. It is an adjective: you say "fulān yamshī rajilan" (so-and-so walks on foot), meaning not riding. From this is the poet's saying:

"Shall I not fight for my religion on my horse, nor on foot without companions?"

(p-510) Qatada and 'Ikrima read "bi-khaylika wa-rijālika" (with your cavalry and your men).

His saying: ﴿and share with them in wealth﴾ is general to every act of disobedience that people commit with wealth, for spending it in disobedience is the path of Iblis. From this are cigarettes and the like, from this is the prostitute's fee, the price of wine, the gift of the soothsayer, usury, and other things found among people habitually. His saying "wal-awlād" (and children) is general to every disobedient act performed regarding offspring. From this is begetting children through fornication, from this is naming them 'Abd Shams, 'Abd al-Ḥārith, Abu al-Kuwayfir, and every hateful name, from this is the burying of daughters alive which the Arabs used to do, and from this is dyeing them into the religions of disbelief, and other things. As for what al-Naqqash introduced regarding intercourse with jinn and that they impregnate human women, it is all weak.

His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-'idhum" means: give them false hopes with what will not come to pass for them, and tell them that they will not be resurrected. This is sharing in the souls. Then Allah the Exalted informed that He promises them only as delusion from Him, because it does not benefit them at all.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ is a statement from Allah the Blessed and Exalted to Iblis. His saying "My servants" means the believers in disbelief and the pious in disobedience. He specified them as "servants," although it is a general term for all creation, because He intended to honor them and draw attention to them, just as a man says to one of his sons when he sees from him what pleases him: "This is my son," meaning as an alert from him and an honoring of him. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "This is my maternal uncle; let any man show me his maternal uncle." The word "sulṭān" means dominion and overpowering, and interpreting it here as "proof" is weak. Then Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿And your Lord is sufficient, O Muhammad, as a Guardian﴾, protecting the believers and watching over their guidance.

In this matter Iblis analogized and erred. He saw superiority for himself because he saw fire as better than clay, and he was ignorant of the fact that excellences in things lie in where Allah the Blessed and Exalted specifies them, and one does not look to their origins.

Al-Ṭabarī reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Iblis was the one whom Allah commanded, so he took a clay of the earth's surface and created Adam from it. The well-known view, however, is that he was the Angel of Death. Iblis's disbelief lay in his ignorance of the attribute of justice of Allah the Exalted, when pride and arrogance seized him. The root of this was envy, and for this reason it was said: "The first thing with which Allah the Exalted was disobeyed was envy." This appeared from Iblis in his saying: ﴿Tell me, is this the one You have honored?﴾ and ﴿I am better than him﴾ [Ṣād 38:76], as Allah the Exalted mentioned in another verse. This is the clear text that his action was not upright.

The "ka" in his saying "arā'aytaka" is the particle of address and emphasis for alerting, having no place in i'rab (grammatical case analysis); it is therefore superfluous. The meaning of "ara'ayt" is like "a-ta'ammalt" (have you considered?). It is as if the speaker is alerting the addressee so that he gathers his attention for what is stated after it. Sibawayh said it means "akhbirnī" (tell me), and he gave the example: "Arā'aytaka Zayd, a-yu'minu huwa?" (Tell me about Zayd, does he believe?)

(p-507) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Zajjaj said it regarding "āyātinā" (Our signs) and did not give an example. Sibawayh's statement is correct where a question follows it, as in his example. The "ka" in this verse is as I have said, and it is not the one Sibawayh mentioned, may Allah have mercy on him.

Ibn Kathir read "akhkharta-nī" with a yā' in both pause and connection, and this is the original form. This position is not like a rhyme where omission is good, as in the verse of al-A'sha:

"Will my wandering in the wilderness, from fear of death, prevent it from coming to me?"

Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read with a yā' in connection and omit it in pause. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "akhkharta-n" with the yā' omitted in both connection and pause. This is an assimilation to the yā' of "qāḍin" and similar words, because it is a final yā' preceded by a kasra. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ [Hud 11:105].

His saying "la-aḥtanikanna" means "la-umīlanna" (I will surely incline them) and "la-ajurrannna" (I will surely lead them). It is derived from "taḥnīk al-dābba" (bridling the animal), which is to tie a rope or something else around its jaw so that it becomes docile. The year "taḥtanik al-māl" means it devours the wealth, that is, it chews it up. From this is the poet's saying:

"We complain to You of a year that has crushed us, hardship upon hardship, and weakened us, and has devoured our wealth and oppressed us."

(p-508) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

From this poetry al-Ṭabarī said regarding "la-aḥtanikanna": "la-astaʾṣilanna" (I will surely uproot). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, expressed it as "la-astawliyanna" (I will surely take control). Ibn Zayd said: "la-uḍillanna" (I will surely lead astray).

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a substitution of the word, not an explanation of it.

Iblis passed this judgment on the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, because he saw the creation as hollow, with differing parts, combined with desires and accidents such as anger and the like. Then he made an exception of the few, because he knew that among his descendants there would be some who would be steadfast in obedience to Allah the Exalted.

His saying, Exalted is He, "Go," and what follows it of commands, is in the form of "if'al" (imperative) used for threat, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:40]. "Tabi'aka" (follows you) means: in the path of disbelief to which you call. So the verse concerns the disbelievers and those among the disobedient upon whom the threat is executed. His saying, Exalted is He, "jazā'an" (as a recompense) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), and "al-mawfūr" means "complete."

"Istafziz" means: deceive and trick until he falls into your will. You say: "Istafazzanī fulān fī kadhā" (So-and-so provoked me into such-and-such) when he tricked you until you fell into a matter he intended. From lightness (khiffa) the calf of a cow is called "fazz." From this is Zuhayr's saying:

"As a wild ass calf flees from a predator, having feared the eyes, so it is not seen by the sharp-eyed."

(p-509) As for "al-ṣawt" (voice) here, it has been said that it means singing, flutes and entertainments, because these are all sounds specific to disobedience, and so they are attributed to Satan. This was said by Mujahid. It has also been said that it means: by your calling them to your obedience. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "His voice is the call of every sinner to the disobedience of Allah the Exalted."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that "al-ṣawt" encompasses all of that.

His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-ajlib" means "hawwil" (frighten), and "al-jalaba" is a loud, mixed, terrifying sound. Al-Ḥasan read "wa-ijlub" with a connecting alif and a ḍamma on the lām. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿with your cavalry and your infantry﴾ has been said to be a metaphor and figurative expression meaning: "Exert your effort and exhaust your utmost." It has also been said that it means he has cavalry and infantry from among the jinn, as said by Qatada. It has also been said that the meaning is the horsemen and foot soldiers of mankind who act in falsehood, for they are all helpers of Iblis against others, as said by Mujahid. The majority read "wa-rajlika" with a sukun on the jīm, which is the plural of rājil (foot soldier), like tājir and tajr (merchant and merchants), ṣāḥib and ṣaḥb (companion and companions), shārib and sharb (drinker and drinkers). Ḥafs from 'Asim read "wa-rajilika" with a kasra on the jīm, on the pattern fa'il, and likewise al-Ḥasan and Abu 'Amr (in one transmission) read it. It is an adjective: you say "fulān yamshī rajilan" (so-and-so walks on foot), meaning not riding. From this is the poet's saying:

"Shall I not fight for my religion on my horse, nor on foot without companions?"

(p-510) Qatada and 'Ikrima read "bi-khaylika wa-rijālika" (with your cavalry and your men).

His saying: ﴿and share with them in wealth﴾ is general to every act of disobedience that people commit with wealth, for spending it in disobedience is the path of Iblis. From this are cigarettes and the like, from this is the prostitute's fee, the price of wine, the gift of the soothsayer, usury, and other things found among people habitually. His saying "wal-awlād" (and children) is general to every disobedient act performed regarding offspring. From this is begetting children through fornication, from this is naming them 'Abd Shams, 'Abd al-Ḥārith, Abu al-Kuwayfir, and every hateful name, from this is the burying of daughters alive which the Arabs used to do, and from this is dyeing them into the religions of disbelief, and other things. As for what al-Naqqash introduced regarding intercourse with jinn and that they impregnate human women, it is all weak.

His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-'idhum" means: give them false hopes with what will not come to pass for them, and tell them that they will not be resurrected. This is sharing in the souls. Then Allah the Exalted informed that He promises them only as delusion from Him, because it does not benefit them at all.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ is a statement from Allah the Blessed and Exalted to Iblis. His saying "My servants" means the believers in disbelief and the pious in disobedience. He specified them as "servants," although it is a general term for all creation, because He intended to honor them and draw attention to them, just as a man says to one of his sons when he sees from him what pleases him: "This is my son," meaning as an alert from him and an honoring of him. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "This is my maternal uncle; let any man show me his maternal uncle." The word "sulṭān" means dominion and overpowering, and interpreting it here as "proof" is weak. Then Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿And your Lord is sufficient, O Muhammad, as a Guardian﴾, protecting the believers and watching over their guidance.

(p-٥١١) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Your Lord is the One who drives the ships for you through the sea, so that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed, He is ever Merciful to you.﴾ ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those whom you invoke vanish except Him. But when He delivers you to land, you turn away. And man is ever ungrateful.﴾ ﴿Do you then feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you, or send against you a storm of stones, and then you will find no protector for yourselves?﴾ ﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not return you to it another time and send against you a violent wind to drown you because of your disbelief, and then you will find no avenger against Us for it?﴾

"Al-izjā'" (driving along, propelling): driving what moves slowly, whether because of weakness, the heaviness of a load, or something else. Thus weak camels are "tuzjā" (driven), and from this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

﴿Upon beasts that bear them, driven, emaciated﴾

Clouds are also "tuzjā" (driven), and from this is the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that God drives the clouds?﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. The "biḍā'a al-muzjāt" (the meagre merchandise) is that which, because of its deficiency, needs to be pushed along with an intercession and carried by helpers to the one who accepts it. The driving of ships (izjā' al-fulk) is their propulsion by gentle winds and by oars. "Al-fulk" here is plural. "Al-baḥr" (the sea): abundant water, whether sweet or salt, and the name has become especially established for this well-known body of water in which ships run. The words "so that you may seek of His bounty" (li-tabtaghū min faḍlihi) is an expression that includes the sea and the seeking of reward through pilgrimage, raid, or the like. There is no disagreement about the permissibility of sailing for pilgrimage, jihad, and livelihood. There is disagreement about whether it is obligatory for pilgrimage, I mean for much of it, and about whether it is disliked for trade and for increasing wealth. The Messenger of God ﷺ was informed of sailing for a raid in the hadith of Umm Ḥarām. It has also been related from him that he said: "I will never sail the sea," and this is a hadith which may be understood as an opinion he held for himself, or it may be understood that this was revealed to him. This verse is a reminder of the favours of God and His bounty upon His servants.

(p-٥١٢) "Al-ḍurr" (harm) is a term that includes the fear of drowning and the restraint of walking, and its most terrifying states are the turbulence and surging of the waves. The words of God, the Exalted, "ḍalla" (vanished), mean: perished and was lost. It is an expression of contempt for whoever claims a god other than God, blessed and exalted is He. The meaning of this verse is that the disbelievers only believe of their idols that they intercede and that they have some merit. Each of them, by innate nature, knows with a knowledge he cannot repel that the idols have no action in great calamities. So God made them realise this at sea. The words of God, the Exalted, "kafūran" (ungrateful) means: towards the blessings. "Al-insān" (man) here is generic, and almost no one renders the thanks of God as it is due. Al-Zajjāj said: "Al-insān" is intended to mean the disbelievers.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is not a skilful view.

The words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Do you then feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you﴾, the verse.

The meaning: Do you then, O you who turn away and forget the hardship once you have come to ease, feel secure that God will not cause the land to swallow you in your place on dry ground, since you are in the grip of His power both at sea and on land?

"Al-ḥāṣib" (the storm of stones): the wind that strikes with hail, stones, and the like. From this is the verse of the poet:

﴿Facing the north of Syria, it strikes us
with a stone-storm like scattered cotton fibre﴾

And from this is the verse of al-Akhṭal:

﴿The thornbushes are pelted with a stone-storm of their snow,
until it spends the night upon the thornbushes in heaps﴾

And from this is the stone-storm (al-ḥāṣib) that struck the people of Lūṭ. "Al-ḥaṣb" is pelting with small pebbles, which are small stones.

Nāfi', 'Āṣim, Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī read "yakhsifu" with the "yā'" (ya), meaning God causes to sink. Likewise "yursila," "yu'īdakum," "fa-yursilu," and "fa-yughriqakum." Ibn Kathīr and Abū 'Amr read all of that with the "nūn" (nun). Abū Ja'far and Mujāhid read "fa-tughriqakum" with the "tā'" (ta), meaning the wind. Ḥamīd read "fa-nughriqkum" with the "nūn" lightly, and assimilated the "qāf" into the "kāf"; this was related from Abū 'Amr and Ibn Muḥaysin. Al-Ḥasan and Abū Rajā' read "fa-nugharriqakum" with a doubled "rā'." "Al-wakīl" is the one who manages affairs. "Al-qāṣif" is the one who breaks everything thrown into it and smashes it. "Tāratan" (another time): its plural is "tārāt" and "tīar," and its meaning is "another time." Abū Ja'far read "min al-riyāḥ" (from the winds) in the plural. "Al-tabī'" is the one who seeks vengeance, or a debt, or something like this. From this is the verse of the poet:

﴿They went out, and their gazelles went out with them, as though they were
guaranteed, firm-resolved, with ropes binding them, pursuers﴾

From this word is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When one of you is passed on to a wealthy person, let him follow (fa-l-yatba')." So the meaning is: you will find no one who follows up our action against you and seeks your help.
