Clouds are also "tuzjā" (driven), and from this is the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Do you not see that God drives the clouds?﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. The "biḍā'a al-muzjāt" (the meagre merchandise) is that which, because of its deficiency, needs to be pushed along with an intercession and carried by helpers to the one who accepts it. The driving of ships (izjā' al-fulk) is their propulsion by gentle winds and by oars. "Al-fulk" here is plural. "Al-baḥr" (the sea): abundant water, whether sweet or salt, and the name has become especially established for this well-known body of water in which ships run. The words "so that you may seek of His bounty" (li-tabtaghū min faḍlihi) is an expression that includes the sea and the seeking of reward through pilgrimage, raid, or the like. There is no disagreement about the permissibility of sailing for pilgrimage, jihad, and livelihood. There is disagreement about whether it is obligatory for pilgrimage, I mean for much of it, and about whether it is disliked for trade and for increasing wealth. The Messenger of God ﷺ was informed of sailing for a raid in the hadith of Umm Ḥarām. It has also been related from him that he said: "I will never sail the sea," and this is a hadith which may be understood as an opinion he held for himself, or it may be understood that this was revealed to him. This verse is a reminder of the favours of God and His bounty upon His servants.

(p-٥١٢) "Al-ḍurr" (harm) is a term that includes the fear of drowning and the restraint of walking, and its most terrifying states are the turbulence and surging of the waves. The words of God, the Exalted, "ḍalla" (vanished), mean: perished and was lost. It is an expression of contempt for whoever claims a god other than God, blessed and exalted is He. The meaning of this verse is that the disbelievers only believe of their idols that they intercede and that they have some merit. Each of them, by innate nature, knows with a knowledge he cannot repel that the idols have no action in great calamities. So God made them realise this at sea. The words of God, the Exalted, "kafūran" (ungrateful) means: towards the blessings. "Al-insān" (man) here is generic, and almost no one renders the thanks of God as it is due. Al-Zajjāj said: "Al-insān" is intended to mean the disbelievers.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is not a skilful view.

The words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Do you then feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you﴾, the verse.

The meaning: Do you then, O you who turn away and forget the hardship once you have come to ease, feel secure that God will not cause the land to swallow you in your place on dry ground, since you are in the grip of His power both at sea and on land?

"Al-ḥāṣib" (the storm of stones): the wind that strikes with hail, stones, and the like. From this is the verse of the poet:

﴿Facing the north of Syria, it strikes us
with a stone-storm like scattered cotton fibre﴾

And from this is the verse of al-Akhṭal:

﴿The thornbushes are pelted with a stone-storm of their snow,
until it spends the night upon the thornbushes in heaps﴾

And from this is the stone-storm (al-ḥāṣib) that struck the people of Lūṭ. "Al-ḥaṣb" is pelting with small pebbles, which are small stones.

Nāfi', 'Āṣim, Ibn 'Āmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī read "yakhsifu" with the "yā'" (ya), meaning God causes to sink. Likewise "yursila," "yu'īdakum," "fa-yursilu," and "fa-yughriqakum." Ibn Kathīr and Abū 'Amr read all of that with the "nūn" (nun). Abū Ja'far and Mujāhid read "fa-tughriqakum" with the "tā'" (ta), meaning the wind. Ḥamīd read "fa-nughriqkum" with the "nūn" lightly, and assimilated the "qāf" into the "kāf"; this was related from Abū 'Amr and Ibn Muḥaysin. Al-Ḥasan and Abū Rajā' read "fa-nugharriqakum" with a doubled "rā'." "Al-wakīl" is the one who manages affairs. "Al-qāṣif" is the one who breaks everything thrown into it and smashes it. "Tāratan" (another time): its plural is "tārāt" and "tīar," and its meaning is "another time." Abū Ja'far read "min al-riyāḥ" (from the winds) in the plural. "Al-tabī'" is the one who seeks vengeance, or a debt, or something like this. From this is the verse of the poet:

﴿They went out, and their gazelles went out with them, as though they were
guaranteed, firm-resolved, with ropes binding them, pursuers﴾

From this word is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When one of you is passed on to a wealthy person, let him follow (fa-l-yatba')." So the meaning is: you will find no one who follows up our action against you and seeks your help.

(p-514) Allah the Exalted says:

﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam and carried them on land and sea and provided for them of the good things and preferred them over much of what We have created, with [definite] preference.﴾ ﴿[Mention] the Day We will call every company of people with their leader. Then whoever is given his record in his right hand - those will read their records, and they will not be wronged even as much as the thread in a date pit.﴾ ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter and even more astray in way.﴾ ﴿And indeed, they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, to substitute for it other than it; and then they would have taken you as a friend.﴾ ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined to them a little.﴾ ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us.﴾

"Karramnā" is the intensive form of "karuma," so the meaning is: He made for them karam, that is, honor and excellence. This is the karam of freedom from deficiency, not the karam of wealth; it is like when you say "a noble garment" (thawb karīm), meaning its qualities are abundant.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse is one in which Allah enumerates what He has singled out for the children of Adam from among all other animals. The jinn are the numerous ones who are inferior, and the angels are those who are excluded from the numerous inferior ones. He carried them on land and sea, in a manner that is not suitable for any animal other than the children of Adam: to carry by their own will, intention and management on both land and sea together. And [He provided for them] "of the good things," and no animal benefits from provision as the children of Adam benefit; for they earn wealth specifically and not animals, they wear clothes, and they eat prepared foods, whereas the utmost any animal does is eat raw flesh or unprepared food. And "rizq" (provision) is everything from which benefit can be validly derived. Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: the preference is that he eats with his hands, while the rest of the animals eat with their mouths. Others said: and that he looks out from a higher vantage than any animal, walks upright, and similar preferences.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is unrefined, because animals of this kind possess that by which they would surpass the son of Adam, such as the running and hearing and sight of the horse, the strength of the elephant, the bravery of the lion, and the generosity of the rooster. Honor and preference come only through the intellect, by which he rules over all animals, by which he knows Allah the Exalted, understands His speech, and arrives at His bliss. (p-515) A group said: this verse necessitates the excellence of the angels over mankind, since they are the exception [in the verse's wording], and Allah the Blessed and Exalted has said: ﴿Nor the angels who are near [to Allah]﴾ [al-Nisa’: 172].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This does not necessarily follow from the verse. Rather, the preference between mankind and jinn is not what the verse intends; it may be that the angels are superior, it may be that they are equal, and the excellence of the angels is established from other places in the Sharia.

As for His saying: ﴿[Mention] the Day We will call every company of people with their leader﴾, the verse. The word "yawma" (the day) may be read as an accusative of time, with its governing verb being an implied verb whose estimate is: "remember," or a verb indicated by His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾, its estimate being: "and they will not be wronged on the Day We call," and then the latter "yuzlamūn" explains it. It is also permissible that it be governed by "faḍḍalnāhum" (We preferred them), since the superiority of mankind over the rest of the animals on the Day of Resurrection is clear, for they are the ones who are blessed, addressed, held accountable, and who possess capability. However, this is refuted by the fact that the disbelievers on that day are the greatest losers of all animals, since the disbeliever says: ﴿Would that I had been dust!﴾ [al-Naba’: 40]; and "nadʻū" cannot govern it because it is a genitive complement of it (i.e., it is in construct with it).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that "yawma" is in an indeclinable accusative form, because it is attached to something that is not fully declinable; its position would then be nominative as a subject, and the predicate would be in the division that follows in His saying: ﴿whoever is given﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and whoever was﴾.

(p-516) Al-Jumhur read "nadʻū" with the plural "we" (nūn of majesty). Mujahid read "yadʻū" with the yā', meaning: Allah calls; this is also related from ʿĀṣim. Al-Hasan read "yudʻā" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a sukūn on the wāw; its original form is "yudʻā," but it is a dialect of some Arabs who change this alif into a wāw, saying "afʻū" and "ḥublū." Abu al-Fath and Abu ʿAli mention these two in the discussion of "aʿmā" later on. Al-Hasan also read "kullu" in the nominative, meaning: "yudʻā kullu" (every company is called). Abu ʿAmr al-Dani related from al-Hasan that he read "yudʻā kullu." "Al-unās" is a collective noun with no singular from its own form.

As for His saying: "bi-imāmihim" (with their leader), it may mean: "by the name of their leader," and it may mean: "together with their leader." According to the first interpretation, one would say: "O community of Muhammad, peace be upon him," and "O followers of Pharaoh," and the like; and according to the second interpretation, every nation comes with its leader, whether a guide or a misleader. The exegetes differed concerning the imām: Mujahid and Qatadah said: their prophet. Abu Zayd said: their book that was revealed to them. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: their record that contains their deeds. A group said: whoever they follow, whether a guide or a misleader. The word "imām" encompasses all of this, because the imām is that which is followed and by which one is guided in the direction (of one's aim); from this it is said of a mason's line: imām. A poet describing an arrow-shaft said:

*"I straightened it until it was complete and even, / like the marrow of a shin or like the spine of an imām."*

(p-517) From this, the road is also called imām, because it is followed toward destinations until one reaches the intended goal.

As for His saying: ﴿Then whoever is given his record in his right hand﴾, it is literally indicative that on the Day of Resurrection there are scrolls that fly about and are placed in the right hands of the people of faith, and in the left of the people of disbelief, and placed in the right hands of the sinners upon whom the threat takes effect; they will thereby learn that they are not eternal in the Fire. His blessed and exalted saying: ﴿they will read their records﴾ is an expression of joy in them, meaning: they will repeat them and pass them to one another. His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged even as much as a fatīl﴾ means: not even less or more. This is the implied meaning of the discourse; what is left unstated has the same ruling as what is stated, like His saying: ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾ [al-Isra’: 23], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] an atom's weight﴾ [al-Nisa’: 40], and this is abundant. The meaning of the verse is that they will not be deprived of any part of the reward of their good deeds. "Fatīl" is the thread that is in the split of a date pit, and it is used as a proverb for smallness and insignificance of worth.

His saying: ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world]﴾, the verse. Muhammad ibn Abi Musa said: the reference of "hādhihi" (this) is to the blessings which He mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾; meaning: whoever was blind to thanking these blessings and to believing in their Giver, then he is blind regarding the matters and affairs of the Hereafter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The second "aʿmā" may be understood in the same sense as the first, as a metaphor for one blind of sight; and it may be an elative form, meaning: more blind. The "blindness" in this verse is blindness of the heart in both instances. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the reference of "hādhihi" is to this world, meaning: whoever was blind in this world to looking at the signs of Allah the Blessed and Exalted and His lessons, and to believing in His signs, ﴿then he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾; this may be by omitting a noun, meaning: regarding the matter of the Hereafter, or it may mean: then he will be blind on the Day of Resurrection, in the sense that he is bewildered, no right course is directed to him, and no success appears to him. Mujahid said: "blind in the Hereafter" means blind to his proof.

(p-518) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning to me is that the reference of "hādhihi" is to this world, i.e., whoever in this worldly life of his, and at the time of his perception and understanding, was blind to reflecting upon the signs of Allah the Exalted, then in the Hereafter he will be even more bewildered and blinder, because he has experienced loss and seen the signs of punishment. With this interpretation there is a parallel with the preceding verses that mention whoever is given his record in his right hand; and if we take His saying "fil-ākhirah" (in the Hereafter) to mean "regarding the matter of the Hereafter," the parallel between the two is not sustained.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, and Hafs from ʿĀṣim read "aʿmā" in both places without imāla (inclination). Hamza, al-Kisa’i, and ʿĀṣim (in a variant from him) read it in both places with imāla. Abu ʿAmr read the first with imāla and the second without, interpreting it in the sense of "more blind," and therefore did not incline it. Abu ʿAmr said: imāla is only proper at word-endings, and "aʿmā" is not like that, because its estimate is "aʿmā min kadhā" (blinder than such-and-such), so it is not complete except in saying "min kadhā," as is similar to it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He made him "more astray in way" in the Hereafter because the disbeliever in this world is able to believe and be saved, whereas in the Hereafter that is not possible for him; so he is more astray in way, more bewildered, and nearer to punishment. Sibawayh's statement, "one does not say aʿmā min kadhā, just as one says mā aydāh" (how strong he is), applies only to blindness of the eye, in which there is no gradation; but in blindness of the heart, that is said, because gradation occurs in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Makki mentioned regarding this verse that the first blindness is blindness of the eye from guidance. This is clearly flawed, and Allah is the Helper.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾, the verse. The "in" here, according to Sibawayh, is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and the lām in His saying "layaftinūnaka" is the lām of emphasis. According to al-Farra’, this "in" means "mā" (not), and the lām means "innamā" (only). The pronoun in His saying "kādū" (they had almost) is said to refer to Quraysh, and it is said to refer to Thaqif. As for Quraysh, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: the verse was revealed because they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We will not leave you to touch the Black Stone until you touch our idols," as a demand by way of legislation for that. al-Tabari and others said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ resolved to show them that, while his heart rejected it, so the verse was revealed concerning that. al-Zajjaj said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to himself: "What harm is there in my doing that for them, when Allah knows what is in my heart?" Ibn Ishaq and others said: they gathered one night, exalted him, and said to him: "You are our master, but: turn to some of our affair and we will turn to some of yours," so the verse was revealed concerning that.

(p-519) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. al-Zajjaj related that it was said the verse concerns what they wanted of driving away the poor among his companions.

As for Thaqif, Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and others said: because they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to defer them, after their conversion, for a year during which they would worship al-Lat, saying: "We want to take what is offered to it; but if you fear that the Arabs will object to you for this, then say: Allah revealed that to me." So the verse was revealed concerning that. Whoever holds this view must consider the verse Medinan, and that has been related; while those who hold the other views related that it is Meccan.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Everything that was desired of the Prophet ﷺ according to these differing reports, Allah the Exalted has revealed to him the opposite of it, whether in a miracle or not in a miracle; and his act, were it to have occurred, would be a fabrication against Allah, since all his deeds and sayings are entirely sharia.

His saying: ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ is a warning concerning what Allah the Exalted saved him from, namely opposing the disbelievers and allying with them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 70–75 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying, ﴿Had We not made you firm﴾ to the end of the verse, is an enumeration of a blessing upon the Prophet (ﷺ). It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) (p-520)

"Al-rukun" (الرُكُونُ) means bracing the back toward the matter, or resolving upon the direction of inclining toward it, as a person leans on a corner (rukn) of walls. From it is His saying, related as a narrative: ﴿Or I could take refuge in a strong pillar﴾ [Hud: 80]. The majority of reciters (Jumhur) read "tarkanu" (تَرْكَنُ) with a fatha on the kaf, while Ibn Musarrif, Qatada, and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq read "turkunu" (تُرْكُنُ) with a damma on the kaf.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not incline, but he came close, according to the measure of his concern, to agreeing with them, out of hope of winning them over. Ibn al-Anbari held that its meaning is: "They almost said about you that you had inclined," and similar. In this he went to negating the Prophet's (ﷺ) concern with that, and so he loaded the wording with what it cannot bear. His saying, ﴿a little thing﴾, refutes that. This concern on the part of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only a passing thought that could not be warded off, and for this reason it was said "kidta" (كِدْتَ, "you almost"), which indicates that he did not incline. Then it was said ﴿a little thing﴾, since the closeness implied by "kidta" was slight, a fleeting thought that did not become firm in the soul. This concern is like the concern of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the statement regarding both is one. His saying, ﴿Then We would have made you taste﴾, also refutes what Ibn al-Anbari held.

His saying, ﴿double the life and double the death﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Dahhak said: it means double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The meaning is that what this sin deserves of our punishment in this world and the Hereafter, We would have doubled for you. This doubling is common for the Prophet (ﷺ) in his reward and his pain, and in the punishment of his wives. The rest of the verse is clear.

Then whoever is given his record in his right hand - those will read their records, and they will not be wronged even as much as the thread in a date pit.﴾ ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter and even more astray in way.﴾ ﴿And indeed, they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, to substitute for it other than it; and then they would have taken you as a friend.﴾ ﴿And had We not given you firmness, you would have almost inclined to them a little.﴾ ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us.﴾

"Karramnā" is the intensive form of "karuma," so the meaning is: He made for them karam, that is, honor and excellence. This is the karam of freedom from deficiency, not the karam of wealth; it is like when you say "a noble garment" (thawb karīm), meaning its qualities are abundant.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse is one in which Allah enumerates what He has singled out for the children of Adam from among all other animals. The jinn are the numerous ones who are inferior, and the angels are those who are excluded from the numerous inferior ones. He carried them on land and sea, in a manner that is not suitable for any animal other than the children of Adam: to carry by their own will, intention and management on both land and sea together. And [He provided for them] "of the good things," and no animal benefits from provision as the children of Adam benefit; for they earn wealth specifically and not animals, they wear clothes, and they eat prepared foods, whereas the utmost any animal does is eat raw flesh or unprepared food. And "rizq" (provision) is everything from which benefit can be validly derived. Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: the preference is that he eats with his hands, while the rest of the animals eat with their mouths. Others said: and that he looks out from a higher vantage than any animal, walks upright, and similar preferences.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is unrefined, because animals of this kind possess that by which they would surpass the son of Adam, such as the running and hearing and sight of the horse, the strength of the elephant, the bravery of the lion, and the generosity of the rooster. Honor and preference come only through the intellect, by which he rules over all animals, by which he knows Allah the Exalted, understands His speech, and arrives at His bliss. (p-515) A group said: this verse necessitates the excellence of the angels over mankind, since they are the exception [in the verse's wording], and Allah the Blessed and Exalted has said: ﴿Nor the angels who are near [to Allah]﴾ [al-Nisa’: 172].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This does not necessarily follow from the verse. Rather, the preference between mankind and jinn is not what the verse intends; it may be that the angels are superior, it may be that they are equal, and the excellence of the angels is established from other places in the Sharia.

As for His saying: ﴿[Mention] the Day We will call every company of people with their leader﴾, the verse. The word "yawma" (the day) may be read as an accusative of time, with its governing verb being an implied verb whose estimate is: "remember," or a verb indicated by His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾, its estimate being: "and they will not be wronged on the Day We call," and then the latter "yuzlamūn" explains it. It is also permissible that it be governed by "faḍḍalnāhum" (We preferred them), since the superiority of mankind over the rest of the animals on the Day of Resurrection is clear, for they are the ones who are blessed, addressed, held accountable, and who possess capability. However, this is refuted by the fact that the disbelievers on that day are the greatest losers of all animals, since the disbeliever says: ﴿Would that I had been dust!﴾ [al-Naba’: 40]; and "nadʻū" cannot govern it because it is a genitive complement of it (i.e., it is in construct with it).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also possible that "yawma" is in an indeclinable accusative form, because it is attached to something that is not fully declinable; its position would then be nominative as a subject, and the predicate would be in the division that follows in His saying: ﴿whoever is given﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and whoever was﴾.

(p-516) Al-Jumhur read "nadʻū" with the plural "we" (nūn of majesty). Mujahid read "yadʻū" with the yā', meaning: Allah calls; this is also related from ʿĀṣim. Al-Hasan read "yudʻā" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a sukūn on the wāw; its original form is "yudʻā," but it is a dialect of some Arabs who change this alif into a wāw, saying "afʻū" and "ḥublū." Abu al-Fath and Abu ʿAli mention these two in the discussion of "aʿmā" later on. Al-Hasan also read "kullu" in the nominative, meaning: "yudʻā kullu" (every company is called). Abu ʿAmr al-Dani related from al-Hasan that he read "yudʻā kullu." "Al-unās" is a collective noun with no singular from its own form.

As for His saying: "bi-imāmihim" (with their leader), it may mean: "by the name of their leader," and it may mean: "together with their leader." According to the first interpretation, one would say: "O community of Muhammad, peace be upon him," and "O followers of Pharaoh," and the like; and according to the second interpretation, every nation comes with its leader, whether a guide or a misleader. The exegetes differed concerning the imām: Mujahid and Qatadah said: their prophet. Abu Zayd said: their book that was revealed to them. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: their record that contains their deeds. A group said: whoever they follow, whether a guide or a misleader. The word "imām" encompasses all of this, because the imām is that which is followed and by which one is guided in the direction (of one's aim); from this it is said of a mason's line: imām. A poet describing an arrow-shaft said:

*"I straightened it until it was complete and even, / like the marrow of a shin or like the spine of an imām."*

(p-517) From this, the road is also called imām, because it is followed toward destinations until one reaches the intended goal.

As for His saying: ﴿Then whoever is given his record in his right hand﴾, it is literally indicative that on the Day of Resurrection there are scrolls that fly about and are placed in the right hands of the people of faith, and in the left of the people of disbelief, and placed in the right hands of the sinners upon whom the threat takes effect; they will thereby learn that they are not eternal in the Fire. His blessed and exalted saying: ﴿they will read their records﴾ is an expression of joy in them, meaning: they will repeat them and pass them to one another. His saying: ﴿and they will not be wronged even as much as a fatīl﴾ means: not even less or more. This is the implied meaning of the discourse; what is left unstated has the same ruling as what is stated, like His saying: ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾ [al-Isra’: 23], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong [anyone] an atom's weight﴾ [al-Nisa’: 40], and this is abundant. The meaning of the verse is that they will not be deprived of any part of the reward of their good deeds. "Fatīl" is the thread that is in the split of a date pit, and it is used as a proverb for smallness and insignificance of worth.

His saying: ﴿And whoever was blind in this [world]﴾, the verse. Muhammad ibn Abi Musa said: the reference of "hādhihi" (this) is to the blessings which He mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾; meaning: whoever was blind to thanking these blessings and to believing in their Giver, then he is blind regarding the matters and affairs of the Hereafter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The second "aʿmā" may be understood in the same sense as the first, as a metaphor for one blind of sight; and it may be an elative form, meaning: more blind. The "blindness" in this verse is blindness of the heart in both instances. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the reference of "hādhihi" is to this world, meaning: whoever was blind in this world to looking at the signs of Allah the Blessed and Exalted and His lessons, and to believing in His signs, ﴿then he will be blind in the Hereafter﴾; this may be by omitting a noun, meaning: regarding the matter of the Hereafter, or it may mean: then he will be blind on the Day of Resurrection, in the sense that he is bewildered, no right course is directed to him, and no success appears to him. Mujahid said: "blind in the Hereafter" means blind to his proof.

(p-518) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning to me is that the reference of "hādhihi" is to this world, i.e., whoever in this worldly life of his, and at the time of his perception and understanding, was blind to reflecting upon the signs of Allah the Exalted, then in the Hereafter he will be even more bewildered and blinder, because he has experienced loss and seen the signs of punishment. With this interpretation there is a parallel with the preceding verses that mention whoever is given his record in his right hand; and if we take His saying "fil-ākhirah" (in the Hereafter) to mean "regarding the matter of the Hereafter," the parallel between the two is not sustained.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, and Hafs from ʿĀṣim read "aʿmā" in both places without imāla (inclination). Hamza, al-Kisa’i, and ʿĀṣim (in a variant from him) read it in both places with imāla. Abu ʿAmr read the first with imāla and the second without, interpreting it in the sense of "more blind," and therefore did not incline it. Abu ʿAmr said: imāla is only proper at word-endings, and "aʿmā" is not like that, because its estimate is "aʿmā min kadhā" (blinder than such-and-such), so it is not complete except in saying "min kadhā," as is similar to it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He made him "more astray in way" in the Hereafter because the disbeliever in this world is able to believe and be saved, whereas in the Hereafter that is not possible for him; so he is more astray in way, more bewildered, and nearer to punishment. Sibawayh's statement, "one does not say aʿmā min kadhā, just as one says mā aydāh" (how strong he is), applies only to blindness of the eye, in which there is no gradation; but in blindness of the heart, that is said, because gradation occurs in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Makki mentioned regarding this verse that the first blindness is blindness of the eye from guidance. This is clearly flawed, and Allah is the Helper.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾, the verse. The "in" here, according to Sibawayh, is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and the lām in His saying "layaftinūnaka" is the lām of emphasis. According to al-Farra’, this "in" means "mā" (not), and the lām means "innamā" (only). The pronoun in His saying "kādū" (they had almost) is said to refer to Quraysh, and it is said to refer to Thaqif. As for Quraysh, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: the verse was revealed because they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We will not leave you to touch the Black Stone until you touch our idols," as a demand by way of legislation for that. al-Tabari and others said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ resolved to show them that, while his heart rejected it, so the verse was revealed concerning that. al-Zajjaj said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to himself: "What harm is there in my doing that for them, when Allah knows what is in my heart?" Ibn Ishaq and others said: they gathered one night, exalted him, and said to him: "You are our master, but: turn to some of our affair and we will turn to some of yours," so the verse was revealed concerning that.

(p-519) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9]. al-Zajjaj related that it was said the verse concerns what they wanted of driving away the poor among his companions.

As for Thaqif, Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and others said: because they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to defer them, after their conversion, for a year during which they would worship al-Lat, saying: "We want to take what is offered to it; but if you fear that the Arabs will object to you for this, then say: Allah revealed that to me." So the verse was revealed concerning that. Whoever holds this view must consider the verse Medinan, and that has been related; while those who hold the other views related that it is Meccan.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Everything that was desired of the Prophet ﷺ according to these differing reports, Allah the Exalted has revealed to him the opposite of it, whether in a miracle or not in a miracle; and his act, were it to have occurred, would be a fabrication against Allah, since all his deeds and sayings are entirely sharia.

His saying: ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾ is a warning concerning what Allah the Exalted saved him from, namely opposing the disbelievers and allying with them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 70–75 (part 2 of 2):

And His saying, ﴿Had We not made you firm﴾ to the end of the verse, is an enumeration of a blessing upon the Prophet (ﷺ). It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) (p-520)

"Al-rukun" (الرُكُونُ) means bracing the back toward the matter, or resolving upon the direction of inclining toward it, as a person leans on a corner (rukn) of walls. From it is His saying, related as a narrative: ﴿Or I could take refuge in a strong pillar﴾ [Hud: 80]. The majority of reciters (Jumhur) read "tarkanu" (تَرْكَنُ) with a fatha on the kaf, while Ibn Musarrif, Qatada, and 'Abdullah ibn Abi Ishaq read "turkunu" (تُرْكُنُ) with a damma on the kaf.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not incline, but he came close, according to the measure of his concern, to agreeing with them, out of hope of winning them over. Ibn al-Anbari held that its meaning is: "They almost said about you that you had inclined," and similar. In this he went to negating the Prophet's (ﷺ) concern with that, and so he loaded the wording with what it cannot bear. His saying, ﴿a little thing﴾, refutes that. This concern on the part of the Prophet (ﷺ) was only a passing thought that could not be warded off, and for this reason it was said "kidta" (كِدْتَ, "you almost"), which indicates that he did not incline. Then it was said ﴿a little thing﴾, since the closeness implied by "kidta" was slight, a fleeting thought that did not become firm in the soul. This concern is like the concern of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the statement regarding both is one. His saying, ﴿Then We would have made you taste﴾, also refutes what Ibn al-Anbari held.

His saying, ﴿double the life and double the death﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Dahhak said: it means double the punishment of life and double the punishment of death.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The meaning is that what this sin deserves of our punishment in this world and the Hereafter, We would have doubled for you. This doubling is common for the Prophet (ﷺ) in his reward and his pain, and in the punishment of his wives. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 76–79 (part 1 of 2):

(p-521) His Exalted and Majestic saying:
﴿And indeed they almost incited you to drive you out of the land, but then they would not have remained after you except a little.﴾ ﴿[This is] the way of those We sent before you of Our messengers, and you will not find in Our way any alteration.﴾ ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night and [also] the recitation of dawn. Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾ ﴿And from the night, pray with it as additional worship for you; it is expected that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾

Ḥaḍramī said: The pronoun in "kādū" refers to the Jews of Madina and its surroundings, such as Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and others, because they set out to scheme against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They said: "This land is not the land of the prophets; the land of the prophets is in al-Shām. But you fear the Romans. So if you are a prophet, go out to it, for Allah will protect you just as He protected other prophets." So the verse was revealed concerning that, and Allah informed that if His Messenger had gone out, they would not have remained after him except a little.

Al-Naqqāsh related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out because of their saying, and encamped at Dhū al-Ḥulayfa, waiting for his companions, and then the verse was revealed to him, so he returned.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is weak; it is not found in any biography or in any book that is relied upon, and Dhū al-Ḥulayfa is not on the route to al-Shām.

Another group said: the pronoun in "kādū" refers to Quraysh. Al-Zajjāj related that their incitement was what they had agreed upon in Dār al-Nadwa concerning killing him. The "land" in this view is general, meaning the world, as if he said: "they would drive you out of the world." According to all the other opinions, it is a specific land, either Makka or Madina, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 33], or its meaning is: from the land in which they have their control and enjoyment. Ibn 'Abbās and Qatāda said: the incitement of Quraysh was what they went to of expelling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makka, just as they had earlier gone to besiege him in the mountain pass. This incitement of theirs occurred after the revelation of the verse; they constricted him until he left, and they pursued him to the cave and other things, and [Allah] carried out the threat against them, that they would not remain after him except a little, on the day of Badr.

Mujāhid said: Quraysh went toward this, but it did not happen from them, because when Allah willed to preserve Quraysh and not to uproot them, He permitted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to emigrate. So he left the land by Allah's permission, not by Quraysh's subjugation, and Quraysh was spared, and from them and their descendants those who embraced Islam became Muslims. He said: Had Quraysh expelled him, they would have been punished. Mujāhid, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the pronoun in "yalbathūn" is general, referring to all of them. In the codex of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd it reads: "wa-idhan lā yalbathū" with the nūn dropped and "idhan" operative, whereas the rest of the readers nullified it and affirmed the nūn. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ recited: "yulabbathūn" with a damma on the yā', a shadda on the bā', and a fatḥa on the lām; and the like was related from Yaʿqūb except that he read the bā' with a kasra. ʿAṭāʾ recited: "baʿdaka illā qalīlan," whereas the majority read "khalfaka"; Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read "khilāfaka," and the meaning is one. From it is the poet's saying:
"ʿAqaba al-raddhādu khilāfahā fa-ka-annamā / basaṭa al-shawāṭib baynahunna ḥaṣīran"
And from it is His saying: ﴿those who were left behind rejoiced in their seat, contrary to the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 81], according to some of its interpretations, meaning: after the departure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This word necessarily involves the omission of a governed noun, because the estimate in our verse is "khilāfa khurūjika," and in the poet's verse "khilāfa inbisāṭi al-shams" or something similar.

Abū ʿAlī said: They used these adverbial nouns only when they are attached to concrete nouns that are not events, so they did not prefer attaching them to anything other than what their speech had been accustomed to, just as when they came in the accusative in their speech they left them in their state when they occurred in a non-accusative position, as in His saying: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those beneath that﴾ [al-Jinn: 11], and His saying: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection He will separate you﴾ [al-Mumtaḥana: 3].

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
As for His saying "sunnata," it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the accusative by the deletion of the preposition, because the meaning is "like the sunna," so he deleted the kāf and put it in the accusative.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
It follows from this that one should not stop at His saying "qalīlan."

The meaning of the verse is the report that the sunna of Allah the Exalted regarding the earlier nations and His custom is that when a nation drives out its prophet from among them, punishment befalls them and destruction uproots them, so they do not remain after him except a little.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ and the rest of the verse. By the consensus of the exegetes, this refers to the obligatory prayers.

Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Burda, al-Ḥasan, and the majority said: "dulūk al-shams" is its decline (zawāl), and it refers to Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr; "ghasaq al-layl" refers to Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ; and "qurʾān al-fajr" means the Ṣubḥ prayer. So the verse, according to this, encompasses all the prayers. Ibn Masʿūd related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Jibrīl came to me at the decline of the sun when it passed the zenith, and he led me in Ẓuhr prayer." Jābir related that the Prophet (ﷺ) went out from his presence, having eaten, and the sun had passed its zenith, and he said: "Go out, Abū Bakr, for this is the time when the sun has declined."

Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "dulūk al-shams" is its setting (ghurūb), and the reference by it is to Maghrib. "Ghasaq al-layl" is the gathering of its darkness, so the reference is to ʿAtma. "Qurʾān al-fajr" is the Ṣubḥ prayer. According to this interpretation, no reference is made to Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The first opinion is more correct because of its generality over the prayers, and both are, linguistically, good meanings. "Dulūk" is inclination in the language. Its beginning is the zenith and its end is Maghrib, and from the time of zenith to sunset it is called "dulūk," because the sun is in a state of inclination. So Allah mentioned the prayers that occur during the dulūk and at it, and thus Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, and Maghrib enter into it, and it is valid that Maghrib is included in "ghasaq al-layl." From "dulūk," which is inclination, is the saying of the Bedouin to al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan: "Does a man dālik his wife?" He meant: does he incline with her toward delaying the payment of her debt? Al-Ḥasan said to him: "Yes, if he is mulḥif," meaning impoverished. From it is the saying of Dhū al-Rumma:
"Maṣābīḥ laysat bi-l-lawātī taqūduhā / nujūmun wa-lā bi-l-āfilāti al-dawālik"
And from that is the saying of the poet:
"Hādhā makānu qadamayya Rabāḥ / ghadwatan ḥattā dalakat Barāḥ"
(p-525) It is also related as "bi-Barāḥ" with a kasra on the bā'. Abū ʿUbayda, al-Aṣmaʿī, and Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī said: its meaning is "by the palm of the viewer," who shades himself with it always, so as to see how its inclination is and what remains of it. This is similar to the saying of al-Ḥajjāj:
"Wa-l-shamsu qad kādat takūnu danafan / adfaʿuhā bi-l-rāḥi kay tazḥalafā"
Al-Ṭabarī mentioned from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "dalakat bi-Barāḥ, meaning: by Barāḥ as a place." He said: if this is from the tafsir of Ibn Masʿūd, then he is most knowing; and if it is from the speech of a transmitter, then the people of gharīb are most knowing of it.
The first verse is also related as: "ghadwatan ḥattā halakat Barāḥ" with a fatḥa on the bā', on the pattern of Qaṭām and Ḥizām, and it is a name of the sun.

"Ghasaq al-layl" is its gathering and the thickening of its darkness. The poet said:
"Āba hādhā al-layl idh ghasaqā"
Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "ghasaq al-layl" is its beginning.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, its estimate being: "and recite the recitation of dawn." It is also valid that it be in the accusative by coordination with "al-ṣalāh," meaning: "and establish the recitation of dawn." He expressed the Ṣubḥ prayer specifically by "the Qurʾān" because the Qurʾān is its core, since its recitation is long and laborious. It is also valid that "qurʾāna" be in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ). His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ means: it is witnessed by the guardian angels of the day and the guardian angels of the night, as stated in the well-known hadith in his words, upon him be peace: "Angels succeed one another among you, angels by night and angels by day, and they gather at the Ṣubḥ prayer and the ʿAṣr prayer," the hadith in full, related from Abū Hurayra and others. On this interpretation the majority proceeded.

Al-Ṭabarī mentioned a hadith from Ibn ʿAskar, through the route of Abū al-Dardāʾ, regarding His saying: ﴿was witnessed﴾. Muḥammad ibn Sahl ibn ʿAskar said: (Allah witnesses it, and His angels). He mentioned in that hadith that Allah, blessed and exalted, descends in the last part of the night, and similar things that are not strong.

(p-527) His saying the Exalted: ﴿And from the night﴾: "min" is partitive, and the estimate is: "and a time from the night," meaning: establish a time from the night. The pronoun in "bihi" returns to this estimated noun. It is also possible that it returns to the Qurʾān, although no mention of it has preceded absolutely, just as the pronoun is absolute, but it occurred as an addition to "al-fajr." "Tahajjad" means: cast off sleep from yourself. "Hujūd" is sleep; it is said: "hajada yahjudu" with a damma on the jīm, "hujūdan," when he slept. From it is the saying of the poet:
"Alā ṭaraqatnā wa-l-rifāqu hujūdun / fa-bātat bi-ʿillāti al-nawāli tajūdu"
And from it is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:
"Fa-ḥayyāki wudduñ mā hadāki li-fityatin / wa-khūṣin bi-aʿlā dhī ṭuwālatin hujjadi"
This verb operates on the pattern of: taḥarraba, taḥarraja, ta'aththama, taḥannatha. Similar to it is: ﴿so you would remain amazed﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 65], meaning: you would regret, that is, you would cast fruit away from yourselves, and it is the expansion and joy of the soul. It is said: "a man is fakih" when he is much given to joy and laughter. So the meaning is: and a time from the night, stay awake with it in prayer and recitation. The hadith in full is in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, so we have abridged it. And because of that possibility which it has for the pleasure of all the world, believers and disbelievers alike, he said: "I am the master of the children of Ādam and there is no boasting." And "ʿasā" from Allah is binding, and "maqāman" is in the accusative as an adverbial noun.

Among the strange features of the hadith of intercession is its abridgment of the meaning. The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I should translate this faithfully. Here is the translation:

It is fitting that this be interpreted in accordance with what we have said: that it applies to his community and to others; or it may be said that each of the two is a praiseworthy station (maqam mahmud). Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 76–79 (part 1 of 2):

(p-521) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾ ﴿And from the night, pray with it as additional worship for you; it is expected that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾

Ḥaḍramī said: The pronoun in "kādū" refers to the Jews of Madina and its surroundings, such as Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and others, because they set out to scheme against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They said: "This land is not the land of the prophets; the land of the prophets is in al-Shām. But you fear the Romans. So if you are a prophet, go out to it, for Allah will protect you just as He protected other prophets." So the verse was revealed concerning that, and Allah informed that if His Messenger had gone out, they would not have remained after him except a little.

Al-Naqqāsh related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out because of their saying, and encamped at Dhū al-Ḥulayfa, waiting for his companions, and then the verse was revealed to him, so he returned.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is weak; it is not found in any biography or in any book that is relied upon, and Dhū al-Ḥulayfa is not on the route to al-Shām.

Another group said: the pronoun in "kādū" refers to Quraysh. Al-Zajjāj related that their incitement was what they had agreed upon in Dār al-Nadwa concerning killing him. The "land" in this view is general, meaning the world, as if he said: "they would drive you out of the world." According to all the other opinions, it is a specific land, either Makka or Madina, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 33], or its meaning is: from the land in which they have their control and enjoyment. Ibn 'Abbās and Qatāda said: the incitement of Quraysh was what they went to of expelling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makka, just as they had earlier gone to besiege him in the mountain pass. This incitement of theirs occurred after the revelation of the verse; they constricted him until he left, and they pursued him to the cave and other things, and [Allah] carried out the threat against them, that they would not remain after him except a little, on the day of Badr.

Mujāhid said: Quraysh went toward this, but it did not happen from them, because when Allah willed to preserve Quraysh and not to uproot them, He permitted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to emigrate. So he left the land by Allah's permission, not by Quraysh's subjugation, and Quraysh was spared, and from them and their descendants those who embraced Islam became Muslims. He said: Had Quraysh expelled him, they would have been punished. Mujāhid, may Allah have mercy on him, held that the pronoun in "yalbathūn" is general, referring to all of them. From it is the poet's saying:
"ʿAqaba al-raddhādu khilāfahā fa-ka-annamā / basaṭa al-shawāṭib baynahunna ḥaṣīran"
And from it is His saying: ﴿those who were left behind rejoiced in their seat, contrary to the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 81], according to some of its interpretations, meaning: after the departure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This word necessarily involves the omission of a governed noun, because the estimate in our verse is "khilāfa khurūjika," and in the poet's verse "khilāfa inbisāṭi al-shams" or something similar.

Abū ʿAlī said: They used these adverbial nouns only when they are attached to concrete nouns that are not events, so they did not prefer attaching them to anything other than what their speech had been accustomed to, just as when they came in the accusative in their speech they left them in their state when they occurred in a non-accusative position, as in His saying: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those beneath that﴾ [al-Jinn: 11], and His saying: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection He will separate you﴾ [al-Mumtaḥana: 3].

As for His saying "sunnata," it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the accusative by the deletion of the preposition, because the meaning is "like the sunna," so he deleted the kāf and put it in the accusative.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
It follows from this that one should not stop at His saying "qalīlan."

The meaning of the verse is the report that the sunna of Allah the Exalted regarding the earlier nations and His custom is that when a nation drives out its prophet from among them, punishment befalls them and destruction uproots them, so they do not remain after him except a little.

Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "dulūk al-shams" is its setting (ghurūb), and the reference by it is to Maghrib. The first opinion is more correct because of its generality over the prayers, and both are, linguistically, good meanings. "Dulūk" is inclination in the language. "Maṣābīḥ laysat bi-l-lawātī taqūduhā / nujūmun wa-lā bi-l-āfilāti al-dawālik"
And from that is the saying of the poet:
"Hādhā makānu qadamayya Rabāḥ / ghadwatan ḥattā dalakat Barāḥ"

This is similar to the saying of al-Ḥajjāj:
"Wa-l-shamsu qad kādat takūnu danafan / adfaʿuhā bi-l-rāḥi kay tazḥalafā"
Al-Ṭabarī mentioned from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "dalakat bi-Barāḥ, meaning: by Barāḥ as a place." He said: if this is from the tafsir of Ibn Masʿūd, then he is most knowing; and if it is from the speech of a transmitter, then the people of gharīb are most knowing of it.
The first verse is also related as: "ghadwatan ḥattā halakat Barāḥ" with a fatḥa on the bā', on the pattern of Qaṭām and Ḥizām, and it is a name of the sun.

"Ghasaq al-layl" is its gathering and the thickening of its darkness. The poet said:
"Āba hādhā al-layl idh ghasaqā"
Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "ghasaq al-layl" is its beginning.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, its estimate being: "and recite the recitation of dawn." It is also valid that it be in the accusative by coordination with "al-ṣalāh," meaning: "and establish the recitation of dawn." He expressed the Ṣubḥ prayer specifically by "the Qurʾān" because the Qurʾān is its core, since its recitation is long and laborious. It is also valid that "qurʾāna" be in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ). His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ means: it is witnessed by the guardian angels of the day and the guardian angels of the night, as stated in the well-known hadith in his words, upon him be peace: "Angels succeed one another among you, angels by night and angels by day, and they gather at the Ṣubḥ prayer and the ʿAṣr prayer," the hadith in full, related from Abū Hurayra and others. On this interpretation the majority proceeded.

Al-Ṭabarī mentioned a hadith from Ibn ʿAskar, through the route of Abū al-Dardāʾ, regarding His saying: ﴿was witnessed﴾. Muḥammad ibn Sahl ibn ʿAskar said: (Allah witnesses it, and His angels). He mentioned in that hadith that Allah, blessed and exalted, descends in the last part of the night, and similar things that are not strong.

Ibn Masʿūd related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Jibrīl came to me at the decline of the sun when it passed the zenith, and he led me in Ẓuhr prayer." Jābir related that the Prophet (ﷺ) went out from his presence, having eaten, and the sun had passed its zenith, and he said: "Go out, Abū Bakr, for this is the time when the sun has declined."

Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Zayd ibn Aslam said: "dulūk al-shams" is its setting (ghurūb), and the reference by it is to Maghrib. "Ghasaq al-layl" is the gathering of its darkness, so the reference is to ʿAtma. "Qurʾān al-fajr" is the Ṣubḥ prayer. According to this interpretation, no reference is made to Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The first opinion is more correct because of its generality over the prayers, and both are, linguistically, good meanings. "Dulūk" is inclination in the language. Its beginning is the zenith and its end is Maghrib, and from the time of zenith to sunset it is called "dulūk," because the sun is in a state of inclination. So Allah mentioned the prayers that occur during the dulūk and at it, and thus Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, and Maghrib enter into it, and it is valid that Maghrib is included in "ghasaq al-layl." From "dulūk," which is inclination, is the saying of the Bedouin to al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan: "Does a man dālik his wife?" He meant: does he incline with her toward delaying the payment of her debt? Al-Ḥasan said to him: "Yes, if he is mulḥif," meaning impoverished. From it is the saying of Dhū al-Rumma:
"Maṣābīḥ laysat bi-l-lawātī taqūduhā / nujūmun wa-lā bi-l-āfilāti al-dawālik"
And from that is the saying of the poet:
"Hādhā makānu qadamayya Rabāḥ / ghadwatan ḥattā dalakat Barāḥ"
(p-525) It is also related as "bi-Barāḥ" with a kasra on the bā'. Abū ʿUbayda, al-Aṣmaʿī, and Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī said: its meaning is "by the palm of the viewer," who shades himself with it always, so as to see how its inclination is and what remains of it. This is similar to the saying of al-Ḥajjāj:
"Wa-l-shamsu qad kādat takūnu danafan / adfaʿuhā bi-l-rāḥi kay tazḥalafā"
Al-Ṭabarī mentioned from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "dalakat bi-Barāḥ, meaning: by Barāḥ as a place." He said: if this is from the tafsir of Ibn Masʿūd, then he is most knowing; and if it is from the speech of a transmitter, then the people of gharīb are most knowing of it.
The first verse is also related as: "ghadwatan ḥattā halakat Barāḥ" with a fatḥa on the bā', on the pattern of Qaṭām and Ḥizām, and it is a name of the sun.

"Ghasaq al-layl" is its gathering and the thickening of its darkness. The poet said:
"Āba hādhā al-layl idh ghasaqā"
Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "ghasaq al-layl" is its beginning.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, its estimate being: "and recite the recitation of dawn." It is also valid that it be in the accusative by coordination with "al-ṣalāh," meaning: "and establish the recitation of dawn." He expressed the Ṣubḥ prayer specifically by "the Qurʾān" because the Qurʾān is its core, since its recitation is long and laborious. It is also valid that "qurʾāna" be in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ). His saying: ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ means: it is witnessed by the guardian angels of the day and the guardian angels of the night, as stated in the well-known hadith in his words, upon him be peace: "Angels succeed one another among you, angels by night and angels by day, and they gather at the Ṣubḥ prayer and the ʿAṣr prayer," the hadith in full, related from Abū Hurayra and others. On this interpretation the majority proceeded.

Al-Ṭabarī mentioned a hadith from Ibn ʿAskar, through the route of Abū al-Dardāʾ, regarding His saying: ﴿was witnessed﴾. Muḥammad ibn Sahl ibn ʿAskar said: (Allah witnesses it, and His angels). He mentioned in that hadith that Allah, blessed and exalted, descends in the last part of the night, and similar things that are not strong.

(p-527) His saying the Exalted: ﴿And from the night﴾: "min" is partitive, and the estimate is: "and a time from the night," meaning: establish a time from the night. The pronoun in "bihi" returns to this estimated noun. It is also possible that it returns to the Qurʾān, although no mention of it has preceded absolutely, just as the pronoun is absolute, but it occurred as an addition to "al-fajr." "Alā ṭaraqatnā wa-l-rifāqu hujūdun / fa-bātat bi-ʿillāti al-nawāli tajūdu"
And from it is the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:
"Fa-ḥayyāki wudduñ mā hadāki li-fityatin / wa-khūṣin bi-aʿlā dhī ṭuwālatin hujjadi"
This verb operates on the pattern of: taḥarraba, taḥarraja, ta'aththama, taḥannatha. Similar to it is: ﴿so you would remain amazed﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 65], meaning: you would regret, that is, you would cast fruit away from yourselves, and it is the expansion and joy of the soul. It is said: "a man is fakih" when he is much given to joy and laughter. So the meaning is: and a time from the night, stay awake with it in prayer and recitation. Al-Aswad, ʿAlqama, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad said: tahajjud is after a sleep. Al-Ḥajjāj ibn ʿAmr said: tahajjud is only after a nap. Al-Ḥasan said: tahajjud is whatever occurs after the late ʿIshāʾ prayer.

The verse may allow that this is by way of recommendation in voluntary worship, and the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) while the intended meaning is him and his community, like his address in His saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. Mujāhid said: it is only a supererogatory act for the Prophet (ﷺ), because he is forgiven, and people expiate their sins by the like of it. He explained that the Prophet (ﷺ) had been forgiven what preceded and what followed of his sins since the year of Ḥudaybiya, so his supererogatory acts and his seeking forgiveness were virtuous deeds and acts of nearness superior to the supererogatory acts of his community; because theirs may either make up for their obligations or erase their errors. One may conceive of someone with no sin performing supererogatory acts, so his supererogation is a grace, like a Christian who becomes Muslim or a child who reaches puberty. Al-Ṭabarī weakened Mujāhid's opinion.

The hadith in full is in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, so we have abridged it. And "ʿasā" from Allah is binding, and "maqāman" is in the accusative as an adverbial noun.

I should translate this faithfully. Here is the translation:

It is fitting that this be interpreted in accordance with what we have said: that it applies to his community and to others; or it may be said that each of the two is a praiseworthy station (maqam mahmud). Whoever denies its permissibility, (his denial is) on the basis of its interpretation.

Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾ ﴿And from the night, pray with it as additional worship for you; it is expected that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾

Ḥaḍramī said: The pronoun in "kādū" refers to the Jews of Madina and its surroundings, such as Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and others, because they set out to scheme against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They said: "This land is not the land of the prophets; the land of the prophets is in al-Shām. But you fear the Romans. So if you are a prophet, go out to it, for Allah will protect you just as He protected other prophets." So the verse was revealed concerning that, and Allah informed that if His Messenger had gone out, they would not have remained after him except a little.

Al-Naqqāsh related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out because of their saying, and encamped at Dhū al-Ḥulayfa, waiting for his companions, and then the verse was revealed to him, so he returned.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is weak; it is not found in any biography or in any book that is relied upon, and Dhū al-Ḥulayfa is not on the route to al-Shām.

Another group said: the pronoun in "kādū" refers to Quraysh. Al-Zajjāj related that their incitement was what they had agreed upon in Dār al-Nadwa concerning killing him. The "land" in this view is general, meaning the world, as if he said: "they would drive you out of the world." According to all the other opinions, it is a specific land, either Makka or Madina, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿or be exiled from the land﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 33], or its meaning is: from the land in which they have their control and enjoyment. Ibn 'Abbās and Qatāda said: the incitement of Quraysh was what they went to of expelling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makka, just as they had earlier gone to besiege him in the mountain pass. This incitement of theirs occurred after the revelation of the verse; they constricted him until he left, and they pursued him to the cave and other things, and [Allah] carried out the threat against them, that they would not remain after him except a little, on the day of Badr.

Mujāhid said: Quraysh went toward this, but it did not happen from them, because when Allah willed to preserve Quraysh and not to uproot them, He permitted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to emigrate. So he left the land by Allah's permission, not by Quraysh's subjugation, and Quraysh was spared, and from them and their descendants those who embraced Islam became Muslims. "ʿAqaba al-raddhādu khilāfahā fa-ka-annamā / basaṭa al-shawāṭib baynahunna ḥaṣīran"

This word necessarily involves the omission of a governed noun, because the estimate in our verse is "khilāfa khurūjika," and in the poet's verse "khilāfa inbisāṭi al-shams" or something similar.

Abū ʿAlī said: They used these adverbial nouns only when they are attached to concrete nouns that are not events, so they did not prefer attaching them to anything other than what their speech had been accustomed to, just as when they came in the accusative in their speech they left them in their state when they occurred in a non-accusative position, as in His saying: ﴿And among us are the righteous, and among us are those beneath that﴾ [al-Jinn: 11], and His saying: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection He will separate you﴾ [al-Mumtaḥana: 3].

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
As for His saying "sunnata," it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the accusative by the deletion of the preposition, because the meaning is "like the sunna," so he deleted the kāf and put it in the accusative.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
It follows from this that one should not stop at His saying "qalīlan."

The meaning of the verse is the report that the sunna of Allah the Exalted regarding the earlier nations and His custom is that when a nation drives out its prophet from among them, punishment befalls them and destruction uproots them, so they do not remain after him except a little.

Abu Haywa, Qatada and Hamid read مَدْخَلَ and مَخْرَجَ with a fatḥah on the mīm, so it does not follow أَدْخِلْنِي; rather the implied sense is "He caused me to enter, so I enter an entrance," because it is derived from دَخَلَ. The word الصِّدْقُ here is an attribute that requires the removal of blame and the comprehensiveness of praise, as you say: "a man of sincerity (رَجُلُ صِدْقٍ)," meaning one who combines the excellences.

As for His saying, ﴿and grant me from Yourself an authority to help me﴾, Mujahid and others said: a proof, meaning, "Help me by its clarification against the disbelievers." Al-Hasan and Qatada said: he means a protective force, leadership, and a sword that supports the religion of Allah the Exalted. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sought that by the command of Allah to him to do so, out of desire for the support of the religion. It is related that Allah the Exalted promised him this, and then fulfilled it for him in his lifetime and completed it after his death.

(p. 531) His saying the Exalted: ﴿And say, "Truth has come, and falsehood has departed"﴾, to the end of the verse. Qatada said: "the truth" is the Qur'an, and "the falsehood" is Satan. A group said: "the truth" is faith, and "the falsehood" is disbelief. Ibn Jurayj said: the truth is jihad, and the falsehood is polytheism. Other things have been said, but the correct view is to generalize the wording to the fullest possible extent, so the expression means: the Law has come with all that it contains, and disbelief has departed with all that it contains. "Falsehood" is everything by which no beneficial end is attained. As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿was bound to depart﴾, the word "was" (كانَ) is not an indication of a past time; rather the meaning is "was, and it is continuing." This is like your saying: "Allah was Knowing, Powerful," and the like.

This verse was revealed in Makkah. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to cite it on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, at the time he struck the idols, and they fell at his striking them with a staff, as is mentioned in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham and elsewhere. The majority read وَنُنَزِّلُ with the nūn, and Mujahid read وَيُنْزِلُ with the yā' lightly; al-Marwazi related it from Hafs. As for His saying the Exalted ﴿of the Qur'an﴾, the word مِنَ may be for the beginning of the extent, and it may be for explaining the kind, as if He said: "And We send down from the Qur'an that which has healing in it." Some interpreters rejected that مِنْ is partitive, out of concern that it would imply that some of it has no healing in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This does not follow. Rather it is correct for مِنْ to be partitive, in view of the fact that its sending down is only in parts. So it is as if He said: "And We send down of the Qur'an" piece by piece, that which in its entirety is healing. His using the word "healing" for the Qur'an is according to its removal of doubt and its uncovering of the veil of the heart for understanding the miracles and the matters indicating Allah the Exalted, which establish His Law. It is also possible that "healing" means its benefit from illnesses by means of incantations (p. 532) and amulets and the like, and its being a manifest mercy. As for His saying the Exalted ﴿but it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾, it means that for them it is blindness, since they are addressed in the condition of one who does not understand and is not instructed.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man﴾, to the end of the verse. "Man" in this verse is not meant in its general sense; rather it means some of them, namely the disbelievers. This is like your saying in anger: "There is no good in friends, and no trustworthiness in people," where you generalize for emphasis while meaning some. This accords with the mention of the wrongdoers and loss in the verse. It was said: thus the mention of the disbelievers is connected. It is also possible that "man" in this verse is general for the species, in the sense that this blameworthy trait is in his nature: the disbeliever goes to excess in turning away, and the sinner takes his share of it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said concerning a believer: "He turned away, so Allah turned away from him." The meaning of أَعْرَضَ ("turned away") is that he turned his side to us. وَنَأى ("and distanced") means he went far. This is also a metaphor, because he acts like one who turns away and distances himself, in abandoning faith in Allah and thankfulness for His blessings upon him. Ibn 'Amir alone read وَنَاءَ, and its meaning is: he rose up going far away; this is the saying of one group. Another group said it is the transposition of the hamzah after the alif from نَأى with the same root, and it is a dialect like رَأى and وراء. A similar word to this one is the poet's saying describing an archer:

؎ Until, when its joints came together, and it leaned heavily upon its left shoulder-blade (وَناءَ فِي شِقِّ الشِّمالِ كاهِلُهُ)

(p. 533) That is, he rose up leaning on his left side.

What I hold is that ناءَ and نَأى are two distinct verbs. وَناءَ بِجانِبِهِ is an expression for bewilderment and self-sufficiency, while ناءَ is an expression for distance and separation.

Then Allah the Exalted described the disbelievers as, when evil touches them, whether from sickness or calamity in property or otherwise, they despair from a direction in which they do not believe in Allah, and do not hope for the workings of His decrees.

Then He, mighty and majestic, said: Say, O Muhammad: ﴿Each works according to his manner﴾, that is, his way, according to his intention and his path which resembles him. It is his shakl (form/likeness). This verse indicates clearly that "man" at first was not meant in its generality; that is, the disbelievers have these attributes, and the believers are the opposite, and each of them acts according to what befits him, and the Lord the Exalted is most knowing of who is guided. Mujahid said: ﴿according to his shākilah﴾ means according to his nature, and he also said: it means according to his own way, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it means according to his side, and Qatada said: it means according to his own way and what he intends, and Ibn Zayd said: it means according to his religion.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The most preferred of these expressions is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿So your Lord is most knowing of who is best guided in way﴾, it is a clear warning.

(p. 530) Allah the Exalted says:

﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself an authority to help me."﴾ ﴿And say, "Truth has come, and falsehood has departed. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to depart."﴾ ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, but it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss.﴾ ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man, he turns away and distances himself, and when evil touches him, he is in despair.﴾ ﴿Say, "Each works according to his manner, but your Lord is most knowing of who is best guided in way."﴾

The apparent meaning of this verse, and the best reading of it, is that it is a supplication that Allah make his condition good in every matter he undertakes, every journey and action he undertakes, and every outcome he awaits from the workings of decrees, in life and in death. It is therefore of the most complete generality. Its meaning is: "My Lord, set right for me my course in all affairs and my breast." The commentators, however, went to the view that it concerns a specific purpose, and then differed in specifying it. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada said: he meant, "Cause me to enter Madinah and cause me to exit Makkah." Within this interpretation, the later in occurrence is put first, for the exit from Makkah is the earlier in speech, since the exit from Makkah came first; yet the place of entry and flight is the more important. Abu Salih and Mujahid said: "Cause me to enter upon the task of conveying the Law, and cause me to exit from it with complete preparation." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The entrance is by death into the grave, and the exit is resurrection." What I have mentioned of complete generality, which encompasses all of this, is more correct.
