[p. 534] The Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

﴿They ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away what We have revealed to you; then you would find for yourself no advocate against Us in that matter.﴾ ﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord. Indeed, His bounty toward you has been great.﴾ ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to be helpers to one another.﴾

As for the pronoun in "they ask you" (yas'alunaka), it is said that it refers to the Jews, and that the verse is Medinan. "'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud narrated that he was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he passed by a field (harth) in Medina, or according to another report, a ruin (kharib), in which there was a group of Jews. Some of them said to others: 'Ask him about the Spirit. If he answers about it, you will know that he is not a prophet.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That is because it was in their Torah (al-Tawrah) that the Spirit is among the things that Allah alone knows, and He does not inform any of His servants of it. Ibn Mas'ud said: Some of them said: "Do not ask him, lest he bring something you dislike."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means, and Allah knows best, that he (the Prophet) would not explain it, so that the proof against them regarding his prophethood would be established. He (Ibn Mas'ud) said: So they asked him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stopped, leaning on a palm-stalk ('asib). I thought he was being inspired, then he recited the verse to them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also said that the verse is Meccan, and that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh. That is because they said: "We will ask Muhammad (peace be upon him) about the People of the Book among the Jews." So they sent to them in Medina al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. The Jews said: "Test him with three questions: ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the Spirit. If he explains the three, he is a liar; and if he is silent about the Spirit, he is a prophet." So the Quraysh asked him about the Spirit. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Tomorrow I will inform you of it," and he did not say "if Allah wills." So revelation was withheld from him for fifteen days, as a reproach for his promise to them without making an exception (istithna'). Then this verse was revealed.

[p. 535] People differed about the Spirit that was asked about: which Spirit is it? A group, which is the majority, said: The question concerned the Spirit that is in living beings (al-ashkhas al-hayawaniyyah), what is it? On this view, "Spirit" (al-ruh) is a generic noun (ism jins), and this is the correct view, and it is the problematic matter for which there is no explanation. Qatadah said: The Spirit asked about is Gabriel (peace be upon him). He said: Ibn 'Abbas used to conceal it. Another group said: It is Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon them both. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: (An angel who has seventy thousand faces; in each face seventy thousand tongues; for each tongue seventy thousand languages; he glorifies Allah, glory be to Him, in all those languages, and from each act of glorification Allah creates an angel who flies with the angels until the Day of Resurrection.) Al-Tabari mentioned it. I do not think this statement is sound from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. Another group said: The Spirit is the Qur'an. All these are explanatory statements, and the first is the most apparent and the most correct.

His saying "of the command of my Lord" (min amr rabbi) allows two interpretations. One is that "command" (al-amr) is a generic noun for affairs, meaning: the Spirit is among the affairs of Allah which He has reserved the knowledge of; so it is an attribution of creation to the Creator. The second is that it is a verbal noun (masdar), from "a command that commands," meaning: the Spirit is among the things that Allah, exalted is He, commanded with the command "Be," and so it came to be. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read "wa ma utu" (what they were given), and Ibn Mas'ud related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). The majority read "wa ma utitum" (what you were given).

There is disagreement about who is addressed by this. One group said: only the questioners, and al-Tabari gave this as a heading, then under that heading he cited from Qatadah that they were the Jews. Another group said: the intended addressees are all the Jews, and on this view is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. Another group said: the entire world, and this is the correct view, because the saying of Allah, exalted is He, to him, "Say: the Spirit...", is only a command to speak to the whole world, since that is how all His speech is; and on this basis the verse is completed as an address to all. It is also possible that it is an address from Allah, exalted is He, to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to all people. The knowledge that all people have is described as little by attributing it to the knowledge of Allah, mighty and majestic, of which the things we know are a very small part, as al-Khidr (peace be upon him) said to Musa (peace be upon him): "My knowledge and your knowledge and the knowledge of all creatures, compared to the knowledge of Allah, is no more than what this sparrow takes from the sea." Al-Khidr meant the knowledge of Allah of these existing things, of which the knowledge of humans is a very small part in relation to what is hidden from them, like the relation of a dot to the sea. As for the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, absolutely, it is unlimited. It is possible that the figurative usage is in al-Khidr's words, "as this sparrow takes," meaning that our knowledge does not diminish anything of the knowledge of Allah, exalted, absolutely; then he gave the example of the sparrow's peck regarding non-diminution, since its diminution is imperceptible, so it is as if it were nonexistent. This is one possibility, but there is a question about it. The Jews said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How is it that you were given only a little knowledge, when we were given the Torah, which is wisdom, and whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good?" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) countered them with the knowledge of Allah, and they were defeated. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stated in some hadiths with his saying: "All of it" (kullan). He meant that the intended "you were given" is the whole of creation. That is because the Jews said to him: "Do you mean us, or your people?" He said: "All of it." And in this sense the verse was revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27]. Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, related this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away what We have revealed to you﴾, to the end of the verse, contains severity toward the Prophet (ﷺ). It is a reproach for his saying "Tomorrow I will inform you," so he was commanded to say: "The Spirit is of the command of my Lord," thus submitting in acceptance to Allah, that He informs whom He wills and withholds from His servants what He wills. Then it was said to him: "And you have been given of knowledge only a little, you, O Muhammad, and all creatures," so Allah, exalted is He, informs whomever He wills from His knowledge and leaves whatever He wills. And if He willed, He would take away the revelation that came to you, and you would have no helper from it. So it is no great matter that you did not bring an explanation about the Spirit, which you intended to explain to the people, and promised them. Ibn Mas'ud related that a red wind will come out from the direction of al-Sham, removing the Qur'an from the copies and from the hearts, and will carry it away; then he recited this verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn Mas'ud intended by reciting the verse to show that the matter is possible to occur, so that the truth of his report would be manifest from the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic. "Al-wakil" (advocate): the one who takes up the matter in support or in litigation, and the like, in terms of being of benefit.

His saying, exalted is He: "Except as a mercy" is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same class), meaning: but a mercy from your Lord keeps that from you. This disjunctive exception specifies in a certain way, but it is not like the connected exception (istithna' muttasil), because the connected exception specifies from the same class or the whole sentence, while the disjunctive exception specifies something external to that. No one denies the occurrence of the disjunctive exception in the Qur'an except a non-Arab, and this has been related from Ibn Khuwayz Mindad. Then He, mighty and majestic, enumerated the greatness of His bounty in singling him out with prophethood, protecting him from the polytheists, and other things that cannot be counted.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together﴾, to the end of the verse.

The occasion of this verse is that a group of the Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, bring us a sign [p. 538] strange, other than this Qur'an, for we are able to bring the like of this." So this verse was revealed, which explicitly challenges them and informs that all creatures, human and jinn, if they gathered together for that, would not be able to do it.

The incapacity regarding the opposition to the Qur'an occurs only in the arrangement (nazm) and the composition (rasf) of its meanings, and the cause of that is the comprehensiveness that is possessed by none except Allah, exalted is He. Humans are necessarily deficient through ignorance, forgetfulness, heedlessness, and various kinds of imperfection. The arrangement of a word that is hidden from them, for the reasons we have mentioned, is the most fitting speech for its meaning. I have discussed this issue at the beginning of this work (al-diwan).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿la ya'tuna﴾ ("they will not produce") is in a place of raising (nominative); "la" is a preface to an oath, and the lam in His saying "la'in" (if) is an announcing lam that is not obligatory, and it may sometimes be omitted, and sometimes this lam comes only to emphasize. The negated verb comes in the jussive (majzum), and this is reliance on the conditional, and from it is the saying of al-A'mash:

"If you are afflicted with us after the aftermath of a battle, you will not find us turning away from the blood of the people."

"Al-zahir" (helper): the supporter. From it is the saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you two back each other against him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], to the end of the verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Arabs understood, by the purity of their understanding, in the discernment of speech and their practice in it, what we do not understand, nor does everyone who has been touched by civilization. So they understood its incapacity necessarily and by direct observation, and those after them knew it by inference and reflection. For each group a definitive knowledge was achieved, but not at one level. This is like the Companions knowing the law (shar') of the Prophet (peace be upon him) and his practices by direct observation, a knowledge of necessity, while we know what is mass-transmitted (mutawatir) of that by the transmission of mass-transmission. So certainty was achieved for all, but at two levels. The masters of eloquence, who have rare insights in discerning speech, understood the inimitability of the Qur'an. Do you not see the understanding of al-Farazdaq of the poetry of Jarir in the poetry of Dhu al-Rummah, in his saying:

"The genealogists count to Tamim..."

all of its verses. And do you not see the story of Jarir in the anecdotes (nawadir) of his with al-Farazdaq regarding al-Farazdaq's saying:

"Why do you look back?"

[p. 540] And in his saying:

"I looked back, that she is under the son of a smith."

And do you not see the saying of the Bedouin: "He was mighty, so he judged, so he cut"? And do you not see the other's argument for resurrection from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2], when he said: "Visiting entails departing."

From this is Bashshar's knowledge of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala's saying regarding the poetry of al-A'sha:

"She disowned me, and what was disowned was not what I disowned."

[p. 541] And from this is the saying of the Bedouin to al-Asma'i: "Who made the generous man need to swear an oath?"

And from their understanding is that, by their spontaneous speech, they produce a prose saying that surpasses refined poetry, and examples of that are preserved. From it are their silencing replies, among other things of their skill in eloquence and that they were at its peak, just as sorcery was in the time of Musa (peace be upon him), and medicine was in the time of 'Isa (peace be upon him). With these understandings they acknowledged incapacity, and the hostile one among them resorted to the sword, and accepted killing and captivity and the exposure of women, though he could have had an escape from that through opposition.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Likewise, the challenge with ten surahs and the challenge with one surah occurred entirely on a single basis, in arrangement specifically. He restricted the ten to "fabricated" (muftarayat) because they said that the Qur'an was fabricated; so right after mentioning that, he called them to bring ten fabricated surahs. Some of them said to others: 'Ask him about the Spirit. If he answers about it, you will know that he is not a prophet.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That is because it was in their Torah (al-Tawrah) that the Spirit is among the things that Allah alone knows, and He does not inform any of His servants of it. Ibn Mas'ud said: Some of them said: "Do not ask him, lest he bring something you dislike."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He means, and Allah knows best, that he (the Prophet) would not explain it, so that the proof against them regarding his prophethood would be established. He (Ibn Mas'ud) said: So they asked him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stopped, leaning on a palm-stalk ('asib). I thought he was being inspired, then he recited the verse to them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also said that the verse is Meccan, and that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh. That is because they said: "We will ask Muhammad (peace be upon him) about the People of the Book among the Jews." So they sent to them in Medina al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. The Jews said: "Test him with three questions: ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the Spirit. If he explains the three, he is a liar; and if he is silent about the Spirit, he is a prophet." So the Quraysh asked him about the Spirit. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Tomorrow I will inform you of it," and he did not say "if Allah wills." So revelation was withheld from him for fifteen days, as a reproach for his promise to them without making an exception (istithna'). Then this verse was revealed.

[p. 535] People differed about the Spirit that was asked about: which Spirit is it? A group, which is the majority, said: The question concerned the Spirit that is in living beings (al-ashkhas al-hayawaniyyah), what is it? On this view, "Spirit" (al-ruh) is a generic noun (ism jins), and this is the correct view, and it is the problematic matter for which there is no explanation. Qatadah said: The Spirit asked about is Gabriel (peace be upon him). He said: Ibn 'Abbas used to conceal it. Another group said: It is Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon them both. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: (An angel who has seventy thousand faces; in each face seventy thousand tongues; for each tongue seventy thousand languages; he glorifies Allah, glory be to Him, in all those languages, and from each act of glorification Allah creates an angel who flies with the angels until the Day of Resurrection.) Al-Tabari mentioned it. I do not think this statement is sound from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. Another group said: The Spirit is the Qur'an. All these are explanatory statements, and the first is the most apparent and the most correct.

His saying "of the command of my Lord" (min amr rabbi) allows two interpretations. One is that "command" (al-amr) is a generic noun for affairs, meaning: the Spirit is among the affairs of Allah which He has reserved the knowledge of; so it is an attribution of creation to the Creator. The second is that it is a verbal noun (masdar), from "a command that commands," meaning: the Spirit is among the things that Allah, exalted is He, commanded with the command "Be," and so it came to be. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read "wa ma utu" (what they were given), and Ibn Mas'ud related it from the Prophet (ﷺ). The majority read "wa ma utitum" (what you were given).

There is disagreement about who is addressed by this. One group said: only the questioners, and al-Tabari gave this as a heading, then under that heading he cited from Qatadah that they were the Jews. Another group said: the intended addressees are all the Jews, and on this view is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. Another group said: the entire world, and this is the correct view, because the saying of Allah, exalted is He, to him, "Say: the Spirit...", is only a command to speak to the whole world, since that is how all His speech is; and on this basis the verse is completed as an address to all. It is also possible that it is an address from Allah, exalted is He, to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to all people. The knowledge that all people have is described as little by attributing it to the knowledge of Allah, mighty and majestic, of which the things we know are a very small part, as al-Khidr (peace be upon him) said to Musa (peace be upon him): "My knowledge and your knowledge and the knowledge of all creatures, compared to the knowledge of Allah, is no more than what this sparrow takes from the sea." Al-Khidr meant the knowledge of Allah of these existing things, of which the knowledge of humans is a very small part in relation to what is hidden from them, like the relation of a dot to the sea. As for the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, absolutely, it is unlimited. It is possible that the figurative usage is in al-Khidr's words, "as this sparrow takes," meaning that our knowledge does not diminish anything of the knowledge of Allah, exalted, absolutely; then he gave the example of the sparrow's peck regarding non-diminution, since its diminution is imperceptible, so it is as if it were nonexistent. This is one possibility, but there is a question about it. The Jews said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How is it that you were given only a little knowledge, when we were given the Torah, which is wisdom, and whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good?" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) countered them with the knowledge of Allah, and they were defeated. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stated in some hadiths with his saying: "All of it" (kullan). He meant that the intended "you were given" is the whole of creation. That is because the Jews said to him: "Do you mean us, or your people?" He said: "All of it." And in this sense the verse was revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqman: 27]. Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, related this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away what We have revealed to you﴾, to the end of the verse, contains severity toward the Prophet (ﷺ). It is a reproach for his saying "Tomorrow I will inform you," so he was commanded to say: "The Spirit is of the command of my Lord," thus submitting in acceptance to Allah, that He informs whom He wills and withholds from His servants what He wills. Then it was said to him: "And you have been given of knowledge only a little, you, O Muhammad, and all creatures," so Allah, exalted is He, informs whomever He wills from His knowledge and leaves whatever He wills. And if He willed, He would take away the revelation that came to you, and you would have no helper from it. So it is no great matter that you did not bring an explanation about the Spirit, which you intended to explain to the people, and promised them. Ibn Mas'ud related that a red wind will come out from the direction of al-Sham, removing the Qur'an from the copies and from the hearts, and will carry it away; then he recited this verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn Mas'ud intended by reciting the verse to show that the matter is possible to occur, so that the truth of his report would be manifest from the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic. "Al-wakil" (advocate): the one who takes up the matter in support or in litigation, and the like, in terms of being of benefit.

His saying, exalted is He: "Except as a mercy" is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same class), meaning: but a mercy from your Lord keeps that from you. This disjunctive exception specifies in a certain way, but it is not like the connected exception (istithna' muttasil), because the connected exception specifies from the same class or the whole sentence, while the disjunctive exception specifies something external to that. No one denies the occurrence of the disjunctive exception in the Qur'an except a non-Arab, and this has been related from Ibn Khuwayz Mindad. Then He, mighty and majestic, enumerated the greatness of His bounty in singling him out with prophethood, protecting him from the polytheists, and other things that cannot be counted.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together﴾, to the end of the verse.

The occasion of this verse is that a group of the Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, bring us a sign [p. 538] strange, other than this Qur'an, for we are able to bring the like of this." So this verse was revealed, which explicitly challenges them and informs that all creatures, human and jinn, if they gathered together for that, would not be able to do it.

The incapacity regarding the opposition to the Qur'an occurs only in the arrangement (nazm) and the composition (rasf) of its meanings, and the cause of that is the comprehensiveness that is possessed by none except Allah, exalted is He. Humans are necessarily deficient through ignorance, forgetfulness, heedlessness, and various kinds of imperfection. The arrangement of a word that is hidden from them, for the reasons we have mentioned, is the most fitting speech for its meaning. I have discussed this issue at the beginning of this work (al-diwan).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿la ya'tuna﴾ ("they will not produce") is in a place of raising (nominative); "la" is a preface to an oath, and the lam in His saying "la'in" (if) is an announcing lam that is not obligatory, and it may sometimes be omitted, and sometimes this lam comes only to emphasize. The negated verb comes in the jussive (majzum), and this is reliance on the conditional, and from it is the saying of al-A'mash:

"If you are afflicted with us after the aftermath of a battle, you will not find us turning away from the blood of the people."

"Al-zahir" (helper): the supporter. From it is the saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you two back each other against him﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], to the end of the verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Arabs understood, by the purity of their understanding, in the discernment of speech and their practice in it, what we do not understand, nor does everyone who has been touched by civilization. So they understood its incapacity necessarily and by direct observation, and those after them knew it by inference and reflection. For each group a definitive knowledge was achieved, but not at one level. This is like the Companions knowing the law (shar') of the Prophet (peace be upon him) and his practices by direct observation, a knowledge of necessity, while we know what is mass-transmitted (mutawatir) of that by the transmission of mass-transmission. So certainty was achieved for all, but at two levels. The masters of eloquence, who have rare insights in discerning speech, understood the inimitability of the Qur'an. Do you not see the understanding of al-Farazdaq of the poetry of Jarir in the poetry of Dhu al-Rummah, in his saying:

"The genealogists count to Tamim..."

all of its verses. And do you not see the story of Jarir in the anecdotes (nawadir) of his with al-Farazdaq regarding al-Farazdaq's saying:

"Why do you look back?"

[p. 540] And in his saying:

"I looked back, that she is under the son of a smith."

And do you not see the saying of the Bedouin: "He was mighty, so he judged, so he cut"? And do you not see the other's argument for resurrection from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 2], when he said: "Visiting entails departing."

From this is Bashshar's knowledge of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala's saying regarding the poetry of al-A'sha:

"She disowned me, and what was disowned was not what I disowned."

[p. 541] And from this is the saying of the Bedouin to al-Asma'i: "Who made the generous man need to swear an oath?"

And from their understanding is that, by their spontaneous speech, they produce a prose saying that surpasses refined poetry, and examples of that are preserved. From it are their silencing replies, among other things of their skill in eloquence and that they were at its peak, just as sorcery was in the time of Musa (peace be upon him), and medicine was in the time of 'Isa (peace be upon him). With these understandings they acknowledged incapacity, and the hostile one among them resorted to the sword, and accepted killing and captivity and the exposure of women, though he could have had an escape from that through opposition.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Likewise, the challenge with ten surahs and the challenge with one surah occurred entirely on a single basis, in arrangement specifically. He restricted the ten to "fabricated" (muftarayat) because they said that the Qur'an was fabricated; so right after mentioning that, he called them to bring ten fabricated surahs. He did not mention "fabrication" in the surah because it had not preceded from them [p. 542] any mention of that before. Rather He said: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]. Yet the mention of a surah did occur together with their mention of fabrication in Surat Hud. People have differed about this position: it was said that they were called to a surah similar in arrangement, unseen matters, and other descriptions; and this was a burden of what cannot be borne, so when it was difficult for them it was lightened by calling them to fabricated surahs. And it was said other than this, which is resolved upon its attainment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 89–92:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And indeed We have explained for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused except disbelief.﴾ ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth,﴾ ﴿or you have a garden of palm trees and grapevines and cause rivers to gush forth within it in abundance,﴾ ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you have claimed, or you bring Allah and the angels before us as a guarantee."﴾

This is a verse calling attention to Allah's favour in the Qur'an upon the world, and a rebuke to the disbelievers for their ugly conduct. "Tasrif al-qawl" (the varied presentation of speech) is the repeated clarification of the meaning. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "ṣarrafnā" with a doubled rā', and al-Ḥasan read "ṣarafnā" with a single rā' and a fatḥa.

His saying, Exalted is He, "min kulli mathal" (from every kind of example): the "min" may be for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), and the object of "ṣarrafnā" is then implied, its sense being: "And indeed We have explained in this Qur'an the admonitions and lessons from every example We have set forth." It may also be an emphatic, superfluous "min", the sense being: "And indeed We have explained every example," and this is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 125].

His saying, Exalted is He, "fa-abā" (but refused) is an expression for the disbelievers' acquisition of disbelief and their turning away from faith. In the expression with "abā" there is intensification. Disbelief as creation and origination is from the act of Allah Exalted is He, while disbelief as acquisition and persistence is from the human being. "Kufūran" is a verbal noun like "khurūj".

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you"﴾, to the end of the verse. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "ḥattā tufajjira" (with a doubled jīm, in the causative form), while 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ḥattā tafjura" with a fatḥa on the tā' (p-543) and a ḍamma on the jīm. In the Qur'an there is "fa-nfajarat" (then it gushed forth), and infajara is the intransitive form (muṭāwi') of fajara, so this supports the second reading. As for the first, it implies intensification in the gushing. "Al-yanbū'" is the flowing water, and it is an intensive adjective (ṣifa mubālagha) that applies only to abundant water.

The Quraysh requested this from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Makkah, and by "the earth" they meant that very place. The word "al-ard" (earth) is used here to mean the land in which the matter under discussion takes place, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or be banished from the land﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 33]; what is meant is: from the land of their movement, their brigandage on the roads and their livelihood. Likewise their demand for a garden was specifically in Makkah, because that was impossible there; otherwise in the rest of the lands it would have been possible for him. They asked him for a matter of divine power in that barren place. The majority read "jannatun". It has also been read "ḥabbatun", as mentioned by al-Mahdawi. His saying, Exalted is He, "fa-tufajjira" is an intensive doubling (taḍ'if mubālagha), not a doubling of transitivity, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the doors were locked﴾ [Yusuf: 23]. "Khilālahā" is an adverbial of place (ẓarf), and its meaning is: within it and in its interior.

A lengthy narration has been reported concerning the saying of this statement to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the gist of which is: "that 'Utba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabi'a, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and others of the elders and chiefs of the Quraysh gathered, and they proposed to him that, if he wished, they would make him king, and if he wished wealth, they would gather much wealth for him, or they would have him treated if he had an illness, and similar such statements. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then called them to Allah and said: 'I have come to you from Allah with a matter in which is the welfare of your religion and your worldly life. If you listen and obey, that is good; otherwise I shall be patient with the command of Allah until Allah judges between me and you by what He wills.' They then said to him: 'If what you claim is true, then cause a spring to gush forth for us, and we will believe you, and let there be a garden for you,' and other demands that they imposed upon him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: 'All of this is up to Allah; it is not incumbent upon me, nor on anything else; I am only submitting to the command of Allah, Exalted is He.'"

(p-544) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the meaning of the hadith. In the wording there is variance and branching narrations, the full recounting of which would be lengthy, so I have abbreviated.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or you cause the sky to fall﴾, to the end of the verse. The majority read "aw tusqiṭa" with a ḍamma on the tā', and "al-samā'a" with a fatḥa (as object). Mujahid read "aw taqṭu'a al-samā'u" (with the sky as subject, the verb ascribed to it), with raf' on "al-samā'". His saying, "kamā za'amta" (as you have claimed), refers to what He recited to them before that in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them up, or We shall cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾ [Saba': 9]. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "kisfan" with a sukun on the sīn, except in al-Rum (Surah 30), where they vowelled it; its meaning is: a single piece. Mujahid said: the sky, all of it. The Arabs say: "kasaftu al-thawb" and the like, meaning I cut it. So "al-kisaf" with a fatḥa on the sīn is the verbal noun, and "al-kisaf" is the cut-off thing. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: or you cause the sky to fall upon us in layers, and its derivation is from "kasaftu al-shay'" when I covered it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Kasafa" in the sense of "covered" is not well known in the lexicographical dictionaries; rather it means "cut", and it seems that the eclipse of the sun and moon is a cutting-off from them. Nafi' and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "kisafan" with a fatḥa on the sīn, meaning pieces, the plural of "kisfa".

His saying, "qabīlan" means: in direct confrontation and visible presence. It has also been said that it means: a guarantor and surety for your truthfulness; from it comes "al-qubala" (surety), and al-qabil and al-mutaqabbil mean the guarantor. It has also been said that it means: a kind and genus with no equal among us. Al-A'raj read "qubulan", which has the sense of confrontation.

His saying, Exalted is He, "fa-abā" (but refused) is an expression for the disbelievers' acquisition of disbelief and their turning away from faith. In the expression with "abā" there is intensification. Disbelief as creation and origination is from the act of Allah Exalted is He, while disbelief as acquisition and persistence is from the human being. "Kufūran" is a verbal noun like "khurūj".

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you"﴾, to the end of the verse. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "ḥattā tufajjira" (with a doubled jīm, in the causative form), while 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ḥattā tafjura" with a fatḥa on the tā' (p-543) and a ḍamma on the jīm. The word "al-ard" (earth) is used here to mean the land in which the matter under discussion takes place, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or be banished from the land﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 33]; what is meant is: from the land of their movement, their brigandage on the roads and their livelihood. This is the meaning of the hadith. In the wording there is variance and branching narrations, the full recounting of which would be lengthy, so I have abbreviated.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 93–95:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascent until you bring down to us a book we can read." Say: "Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"﴾ ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them, except that they said, "Has Allah sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ ﴿Say: "If there were angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down to them from the sky an angel as a messenger."﴾

The exegetes (mufassirun) said: "al-Zukhruf" means gold in this place, while zukhruf is that with which something is adorned, whether gold or otherwise. From it is His saying: ﴿until, when the earth takes on its adornment﴾ [Yunus: 24]. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is: "Or you have a house of gold." His saying: ﴿in the sky﴾ means: in the air, on high. The Arabs call the air "sama'" (sky/height) on high, because it is in the sphere of elevation. It is also possible that they mean the well-known sky, and this is the apparent meaning, because He informed them that the God of creation is in it and that news of it comes to Him. "Tarqa" means: he ascends, and ruqiyy means ascent.

It is narrated that the speaker of this statement was 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, for he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We will not believe you until you bring us a book—he meant his book—containing: From Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya." It is also narrated that their group requested this sort of thing from him, so Allah the Exalted commanded him to say: ﴿Glory be to my Lord﴾, that is, exalting Him above coming with the angels as a clan, and above addressing you with a book as you wished, and above my proposing these things to Him. "Am I anything but a human like you, sent to you with the Law? My duty is only to convey." Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read: "He said, 'Glory be to my Lord,'" in the sense of a report about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he glorified God when they said this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing﴾. This verse is in the sense of rebuke and regret from the Prophet (ﷺ), as though he were saying in wonder at them: "What Allah wills comes to pass. Nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except this trivial pretext, and the outlandish claim unsupported by any proof." Sending humans as messengers is neither novel nor strange, for through them understanding is achieved and the capacity for reflection. Had there been angels in the earth dwelling in it "calmly"—that is, settled in it and residing—the messenger to them would have been from among the angels, so that understanding could be achieved. As for humans, if an angel were sent to them, their natures would recoil from seeing him, their eyes would not bear him, and their hearts would not endure him. Allah has only made their conditions follow their customary course.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verse 96–98:

(p-546) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you. Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing."﴾ ﴿And whoever Allah guides - he is the [rightly] guided; but whoever He leaves astray - never will you find for them allies other than Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf. Their refuge is Hell; whenever it subsides, We increase for them the blaze.﴾ ﴿That is their recompense because they denied Our signs and said, "When we are bones and crumbled particles, will we really be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾

It is narrated that the chiefs of Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the statements mentioned earlier, including offering him kingship and wealth and other things. At the end of their speech they said to him: "Let a group of angels come with you to bear witness to your truthfulness in your prophethood." Al-Mahdawi said: It is narrated that they said to him, "Then who will bear witness for you?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of their words is only a request for a witness, without their mentioning it. So the verse was revealed concerning this, meaning: Allah bears witness between me and you, He who has the knowledge and the sight of all of us, our truthful and our liar. Then He returned the matter to the creation of Allah and His origination of guidance and misguidance in the hearts of humans, meaning: the matter is not in my hand beyond conveying [the message]. And in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so you will never find for them allies other than Him﴾ is a warning.

Then Allah, Exalted, informed that they will be gathered upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf. This has been differed over: it was said that these are metaphors, either because they, from confusion, grief and bewilderment, resemble people with these attributes, or because they do not see what pleases them, do not hear, and do not speak with a proof. And it was said that all of it is literal, and that occurs when they rise from their graves; then Allah, Exalted, returns to them their sight, hearing and speech, so when these are returned to them they see the Fire, hear its roaring, and speak everything that is related of them in that regard.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is said of one who turns away from a matter fearful and distressed: "He departed upon his face," and it is said of a camel: "It is as if it walks upon its face." Whoever says that this is literal in the verse says: Allah, Exalted, empowered them to move upon their faces, just as He empowered them in this world to move upon their feet. And in this meaning there is a hadith: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, how does the disbeliever walk upon his face? He said: 'Is not the One who made him walk upon two legs in this world able to make him walk upon his face in the Hereafter?'" Qatadah said: "Yes, by the might of our Lord."

His, Exalted is He, saying ﴿whenever it subsides﴾ means: whenever it finishes burning them, so the flame standing over them subsides for the time it takes them to be restored, then it flares up again; that is the increase of the blaze. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the increase is in their space, while as for Hell, it remains in its state of intensity and does not experience any lessening. "Khabat al-nar" means: the flame and the ember calmed in their state; "khamadat" means: the ember calmed and weakened; "hamadat" means: it was extinguished entirely. From this word is the saying of the poet:

﴿Whose fire is it, near the morning, at the House, that does not subside?﴾
﴿When it is extinguished, there is cast upon it moist aloes-wood?﴾

And from it is the saying of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

﴿In its midst like a firefly or the lamps of the wick, at times it subsides and at times it shines.﴾

And from it is the saying of al-Qutami:

﴿It subsides for an hour and blazes up for an hour.﴾

His, Exalted is He, saying ﴿That is their recompense﴾: the verse refers to the aforementioned warning of Hell. His saying "with Our signs" encompasses the proofs and arguments that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, and encompasses the signs of the noble Qur'an and what it includes of news, command and prohibition. Then the denial of resurrection became grave for them, and it was singled out for mention despite being within the general category of disbelief in the signs of the noble Qur'an; the reason for singling it out is to magnify it and to alert to the gravity of disbelief in denying it. The differences of the readers concerning the two interrogatives have already been mentioned in other than this place.

"Al-rufat" is the remnant of a thing that decay has reduced to the state of dust, and "al-ba'th" is the moving of a still thing. This interrogation from them is by way of denial and deeming the impossible to be far-fetched according to their claim.

This has been differed over: it was said that these are metaphors, either because they, from confusion, grief and bewilderment, resemble people with these attributes, or because they do not see what pleases them, do not hear, and do not speak with a proof. It is said of one who turns away from a matter fearful and distressed: "He departed upon his face," and it is said of a camel: "It is as if it walks upon its face." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 99–101:

(p. 549) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them? And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt. Yet the wrongdoers insist on nothing but disbelief.﴾ ﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasuries of my Lord's mercy, you would withhold them for fear of spending, for man is ever tight-fisted."﴾ ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs. So ask the Children of Israel: when he came to them, Pharaoh said to him, "I truly think you, Moses, are bewitched."﴾

This verse is an argument against them concerning what they deemed improbable, namely resurrection. They acknowledge God's creation and His bringing into being this whole (universe), of which humankind is a part. They do not deny this. So how can it be valid for them to affirm His creating all of it and bringing it out of the lethargy of non-existence, while denying His restoring some of it? Thus the matter falls within the realm of possibility. The Truthful One, whose miracles are proof (of his truthfulness), has informed us that this possibility will occur. The "seeing" in this verse is seeing of the heart (i.e., understanding). The "term" (ajal) here may be understood as referring to the Resurrection, or to the term of death. On the latter interpretation, "ajal" is a noun of genus, since it is placed in the position of the plural "ājāl" (terms). The purpose of this statement is to demonstrate God's power and His dominion over His creation, and by establishing this, the possibility of His resurrecting them whenever He wills becomes firmly established. There is no god but Him.

His saying, "Yet... insist" ('abā), is an expression for their acquiring (disbelief) and their inclination toward it. The explanation of this verse has already passed above.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Even if you possessed..."﴾, the verse. The rule for "law" (law, "if") is that a verb should follow it, either explicit or implicit, which the explicit verb after it explains. The estimate here is: "Say: if you were to possess, you (yourselves) possess the treasuries." So "antum" is in the nominative as a substitute for the pronoun (in the verb). "Mercy" in this verse means wealth and bounties that are spent on provisions, and for this reason it is called "mercy". "Spending" (infāq), as commonly known, is the dispersal of wealth, and it leads to poverty. So the meaning is: for fear of the consequence of spending. Some lexicographers said: "anfaqa al-rajul" means he became poor.

(p. 550) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and man is ever tight-fisted﴾ means: withholding. It means that in his nature and the extent of his outlook, things come to an end and perish. So if he were to possess the treasuries of God's mercy, he would withhold them for fear of poverty. Likewise, he thinks that the power of God, blessed and exalted, stops short of resurrection. The matter is not so; rather, His power is limitless. He creates whatever He wills from creation, and stores provisions from His mercy, so He does not fear the exhaustion of the treasuries of His mercy. By this consideration, this verse connects with what precedes it. And God is the Giver of success through His mercy. From the (usage of) "iqtār" (straitening) is the verse of Abu Dawud:

"I do not count straitening as non-existence, but the loss of one whom I have been struck by is the true annihilation."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs.﴾ The exegetes and transmitters agree that the five signs mentioned in Surat al-A'raf are among these nine, and they are: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. They differed regarding the other four. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they are his hand, his tongue when its knot was loosed, his staff, and the sea. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are the sea, the staff, the effacement (ṭamsa), and the stone. He said: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God be pleased with him, asked me about this, and I informed him. He said: "What is the effacement?" I said: "Moses supplicated and Aaron said 'Amen', peace be upon them both, so God effaced their wealth and turned it into stones." 'Umar said: "Is understanding anything but this?" Then he called for a case containing curiosities which had belonged to 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Marwan, which he had gathered in Egypt. From it he extracted the hawza, the bayḍa, and the 'adasa, all of which are stones that were from the remains of Pharaoh's wealth. Al-Dahhak said: they are the throwing of the staff twice, the hand, and the knot of his tongue. 'Ikrima, Matar al-Warraq, and al-Sha'bi said: they are the staff, the hand, the years of drought, and the reduction of fruits. Al-Hasan said: they are the staff in its being a serpent, the hand, the years of drought, and "it swallowed what they fabricated" (the staff devouring their falsehood). Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, also said: they are the years of drought in their desert regions, the reduction of fruits in their villages, (p. 551) the hand, and the staff. Musrif narrated from Malik that they are the staff, the hand, the mountain when it was lifted up, and the sea. Ibn Wahb narrated from him that in place of the sea (it is) the stone.

What is necessarily implied by the verse is that God, exalted is He, singled out from the signs of Moses (for mention) nine, though his signs are very numerous, exceeding twenty-four. He described them as "clear" but did not specify them. The scholars differed in identifying them, according to their own reasoning about their clarity, or their transmitted reports (tawqīfiyya) on this matter.

A group said: the signs of Moses, peace be upon him, are meant only as the signs of the Torah, which are commands and prohibitions. Ṣafwān ibn 'Assāl narrated on this matter that "a Jew from the Jews of Medina said to another: 'Come with us to this Prophet, let us ask him about the signs of Moses, peace be upon him.' The other said to him: 'Do not call him a prophet, for if he hears you, he will have four eyes.' They went to the Messenger of God ﷺ and asked him. He said: 'They are: that you not associate anything with God, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, do not walk with an innocent man to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not mock, do not consume usury, do not slander a chaste woman, do not flee on the day of battle, and upon you specifically, O Jews: do not transgress on the Sabbath.'"

The majority recited: ﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾. It was also narrated from al-Kisa'i: "fa-sal" (ask!), according to the dialect of one who says "sa'ala yas'alu". All of this is in the sense of a command to Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: ask your contemporaries about what We have informed you of the unseen of the story. Then He said: ﴿when he came to them﴾, meaning: their forefathers, and He included them in the pronoun since they are from among them. It is possible that it means: "Ask the earlier Children of Israel to whom Moses, peace be upon him, came," and his referring (the Prophet) to their questioning would be by seeking information from them and considering their conditions and what is in their books, similar to the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you﴾. This is like when you admonish someone and say: "Ask the past nations whether any of them remained immortal?" and similar things in which reflection takes the place of asking. Al-Hasan said: "Your asking is your reflection upon the Qur'an."

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, recited: ﴿fa-sa'ala Banī Isrā'īl﴾, meaning: Moses asked Pharaoh for the Children of Israel, that is, he requested them (to be released) so that he might deliver them from the punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: "masḥūran" (bewitched). The exegetes differed regarding it. A group said: it is a passive participle in its original sense, meaning: you have indeed been bewitched, so your speech is disordered and what you bring is not upright. Al-Ṭabarī said: it is a passive participle in the sense of an active participle, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿a veil concealed (mastūr)﴾, and as they said: "mash'ūm" (ill-omened) and "maymūn" (blessed), when in fact it is "shā'im" and "yāmin".

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This cannot be derived except on the basis of the relative form (nisba), meaning: one who possesses sorcery and has mastered it, so you bring these wonders by virtue of that. This is an address of disparagement, so it is correct that "masḥūran" be a passive participle in its literal sense, and also that it be in the sense of "sāḥir" (sorcerer) who opposes us. As for what is reported of them that they said to him, by way of praise: ﴿O sorcerer, pray to your Lord for us﴾, then either those who said this there did not include Pharaoh, or he was among them but he shifted from disparagement to exaltation. There is room for scrutiny in this.

"Mercy" in this verse means wealth and bounties that are spent on provisions, and for this reason it is called "mercy". "Spending" (infāq), as commonly known, is the dispersal of wealth, and it leads to poverty. So the meaning is: for fear of the consequence of spending. Some lexicographers said: "anfaqa al-rajul" means he became poor.

(p. 550) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and man is ever tight-fisted﴾ means: withholding. It means that in his nature and the extent of his outlook, things come to an end and perish. So if he were to possess the treasuries of God's mercy, he would withhold them for fear of poverty. Likewise, he thinks that the power of God, blessed and exalted, stops short of resurrection. The matter is not so; rather, His power is limitless. He creates whatever He wills from creation, and stores provisions from His mercy, so He does not fear the exhaustion of the treasuries of His mercy. By this consideration, this verse connects with what precedes it. And God is the Giver of success through His mercy. From the (usage of) "iqtār" (straitening) is the verse of Abu Dawud:

"I do not count straitening as non-existence, but the loss of one whom I have been struck by is the true annihilation."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs.﴾ The exegetes and transmitters agree that the five signs mentioned in Surat al-A'raf are among these nine, and they are: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. They differed regarding the other four. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they are his hand, his tongue when its knot was loosed, his staff, and the sea. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are the sea, the staff, the effacement (ṭamsa), and the stone. He said: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God be pleased with him, asked me about this, and I informed him. He said: "What is the effacement?" I said: "Moses supplicated and Aaron said 'Amen', peace be upon them both, so God effaced their wealth and turned it into stones." 'Umar said: "Is understanding anything but this?" Then he called for a case containing curiosities which had belonged to 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Marwan, which he had gathered in Egypt. From it he extracted the hawza, the bayḍa, and the 'adasa, all of which are stones that were from the remains of Pharaoh's wealth. Al-Dahhak said: they are the throwing of the staff twice, the hand, and the knot of his tongue. 'Ikrima, Matar al-Warraq, and al-Sha'bi said: they are the staff, the hand, the years of drought, and the reduction of fruits. Al-Hasan said: they are the staff in its being a serpent, the hand, the years of drought, and "it swallowed what they fabricated" (the staff devouring their falsehood). Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, also said: they are the years of drought in their desert regions, the reduction of fruits in their villages, (p. 551) the hand, and the staff. Musrif narrated from Malik that they are the staff, the hand, the mountain when it was lifted up, and the sea. Ibn Wahb narrated from him that in place of the sea (it is) the stone.

What is necessarily implied by the verse is that God, exalted is He, singled out from the signs of Moses (for mention) nine, though his signs are very numerous, exceeding twenty-four. He described them as "clear" but did not specify them. The scholars differed in identifying them, according to their own reasoning about their clarity, or their transmitted reports (tawqīfiyya) on this matter.

A group said: the signs of Moses, peace be upon him, are meant only as the signs of the Torah, which are commands and prohibitions. Ṣafwān ibn 'Assāl narrated on this matter that "a Jew from the Jews of Medina said to another: 'Come with us to this Prophet, let us ask him about the signs of Moses, peace be upon him.' The other said to him: 'Do not call him a prophet, for if he hears you, he will have four eyes.' They went to the Messenger of God ﷺ and asked him. He said: 'They are: that you not associate anything with God, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, do not walk with an innocent man to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not mock, do not consume usury, do not slander a chaste woman, do not flee on the day of battle, and upon you specifically, O Jews: do not transgress on the Sabbath.'"

The majority recited: ﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾. It was also narrated from al-Kisa'i: "fa-sal" (ask!), according to the dialect of one who says "sa'ala yas'alu". All of this is in the sense of a command to Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: ask your contemporaries about what We have informed you of the unseen of the story. Then He said: ﴿when he came to them﴾, meaning: their forefathers, and He included them in the pronoun since they are from among them. It is possible that it means: "Ask the earlier Children of Israel to whom Moses, peace be upon him, came," and his referring (the Prophet) to their questioning would be by seeking information from them and considering their conditions and what is in their books, similar to the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿And ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you﴾. This is like when you admonish someone and say: "Ask the past nations whether any of them remained immortal?" and similar things in which reflection takes the place of asking. Al-Hasan said: "Your asking is your reflection upon the Qur'an."

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, recited: ﴿fa-sa'ala Banī Isrā'īl﴾, meaning: Moses asked Pharaoh for the Children of Israel, that is, he requested them (to be released) so that he might deliver them from the punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: "masḥūran" (bewitched). The exegetes differed regarding it. A group said: it is a passive participle in its original sense, meaning: you have indeed been bewitched, so your speech is disordered and what you bring is not upright. Al-Ṭabarī said: it is a passive participle in the sense of an active participle, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿a veil concealed (mastūr)﴾, and as they said: "mash'ūm" (ill-omened) and "maymūn" (blessed), when in fact it is "shā'im" and "yāmin".

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This cannot be derived except on the basis of the relative form (nisba), meaning: one who possesses sorcery and has mastered it, so you bring these wonders by virtue of that. This is an address of disparagement, so it is correct that "masḥūran" be a passive participle in its literal sense, and also that it be in the sense of "sāḥir" (sorcerer) who opposes us. As for what is reported of them that they said to him, by way of praise: ﴿O sorcerer, pray to your Lord for us﴾, then either those who said this there did not include Pharaoh, or he was among them but he shifted from disparagement to exaltation. There is room for scrutiny in this.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 102–104:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿He said: "You have certainly known that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights. And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed."﴾ ﴿So he intended to scare them off from the land, but We drowned him and those with him, all together.﴾ ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land; and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you together as a mixed throng."﴾

It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and others, that he recited "عَلِمْتُ" (ʿalimtu, "I have known") with a dammah on the tā' of the speaker, and said: "The enemy of Allah never knew, but Moses knew."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This reading is strengthened for one who interprets "مَسْحُورًا" (maskhur, "bewitched") in its literal sense. When Pharaoh accused him of having been bewitched, which corrupted his sight, intellect and speech, he replied that he knows the signs of Allah, that he is not bewitched, but rather that he explains what he brings. This is the reading of al-Kisa'i. The majority read "لَقَدْ عَلِمْتَ" with a fathah on the tā' addressing the second person, so it is as if Moses, peace be upon him, accused him of denying out of obstinacy.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever holds that disbelief occurs out of obstinacy has a connection to this verse, and makes it like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. al-Tabari reported this from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-Zajjaj inclined to it. Yet it remains open to the possibility that Moses's statement was a rebuke to Pharaoh, meaning: "You are in the state of one who knows this, and it is so clear that you know it," and it was not a report about Pharaoh's knowledge.

His saying, Exalted is He: "بَصَائِرَ" (basa'ir) is the plural of "بَصِيرَة" (basirah), which means a path, i.e., paths by which one is guided. Likewise, "basirah" has come to be used for the way the soul sees and believes. The accusative of "بَصَائِرَ" is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

"Al-mathbur" means the one who perishes; this is said by Mujahid. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said it means the defeated. Ibn Zayd said it means the deluded. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he explained it as "the accursed." Some scholars said: At the beginning of his affair, Moses, peace be upon him, used to be distressed, and was commanded to speak gently and sought a minister; but when his soul was strengthened by the powers of prophethood and he became steadfast, he confronted Pharaoh with more than he had been commanded, according to his permissible reasoning. Ibn Zayd said: Moses dared to say to him more than Allah had commanded him. Another group said: Rather, "al-mathbur" means the defeated, the disgraced, and Moses, peace be upon him, would not be one to curse. From the same word is the saying of 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara:

﴾ When I contend with Satan in the ways of error, and whoever inclines in his inclination is mathbur ﴿

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he intended to scare them off from the land﴾, the verse. "Yastafizzahum" means: to unsettle them and disturb them, either by killing or by expulsion. "Al-ard" (the land) here is the land of Egypt. It has been previously mentioned that whenever "al-ard" is mentioned in a general sense, what is meant is what suits the story under discussion, though its generality may be appropriate in some narratives.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse summarizes the stories of the Children of Israel with Pharaoh. It mentions the greatness and gravity of the matter, which are its two extremes: Pharaoh intended to subdue and kill them, which was the beginning of the affair; then "He drowned him," Allah, blessed and exalted, drowned him and his armies, which was the end of the affair. Then Allah, Exalted, mentioned the matter of the Children of Israel after the drowning of Pharaoh, their dwelling in the land of Syria.

﴿The promise of the Hereafter﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. "Al-lafif" means a gathered mass that is intermixed, with some folded into others, so there are no distinct tribes and no separation. Some lexicographers said it is among the collective nouns, with no singular form from its own root. al-Tabari said it is in the sense of the verbal noun, as one says: "I wrapped it wrapping (laffan) and a folded mass (lafifan)."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this there is room for reflection, so consider it.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah 17, verses 105–108:**

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿We sent it down with truth, and with truth it descended. And We sent you not except as a bringer of good news and a warner.﴾ ﴿And a Qur'an which We have divided [into parts], that you might recite it to the people over a period, and We have sent it down in gradual revelation.﴾ ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in prostration."﴾ ﴿And they say, "Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled."﴾

The pronoun in His saying, "anzalnāhu" (We sent it down), refers to the Qur'an mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every [kind of] example﴾ [al-Isrā': 89]. It is also possible that the speech is immediately preceding, and the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, which has been mentioned earlier, due to its fame, as Allah says: ﴿until [the sun] disappeared behind the veil﴾ [Ṣād: 32]. This usage is common.

Al-Zahrāwī said: Its meaning is "with what is required, which is the benefit and rectitude for people, [being] true in itself." His saying, "and with truth it descended," means "with truth in its commands, prohibitions and reports." With this interpretation, the repetition of the word is for a meaning other than the first. Al-Ṭabarī held that the two have one meaning, i.e., with its reports and commands, and with that it descended.

His saying, "wa-Qur'ānan" (and a Qur'an). The position of Sībawayh is that its accusative case is governed by a hidden verb which the following apparent verb explains, i.e., "and We divided a Qur'an." It is also valid that it is conjoined to the kāf (the "you") in "arsalnāka" (We sent you), since sending this and sending down this have one meaning.

Most readers recited "farraqnāhu" with a light pronunciation of the rā'. Its meaning is: We clarified it, made it evident, and made it a criterion (furqān). Ibn 'Abbās, Qatāda, 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn Mas'ūd, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, al-Sha'bī, al-Ḥasan (with a variant), Ḥumayd, and 'Amr ibn Fā'id recited it with a doubled rā' ("farraqnāhu"). However, in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ūd and Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "farraqnāhu 'alayhi li-taqra'ahu," meaning: We sent it down piece by piece, not all at once. This meaning harmonizes with His saying, ﴿that you might recite it to the people over a period﴾. This was among the things that Allah intended by its descent, through causes that occur on earth, in the form of statements and actions, in specific, defined times.

The scholars differed regarding the duration over which the Qur'an was revealed. It was said: twenty-five years. Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: twenty-three years. Qatāda said: twenty years.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is according to the difference of opinion regarding the age of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since revelation came when he was forty years old and it was completed with his death. Al-Ṭabarī narrated from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī that he said: The Qur'an was revealed over eighteen years.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is an unsound statement; it is not authentically established from al-Ḥasan. And Allah knows best.

A group interpreted His saying, ﴿over a period﴾ (ʿalā mukth), meaning: with deliberate, measured recitation and articulation. This is the statement of Mujāhid, Ibn 'Abbās, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd. The other interpretation is: over a period and an extended duration, bit by bit. His saying, ﴿and We have sent it down in gradual revelation﴾, is an emphasis and reinforcement, by means of a verbal noun (maṣdar), of the meaning already mentioned in the wording of the verse.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The readers agreed on the vowelling of the mīm in "mukth" with a ḍamma. It is said "makth" and "mukth" with a ḍamma on the mīm, and "mikth" with a kasra.

His saying, ﴿Say: "Believe in it"﴾ and the rest of the verse. This is a verse of belittling the disbelievers, and within it is a form of threat. The meaning is: You are not a proof, so whether we believe or you disbelieve is the same to us; the harm of that falls only upon yourselves. The proof is rather the people of knowledge before it, who have the described attribute.

People differed about the referent of ﴿those who were given knowledge before it﴾. One group said: they are the believers among the People of the Book. Another group said: they are Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, and those who were like them. It was also said that a group of the People of the Book sat, while still upon their religion, and discussed the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and what had been revealed to him. Some of it was recited to them, so they humbled themselves, glorified Allah, and prostrated to Him, and said: "This is the time of the Prophet mentioned in the Torah, and this is his description, and Allah's promise concerning him is certainly coming to pass." They inclined toward Islam with this inclination, so the verse was revealed concerning them. Another group said: the referent of ﴿those who were given knowledge before it﴾ is Muḥammad (ﷺ), and the pronoun in "qablihi" (before it) refers to the Qur'an, in the same way as the pronoun in "bihi" (in it). His saying, ﴿when it is recited to them﴾ clarifies this. It was also said: both pronouns refer to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and the mention of the Qur'an is resumed in His saying, ﴿when it is recited to them﴾.

His saying, ﴿they fall down upon their chins﴾ (yakhirrūna li-l-adhqān), meaning: to their sides. This is like when you say "he fell on his hand and mouth," meaning to their sides and upon them. Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: the meaning is "to the faces." al-Ḥasan said: "to the beards."

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The adhqān are the lowest parts of the faces, where the two jaws meet, and they are the part of a person's head closest to the ground, especially when he prostrates. The poet said:

*They fell upon the chins of their faces, while birds of prey, swooping, tore at them and plucked [them].*

In His saying, ﴿Indeed, the promise of our Lord﴾ (in kāna wa'du rabbinā), the "in" is, according to Sībawayh, the lightened form of the heavy "inna". The lām after it is the lām of emphasis. According to al-Farrā', it is a negating "in" and the lām is in the sense of "illā" (except). Another meaning is possible in this verse: that His saying, ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe"﴾, is intended for threat rather than belittling. The meaning would be: "You will see what you will be recompensed with." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 17, verses 109–111:

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And they fall down upon their faces weeping, and it increases them in humility.﴾ ﴿Say: "Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names. And do not recite your prayer aloud or quietly, but seek between that a middle way."﴾ ﴿And say: "Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and has no ally out of weakness; and magnify Him with full magnification."﴾

This is an intensification in their description, a praise of them, and an exhortation to everyone who takes on knowledge and acquires some of it to strive to reach this rank. al-Tabari related from al-Taymi that he said: "Whoever has been given knowledge that does not make him weep is surely not one who has been given beneficial knowledge, because Allah, exalted is He, described the scholars, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isra: 107] up to the end of the two verses."

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: "Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful"﴾, and the verse.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the polytheists heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) calling: "O Allah, O Most Merciful," and they said: "Muhammad commands us to call upon one God, yet he calls upon two gods." This was related by Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). Makki said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed the night prayer one night, and in his supplication he said: "O Most Merciful, O Most Compassionate." (p-558) A man among the polytheists heard him, and there was a man in Yamama called al-Rahman. That listener said: "What is the matter with Muhammad that he calls upon the Rahman of Yamama?" So the verse was revealed, clarifying that they are names of one thing: if you call upon Him as Allah, it is He; and if you call upon Him as the Most Merciful, it is He.

Talha ibn Musarrif recited: "Whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names," meaning: to Him belong all the most beautiful names, that is, those which entail the most excellent attributes.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These names are by revelation (tawqif); it is not valid to assign a name to Allah, exalted is He, except by revelation from the Qur'an or the Hadith. It has been related: "Indeed, Allah has ninety-nine names..." the hadith, and al-Tirmidhi and others transmitted all of its wording with a sound chain. The sense of the verse is: whichever of the names you call Him by, you are correct, for to Him belong the most beautiful names.

Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded not to recite his prayer aloud, nor to recite it quietly, which is the whispering that only the speaker himself hears; this is its true meaning, but in the verse it is an expression for lowering the voice, even if it does not reach what we have mentioned. The commentators differed about "prayer" (salat), what is it? Ibn 'Abbas, 'Aisha (may Allah be pleased with them both), and a group said: it is supplication (du'a'). Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the recitation of the Qur'an in prayer; this is by elision of a modifier, the sense being: do not raise the voice in the recitation of your prayer. He said: the reason is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an aloud, so the polytheists heard it and reviled the Qur'an and the One who sent it down, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to take a middle course, so that his companions praying with him could hear and the harm of the polytheists would be removed from him. Ibn Sirin said: the Bedouins used to recite their tashahhud aloud, so the verse was revealed concerning that. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) used to recite quietly, and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to recite aloud. They were asked about that, and (p-559) Abu Bakr said: "I am conversing with my Lord, and He knows my need." 'Umar said: "I drive away the devil and wake the drowsy." When this verse was revealed, it was said to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him): "Raise your voice a little," and it was said to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "Lower your voice a little." 'Aisha also said (may Allah be pleased with her): "By prayer in this verse is meant the tashahhud." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: the meaning is: do not make your prayer good in the open and bad in secret, but follow a middle path that remains constant in every state. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse is a prohibition of what the People of the Gospel and the Torah did, of raising the voice at times so that people raise theirs with him, and lowering it at times so that those behind him fall silent. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said concerning the verse: its meaning is: do not recite aloud in the daytime prayer, nor quietly in the night prayer, and seek a way of complying with the command as it has been laid down for you. This was mentioned by Yahya ibn Sallam and al-Zahrawi. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Whoever makes his ear hear is not whispering."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is related, that it was said to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him): "Raise your voice a little," contradicts this; but what Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said is the original meaning of the language, and "khufut" is used afterward for something louder than that.
